She is nonetheless treated in later Ottoman genealogical tradition as a founding matriarch whose marriage alliance helped bind Osman's frontier principality to established regional families.

entries.name: Edward III of England
entries.desc: Edward III was King of England from 1327 to 1377, known for his military success and for transforming England into one of Europe's most formidable military powers.
entries.tldr: Edward III was King of England from January 1327 until his death in 1377. He is noted for his military success and for restoring royal authority after the disastrous reign of his father, Edward II. Edward III transformed the Kingdom of England into one of the most formidable military powers in Europe. He is also credited with founding the Order of the Garter and initiating the Hundred Years' War with France.

entries.name: Ferdinand I of Portugal
entries.desc: Ferdinand I, sometimes called the Handsome or occasionally the Inconstant, was the King of Portugal from 1367 until his death in 1383. He was also briefly made King of Galicia, in 1369.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand I, sometimes called the Handsome or occasionally the Inconstant, was the King of Portugal from 1367 until his death in 1383. He was also briefly made King of Galicia, in 1369. Facing a lack of legitimate male heirs, his death led to the 1383–85 crisis, also known as the Portuguese interregnum.

entries.name: Go-Komatsu
entries.desc: Emperor Go-Komatsu was the 100th emperor of Japan, according to the traditional order of succession, and the sixth and final Emperor of the Northern Court.
entries.tldr: Installed as a child by the Ashikaga shogunate as the sixth Northern Court emperor during Japan's Nanboku-chō schism, he became sole emperor in 1392 when rival Southern Emperor Go-Kameyama, mediated by shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, surrendered the sacred regalia on a promise the throne would afterward alternate between the two lines. Go-Komatsu never honored that bargain, reigning twenty more years and in 1411 naming his son Shōkō heir, cementing Northern Court dominance permanently. His reign coincided with Yoshimitsu's peak power. He abdicated in 1412 and died in 1433.

entries.name: Jamshīd al-Kāshī
entries.desc: Persian astronomer and mathematician who calculated pi to 16 decimal places under Timurid patronage.
entries.tldr: A Persian astronomer and mathematician working under Timurid patronage, al-Kashi joined the great observatory founded by Ulugh Beg at Samarkand, where his precise calculations of planetary positions and calendars proved invaluable. He calculated the value of pi to sixteen decimal places using an iterative geometric method far more accurate than any before it, and his treatise The Key to Arithmetic advanced the use of decimal fractions in systematic mathematical practice.

entries.name: Henry V of England
entries.desc: King of England from 1413 whose victory at Agincourt in 1415 marked the high point of English fortunes in the Hundred Years' War.
entries.tldr: Henry V, also called Henry of Monmouth, was King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine from 1413 until his death in 1422. His victory at Agincourt in 1415 and his conquest of Normandy gave England the upper hand in the Hundred Years' War and led, by the Treaty of Troyes in 1420, to his recognition as heir and regent of France. This was the high-water mark of the English cause in th…

entries.name: Musa Çelebi
entries.desc: Musa Çelebi was an Ottoman prince and a co-ruler of the empire for three years during the Ottoman Interregnum.
entries.tldr: One of Bayezid I's sons, Musa spent years after the Ottoman defeat at Ankara fighting his brothers for the throne, eventually seizing the empire's European territories and ruling from Edirne while brother Mehmed held Anatolia. He proved a harsh, mistrustful ruler, executing rivals and alienating the nobles and soldiers who had backed him, which fed steady desertions to Mehmed's side. The rivalry ended at the Battle of Camurlu in 1413, where Musa's wounded horse threw him into a marsh and Mehmed's men strangled him on the spot, ending the eleven-year Interregnum.

entries.name: Jan van Eyck
entries.desc: Early Netherlandish painter active in Bruges, renowned as one of the supreme innovators of Early Northern Renaissance oil painting.
entries.tldr: Court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, Jan van Eyck worked in Bruges and became one of the most celebrated innovators of Early Netherlandish painting, prized for his mastery of oil glazes that achieved unprecedented luminosity and minute detail in fabrics, light, and reflection. His Ghent Altarpiece and the enigmatic Arnolfini Portrait, with its convex mirror reflecting the room, remain landmarks of Northern Renaissance art; he often signed works with the motto “Als ich kan.”

entries.name: Maria of Castile, Queen of Aragon
entries.desc: Queen of Aragon and longtime regent of the Crown, effectively governing Aragon for most of Alfonso V's reign while he campaigned in Italy.
entries.tldr: Married to Alfonso V in 1415 in a childless union that grew distant, Maria ran Aragon almost single-handedly once her husband sailed off to conquer Naples in 1420 and never returned. Holding the title of lieutenant-general, she governed through two long regencies, raising funds that helped ransom Alfonso after his capture by rival Italian forces in 1435 and dealing with the fractious Aragonese nobility. Historians credit her with real political skill in a role usually reserved for kings. She died in 1458, having spent most of her marriage as consort in title but head of government in practice.

entries.name: Pius II
entries.desc: Pope (1458–1464) and humanist scholar who called a failed crusade against the Ottoman Empire.
entries.tldr: Born Enea Silvio Piccolomini to an impoverished Sienese family, he built his early career as a celebrated Latin poet and diplomat, even writing a frankly erotic autobiographical novella, before taking holy orders and rising fast through the Church. As pope he indulged his humanist tastes by rebuilding his birthplace into the planned Renaissance town of Pienza. Alarmed by the recent Ottoman capture of Constantinople, he spent his final years organizing a crusade, traveling to Ancona to lead it in 1464, but died there before the fleets arrived and the crusade collapsed with him.

entries.name: Joan of Arc
entries.desc: French peasant who led armies during the Hundred Years' War and was later canonised.
entries.tldr: A peasant girl from Domrémy in northeastern France, Joan claimed visions of saints instructing her to support the Dauphin Charles against English and Burgundian forces during the Hundred Years' War. Given command of troops despite her age and sex, she led the relief of the besieged city of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles crowned king at Reims. Captured by Burgundian allies of England the following year, she was tried for heresy and burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431 at just nineteen; a later retrial nullified the verdict, and she was canonized in 1920.

entries.name: Paul II
entries.desc: Pope from 1464 to 1471, born Pietro Barbo of Venice; known for his love of art and gems and his conflicts with humanist scholars.
entries.tldr: A wealthy Venetian's nephew made cardinal at 23 by his uncle Pope Eugene IV, Pietro Barbo used his fortune to amass one of Rome's great collections of antique gems. As pope he abolished the humanists' College of Abbreviators and cracked down on the Roman Academy, imprisoning and reportedly torturing scholars, including his own future biographer Platina, on suspicion of plotting against him. He gave Rome spectacle instead of scholarship, founding the horse-race carnival still tied to the city and building the vast Palazzo Venezia. He died suddenly in 1471, reportedly after overeating at dinner.

entries.name: Alexander VI
entries.desc: Pope Alexander VI was head of the Catholic Church and leader of the Papal States from 11 August 1492 until his death in 1503.
entries.tldr: Spanish-born pope, born Rodrigo Borgia, who reigned from 1492 to 1503 and became the most notorious Renaissance pope for open nepotism and the ambitions he advanced through his children Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia. His pontificate is remembered for the 1493 papal bulls dividing newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal, later refined by the Treaty of Tordesillas. He used marriage alliances and campaigns led by Cesare to carve out Borgia territories in central Italy. Accusations of simony and scandal have shadowed his reputation ever since.

entries.name: Hans Memling
entries.desc: Hans Memling was a German-Flemish painter who worked in the tradition of Early Netherlandish painting. Born in the Middle Rhine region, he probably spent his childhood in Mainz. During his apprenticeship as a painter he moved to the Netherlands and spent time in the Brussels workshop of Rogier van der Weyden.
entries.tldr: Born in Germany's Middle Rhine region, he trained in the Netherlands, likely in Rogier van der Weyden's Brussels workshop, before settling in Bruges in 1465, building one of the era's largest painting workshops. Blending Jan van Eyck's detail with van der Weyden's restraint, he became Bruges's leading painter of altarpieces and portraits, wealthy enough to rank among its richest residents by 1480. His half-length portrait format was widely imitated by Italian painters, including Ghirlandaio and Botticelli. Major works remain in Bruges's old hospital of St. John, now a museum devoted to him.

entries.name: Ladislaus the Posthumous
entries.desc: Ladislaus the Posthumous, known as Ladislaus V, was Duke of Austria and King of Hungary, Croatia and Bohemia.
entries.tldr: Born four months after the death of his father, Albert II of Habsburg, Ladislaus inherited the crowns of Hungary, Bohemia, and Austria as an infant, giving him the name by which he is known. His minority was dominated by powerful regents, notably his great-uncle Frederick III in Austria and, in Hungary, the general John Hunyadi. He was crowned in each realm as he came of age but exercised little independent power before dying suddenly at seventeen, on the eve of his planned wedding, amid rumors of poisoning historians now attribute more likely to leukemia.

entries.name: Hieronymus Bosch
entries.desc: Hieronymus Bosch was a Dutch painter from Brabant known for his fantastical, moralistic imagery blending religious themes with nightmarish surreal scenes.
entries.tldr: Hieronymus Bosch was a Dutch painter from Brabant. He is one of the most notable representatives of the Early Netherlandish painting school. His work, generally oil on oak wood, mainly contains fantastic illustrations of religious concepts and narratives. His most famous work, The Garden of Earthly Delights, remains one of the most complex and debated triptychs in art history.

entries.name: Leonardo da Vinci
entries.desc: Italian polymath of the Renaissance, painter of the Mona Lisa and prolific inventor.
entries.tldr: Trained in Florence under Andrea del Verrocchio, Leonardo became the archetype of the Renaissance polymath, working as painter, engineer, anatomist, and military designer for patrons including the Sforza of Milan and the French crown. Only a handful of paintings are securely his, among them the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but his true output was far larger: thousands of notebook pages on anatomy, flight, hydraulics, and optics, mostly unpublished in his lifetime. He dissected cadavers to study musculature and sketched flying machines centuries before the technology existed.

entries.name: Ferdinand II of Aragon
entries.desc: Ferdinand II was King of Aragon from 1479 until his death in 1516. As the husband and co-ruler of Queen Isabella I of Castile, he was also King of Castile from 1475 to 1504.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand II was King of Aragon from 1479 until his death in 1516. As the husband and co-ruler of Queen Isabella I of Castile, he was also King of Castile from 1475 to 1504. He reigned jointly with Isabella over a dynastically unified Spain; together, they are known as the Catholic Monarchs.

entries.name: Richard III of England
entries.desc: Richard III was King of England from 26 June 1483 until his death in 1485. He was the last king of the Plantagenet dynasty and its cadet branch the House of York.
entries.tldr: Richard III was King of England from 26 June 1483 until his death in 1485. He was the last king of the Plantagenet dynasty and its cadet branch the House of York. His defeat and death at the Battle of Bosworth Field marked the end of the Middle Ages in England.

entries.name: Bartolomeu Dias
entries.desc: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese explorer who in 1488 became the first European to round the southern tip of Africa, proving a sea route to Asia was possible.
entries.tldr: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese mariner and explorer. In February 1488, he became the first European navigator to round the southern tip of Africa and to demonstrate that the most effective southward route for ships is in the open ocean, well to the west of the African coast. His discoveries were later used by Vasco da Gama to establish a sea route between Europe and Asia.

entries.name: Paul III
entries.desc: Pope Paul III was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 13 October 1534 to his death, in November 1549.
entries.tldr: Pope Paul III was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 13 October 1534 to his death, in November 1549. He convened the Council of Trent and was responsible for the establishment of the Jesuit order.

entries.name: Sri Krishnadevaraya
entries.desc: Krishnadevaraya was emperor of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1509 to 1529. Widely regarded as one of the greatest rulers in Indian history, he presided over the empire at its political and cultural zenith.
entries.tldr: The son of a regent who had seized power to stave off dynastic collapse, Krishnadevaraya took Vijayanagara's throne in 1509 and built it into South India's dominant power. He crushed the Bijapur, Golconda and Bahmani sultans and the Gajapatis of Odisha, seizing the strategic Raichur Doab in 1512 and subjugating Odisha by 1514. A polyglot fluent in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit, he personally composed the Telugu epic Amuktamalyada and patronized a golden age of Telugu literature. His reign is still remembered as the empire's political and cultural peak.

entries.name: Paul IV
entries.desc: Pope (1555–1559) who established the first Roman ghetto and intensified the Roman Inquisition.
entries.tldr: Gian Pietro Carafa, a Neapolitan noble who co-founded the ascetic Theatine order, was elected pope in 1555 at 79 as a hardline voice against Protestantism and moral laxity. His bull that year confined Rome's Jews to a locked, walled ghetto, forcing them into the rag trade and requiring them to wear a badge, a policy that endured for centuries. He turned the Inquisition into a feared instrument of surveillance and torture and launched the first Index of Forbidden Books in 1559. He was so despised that when he died, a mob tore down his statue and threw its head into the Tiber.

entries.name: Ferdinand Magellan
entries.desc: Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese explorer who planned and led the 1519-1522 Spanish expedition to the East Indies, becoming the first European to cross the strait that bears his name.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese explorer best known for planning and leading the 1519–1522 Spanish expedition to the East Indies. During this expedition, he became the first European to encounter the Strait of Magellan, performed the first European crossing of the Pacific Ocean, and made the first known European contact with the Philippines. Magellan himself was killed in battle in the Phil…

entries.name: Martin Luther
entries.desc: German theologian whose Ninety-five Theses sparked the Protestant Reformation.
entries.tldr: An Augustinian friar troubled by the sale of indulgences, he posted 95 propositions for debate on the Wittenberg church door in 1517, challenging papal authority over salvation. Summoned before the Diet of Worms in 1521, he refused to recant, reportedly declaring 'Here I stand, I can do no other,' and was declared an outlaw. In hiding, he translated the New Testament into German, putting scripture in ordinary hands and helping shape the German language. His break with Rome split Western Christianity, though his later antisemitic writings remain a troubling stain on his legacy.

entries.name: Huldrych Zwingli
entries.desc: Huldrych Zwingli was a Swiss Christian theologian, musician, and leader of the Reformation in Switzerland.
entries.tldr: A parish priest in Zurich, Zwingli launched a Reformation independent of and roughly simultaneous with Luther's, preaching that scripture alone, not church tradition, should govern Christian life and stripping Zurich's churches of images, relics, and the Mass. He and Luther could not reconcile their views on the Eucharist at the 1529 Marburg Colloquy, splitting the Protestant movement into separate camps. Zwingli was killed in 1531 fighting alongside Zurich's troops against Catholic cantons at Kappel.

entries.name: Zhengde Emperor
entries.desc: 11th emperor of the Ming dynasty (1505–1521), known for unconventional rule and fondness for military pursuits.
entries.tldr: The Zhengde Emperor ruled Ming China from 1505 to 1521, inheriting the throne as a teenager and quickly rejecting the ceremonial confines expected of an emperor. He built a private pleasure palace called the Leopard Quarter outside the Forbidden City, staffed with exotic animals and entertainers, and enjoyed disguising himself to travel and personally lead campaigns against Mongol raiders. His unconventional rule alarmed Confucian officials, who saw it as a dereliction of duty. He died without an heir after a boating accident, ending his direct line.

entries.name: Francis I of France
entries.desc: Francis I was King of France from 1515 to 1547, a Renaissance patron who brought Italian artists and scholars to his court and waged long rivalry with Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.
entries.tldr: Francis I was King of France from 1515 until his death in 1547. He was the son of Charles, Count of Angoulême, and Louise of Savoy. He succeeded his first cousin once removed and father-in-law Louis XII. Francis was a key figure of the French Renaissance, patronising artists like Leonardo da Vinci and waging the Italian Wars against the Habsburgs.

entries.name: François Rabelais
entries.desc: François Rabelais was a French writer often called the first great French prose author. A Renaissance humanist and Greek scholar, he drew opposition from Protestants and the Catholic Church alike.
entries.tldr: François Rabelais was a French writer who has been called the first great French prose author. A humanist of the French Renaissance and Greek scholar, he attracted opposition from both Protestant theologian John Calvin and from the hierarchy of the Catholic Church. Though in his day he was best known as a physician, scholar, diplomat, and Catholic priest, later he became better known as a satir…

entries.name: Clément Marot
entries.desc: Clément Marot was a French Renaissance poet. He was influenced by the writers of the late 15th century and paved the way for the Pléiade, and is undoubtedly the most important poet at the court of Francis I.
entries.tldr: French Renaissance poet who served at the court of Francis I and is credited with modernizing French verse between the medieval tradition and the Pléiade poets who followed him. His graceful epigrams, elegies, and rondeaux popularized a lighter, more personal style than the rigid forms of his predecessors. His French translation of the Psalms, later adopted by Protestant congregations, made him a target of suspicion during the Reformation, and he was twice forced into exile. He died in Turin, still regarded as the finest French poet of his generation.

entries.name: Heinrich Bullinger
entries.desc: Swiss Reformer and theologian who succeeded Huldrych Zwingli as head of the Church of Zürich and co-authored the Helvetic Confessions.
entries.tldr: Heinrich Bullinger was a Swiss Reformer and theologian, the successor of Huldrych Zwingli as head of the Church of Zürich and a pastor at the Grossmünster. One of the most important leaders of the Swiss Reformation, Bullinger co-authored the Helvetic Confessions and collaborated with John Calvin to work out a Reformed doctrine of the Lord's Supper.

entries.name: Pius V
entries.desc: Pope Pius V, OP, born Antonio Ghislieri, was head of the Catholic Church and leader of the Papal States from 7 January 1566 to his death, in May 1572.
entries.tldr: Born Antonio Ghislieri, a Dominican friar who rose through the Roman Inquisition for his severity, he became the Counter-Reformation's chief enforcer as pope, imposing the Council of Trent's decrees and issuing the standardized Roman Catechism and Missal that shaped Catholic worship for centuries. In 1570 he excommunicated Elizabeth I in the bull Regnans in Excelsis, worsening persecution of English Catholics. He also assembled the Holy League that crushed the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in 1571, crediting the victory to the Virgin Mary. His austerity later earned him canonization as a saint.

entries.name: Giorgio Vasari
entries.desc: Italian Renaissance painter and architect best known for Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, a foundational work of art history.
entries.tldr: Giorgio Vasari was an Italian Renaissance painter, architect, art historian, and biographer known for his work Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, considered the ideological foundation of Western art-historical writing, and still much cited in modern biographies of the many Italian Renaissance artists he covers, including Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, although…

entries.name: Şehzade Mustafa
entries.desc:
Şehzade Mustafa may refer to:Şehzade Mustafa (1450–1474), Ottoman prince, son of Mehmed II and Gülşah Hatun
Şehzade Mustafa, Ottoman prince, son of Suleiman the Magnificent and Mahidevran Hatun
entries.tldr: Şehzade Mustafa was the eldest son of Suleiman the Magnificent, widely seen as capable, popular with the army, and the presumptive Ottoman heir. His rising influence as governor of Amasya threatened the succession hopes of Suleiman's other wife, Hurrem Sultan, and her ally, the grand vizier Rustem Pasha. Accused of plotting rebellion, likely on fabricated evidence from that rivalry, Mustafa was summoned to his father's camp in 1553 and strangled on Suleiman's order. His death, later dramatized in Ottoman and European literature, was among the most consequential Ottoman succession purges.

entries.name: Catherine de' Medici
entries.desc: Catherine de' Medici was Queen of France from 1547 to 1559 by marriage to King Henry II. She was the mother of French kings Francis II, Charles IX, and Henry III, and a cousin to Pope Clement VII.
entries.tldr: Catherine de' Medici was Queen of France from 1547 to 1559 by marriage to King Henry II. She was the mother of French kings Francis II, Charles IX, and Henry III, and a cousin to Pope Clement VII. The years during which her sons reigned have been called "the age of Catherine de' Medici" since she had extensive, albeit at times varying, influence on the political life of France.

entries.name: Henry II of France
entries.desc: Henry II was King of France from 1547 until his death in 1559.
entries.tldr: Henry II was King of France from 1547 until his death in 1559. The second son of Francis I and Claude, Duchess of Brittany, he became Dauphin of France upon the death of his elder brother Francis in 1536.

entries.name: Sixtus V
entries.desc: Pope Sixtus V, born Felice Piergentile, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 24 April 1585 to his death, in August 1590.
entries.tldr: Pope Sixtus V, born Felice Piergentile, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 24 April 1585 to his death, in August 1590. As a youth, he joined the Franciscan order, where he displayed talents as a scholar and preacher, and enjoyed the patronage of Pius V, who made him a cardinal.

entries.name: Ismail II
entries.desc: Ismail II was the third shah of Safavid Iran from 1576 to 1577.
entries.tldr: The third shah of Safavid Iran, Ismail II spent roughly two decades imprisoned in the fortress of Qahqaha by his father, Shah Tahmasp I, who feared his ambition. On finally taking the throne in 1576 he moved swiftly and brutally against rival claimants, executing several of his own brothers to eliminate threats to his rule. His brief, erratic reign ended after little more than a year when he died suddenly in 1577, in circumstances widely believed to involve poison.

entries.name: Leo XI
entries.desc: Pope Leo XI, born Alessandro di Ottaviano de' Medici, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 1 April 1605 to his death, on 27 April 1605.
entries.tldr: Pope Leo XI, born Alessandro di Ottaviano de' Medici, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 1 April 1605 to his death, on 27 April 1605. His pontificate is one of the briefest in history, lasting under a month. He was from the prominent House of Medici originating from Florence.

entries.name: Longqing Emperor
entries.desc: 13th emperor of the Ming dynasty (1567–1572), whose brief reign brought pragmatic diplomatic and trade reforms.
entries.tldr: Born Zhu Zaiji, the Longqing Emperor took the Ming throne in 1567 after the death of his reclusive, Taoist-obsessed father, the Jiajing Emperor, and reversed several of his father's more damaging policies. His short reign is best remembered for lifting the long-standing ban on private maritime trade, opening Chinese ports to silver-driven commerce with Spanish Manila and Japan. He also negotiated a lasting peace with the Mongol leader Altan Khan, ending decades of border warfare. He died after only six years, leaving a young, disengaged successor, the Wanli Emperor.

entries.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
entries.desc: Mary, Queen of Scots, also known as Mary Stuart or Mary I of Scotland, was Queen of Scotland from 14 December 1542 until her forced abdication on 24 July 1567.
entries.tldr: Crowned queen of Scotland at six days old, she was raised in France and briefly became queen consort there through marriage to the French dauphin. Her rule in Scotland collapsed after her marriage to Lord Darnley, his murder, and her hasty remarriage to the chief suspect, Bothwell, which forced her abdication in 1567. She fled to England seeking her cousin Elizabeth I's protection but was instead held captive nineteen years as a rival claimant to the throne. Implicated in a plot against Elizabeth, she was tried and beheaded in 1587, the first legal execution of an anointed monarch.

entries.name: Francis II of France
entries.desc: Francis II was King of France from 1559 to 1560. He was also King of Scotland as the husband of Mary, Queen of Scots, from 1558 until his death in 1560.
entries.tldr: King of France for barely a year and a half, having succeeded his father Henry II after a fatal jousting accident, and already married to Mary, Queen of Scots, making him briefly King consort of Scotland as well. Sickly since childhood and only fifteen when he took the throne, he left governing largely to his wife's powerful Guise uncles, whose aggressive suppression of Protestants helped inflame tensions that erupted into the French Wars of Religion soon after his death. He died of an ear infection that spread to his brain, and the throne passed to his young brother Charles IX.

entries.name: Willem Barents
entries.desc: Willem Barentsz, anglicized as William Barents or Barentz, was a Dutch navigator, cartographer, and Arctic explorer.
entries.tldr: Willem Barentsz, anglicized as William Barents or Barentz, was a Dutch navigator, cartographer, and Arctic explorer. He led three expeditions to the far north of Europe in search of the Northeast Passage, and the Barents Sea is named after him.

entries.name: Jost Bürgi
entries.desc: Jost Bürgi, active primarily at the courts in Kassel and Prague, was a Swiss clockmaker, mathematician, and writer. Burgi was the brother-in-law and adoptive father of Benjamin Bramer.
entries.tldr: A self-taught Swiss instrument maker with no formal mathematical training, Bürgi built astronomical clocks and globes of exceptional precision for the courts of Hesse-Kassel and, later, Emperor Rudolf II in Prague. Working independently of, and slightly before, John Napier, he devised his own system of logarithms to ease astronomical calculation, though he published his tables years after Napier's and to far less attention. In Prague he worked closely with Johannes Kepler, supplying him with instruments for his planetary observations.

entries.name: Paul V
entries.desc: Pope Paul V, born Camillo Borghese, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 16 May 1605 to his death, in January 1621.
entries.tldr: Pope Paul V, born Camillo Borghese, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 16 May 1605 to his death, in January 1621. In 1611, he honored Galileo Galilei as a member of the papal Accademia dei Lincei.

entries.name: Gregory XV
entries.desc: Pope Gregory XV, born Alessandro Ludovisi, was the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 9 February 1621 until his death in 1623.
entries.tldr: Pope Gregory XV, born Alessandro Ludovisi, was the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 9 February 1621 until his death in 1623. He is notable for founding the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith and for the canonization of Saints Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, and others.

entries.name: Carlo Maderno
entries.desc: Carlo Maderno was an Italian architect, born in today’s Ticino, Switzerland, who is remembered as one of the fathers of Baroque architecture.
entries.tldr: Italian architect from Ticino who became the leading figure in early Roman Baroque architecture. He completed St. Peter's Basilica by adding its long nave and dramatic façade, work that gave the church its familiar Latin-cross silhouette. He also designed the façade of Santa Susanna, widely considered the first true Baroque façade in Rome, and worked on the Palazzo Barberini. His innovations in massing and surface decoration shaped Roman architecture for a century after his death.

entries.name: Michael the Brave
entries.desc: Michael the Brave was the Prince of Wallachia, Prince of Moldavia (1600) and de facto ruler of Transylvania (1599–1600). He is considered one of Romania's greatest national heroes.
entries.tldr: A Wallachian prince who fought Ottoman, Habsburg, and Polish domination of the Romanian lands, Michael won victories against the Turks in the 1590s that made him a hero to Christian powers seeking anti-Ottoman allies. In 1599-1600 he seized Transylvania and then Moldavia by force, briefly ruling all three Romanian principalities as one, though the union collapsed within months. Shortly after helping ally Giorgio Basta win a battle, Michael was assassinated on Basta's orders in 1601, his head severed from his body. Nationalists later turned his brief unification into a founding myth.

entries.name: Gaspard Bauhin
entries.desc: Swiss botanist whose Pinax theatri botanici (1623) classified thousands of plants, anticipating Linnaeus’s binomial nomenclature.
entries.tldr: Gaspard Bauhin was a Swiss botanist whose Pinax theatri botanici (1623) described thousands of plants and classified them in a manner that draws comparisons to the later binomial nomenclature of Linnaeus. A disciple of the Italian physician Girolamo Mercuriale, he also contributed to human anatomical nomenclature and taught medicine at Basel.

entries.name: Katō Kiyomasa
entries.desc: Katō Kiyomasa  was a Japanese daimyō of the Azuchi–Momoyama and Edo periods. His court title was Higo no Kami .
entries.tldr: Katō Kiyomasa  was a Japanese daimyō of the Azuchi–Momoyama and Edo periods. His court title was Higo no Kami . His name as a child was Yashamaru, and first name was Toranosuke.

entries.name: Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck
entries.desc: Dutch composer, organist, and pedagogue whose work bridged the Renaissance and Baroque eras; shaped the north German organ tradition.
entries.tldr: A Dutch organist and composer based at Amsterdam's Oude Kerk for most of his life, Sweelinck bridged the Renaissance and Baroque eras through keyboard works that developed the chorale variation and organ fantasia into mature forms. So many German students traveled to study under him that he became known as the “maker of German organists,” and his teaching lineage runs directly through Samuel Scheidt and Dieterich Buxtehude to Johann Sebastian Bach.

entries.name: Wanli Emperor
entries.desc: 14th and longest-reigning Ming emperor (1572–1620), whose 48-year reign ended in prolonged political withdrawal.
entries.tldr: Zhu Yijun took the Ming throne as a child in 1572 under capable regents and briefly presided over the "Three Great Campaigns" defending the empire's borders. His reign was then consumed for over a decade by a bitter succession dispute, as he tried to bypass his eldest son for a younger, favored son, only capitulating in 1601. Embittered, Wanli largely withdrew from court for his final decades, refusing audiences and leaving posts unfilled. Historians see this paralysis, despite his 48-year reign being the Ming dynasty's longest, as a cause of its decline.

entries.name: Michael Praetorius
entries.desc: Michael Praetorius was a German composer, organist, and music theorist, notable for developing musical forms based on Protestant hymns.
entries.tldr: Michael Praetorius was a German composer, organist, and music theorist. He was one of the most versatile composers of his age, being particularly significant in the development of musical forms based on Protestant hymns.

entries.name: Innocent X
entries.desc: Pope (1644–1655) who condemned the Peace of Westphalia and was immortalized by Velázquez's portrait.
entries.tldr: Pope from 1644 to 1655, Innocent X formally condemned the Peace of Westphalia for its concessions to Protestant states, a protest that history ultimately ignored as the treaty reshaped European sovereignty. He commissioned the transformation of Piazza Navona in Rome, including the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone, and sat for Diego Velázquez's searingly honest portrait, of which he is said to have remarked that it was “too truthful.” His reign was also marked by the controversial influence of his sister-in-law, Olimpia Maidalchini.

entries.name: Guido Reni
entries.desc: Guido Reni was an Italian Baroque painter, although his works showed a classical manner. He painted primarily religious works, but also mythological and allegorical subjects.
entries.tldr: Apprenticed at age ten to the Flemish painter Denis Calvaert before joining the rival Carracci academy in Bologna, he split his career between Bologna and Rome, blending Carracci naturalism with classical models like Raphael. His 1614 ceiling fresco Aurora, showing the dawn goddess leading Apollo's chariot, became a defining image of Roman Baroque classicism, endlessly copied by students. He was also a compulsive gambler whose debts reportedly forced him to churn out paintings rapidly late in life. His serene, luminous style made him one of the era's most imitated painters.

entries.name: Taichang Emperor
entries.desc: 15th Ming emperor whose reign lasted less than a month in 1620 before his sudden and mysterious death.
entries.tldr: Zhu Changluo waited decades as a neglected heir before succeeding his father, the Wanli Emperor, in 1620, only to become the shortest-reigning ruler in Ming history. Within days he fell seriously ill with diarrhea and insomnia; a physician's laxative worsened his condition, after which an official offered him mysterious red pills that he took against advice. He died the next morning, not even a month into his reign, touching off the "Red Pill Case," a bitter controversy over whether he was accidentally or deliberately poisoned. His son succeeded him as the Tianqi Emperor.

entries.name: Leopold V, Archduke of Austria
entries.desc: Habsburg archduke who served as Prince-Bishop of Passau and Strasbourg before assuming secular rule over Further Austria.
entries.tldr: A younger son of the Habsburg archduke Charles II of Inner Austria, Leopold was raised for the Church and became Prince-Bishop of both Passau and Strasbourg while young, though he never took full holy orders. In 1619 he set these roles aside for secular rule over Further Austria and Tyrol, territories granted by his cousin, Emperor Ferdinand II, early in the Thirty Years' War. He backed the Catholic cause militarily and worked to consolidate Habsburg control over the fractious Tyrolean estates, and his descendants ruled the region for decades after.

entries.name: Ahmed I
entries.desc: Ottoman sultan who commissioned the Blue Mosque in Istanbul and ruled the empire from 1603 to 1617.
entries.tldr: Ottoman sultan who came to the throne at just thirteen in 1603 and reigned until his death in 1617. He ended a century-old practice of fratricide among Ottoman princes, confining potential rivals to a secluded palace apartment known as the cage rather than having them killed. His reign saw the Peace of Zsitvatorok end the long war with the Habsburgs, alongside continued conflict with Safavid Persia. He is best remembered for commissioning the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, built directly across from Hagia Sophia to rival it in grandeur.

entries.name: Anne Hutchinson
entries.desc: Anne Hutchinson was an English-born religious figure who was an important participant in the Antinomian Controversy which shook the nascent Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1636 to 1638.
entries.tldr: English-born midwife and religious dissenter whose Boston home became a gathering place for discussing Puritan sermons, drawing large audiences that included women, unusual for the time. Her teachings, stressing direct divine revelation over the clergy's authority to interpret grace, triggered the Antinomian Controversy that split the Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1636 to 1638. Tried before the colony's General Court and church, she was banished as a danger to religious order. She resettled in Rhode Island and then Dutch New Netherland, where she was killed in a raid in 1643.

entries.name: John Amos Comenius
entries.desc: Czech philosopher and theologian considered the father of modern education, known for advocating universal schooling in his Didactica Magna.
entries.tldr: John Amos Comenius was a Czech philosopher, pedagogue and theologian who is considered the father of modern education. He served as the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren before becoming a religious refugee and one of the earliest champions of universal education, a concept eventually set forth in his book Didactica Magna. As an educator and theologian, he led schools and advised governme…

entries.name: Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac
entries.desc: French Baroque author known for widely read epistolary essays and as a founding member of the Académie française.
entries.tldr: Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac was a French author in Baroque Précieuses style, best known for his epistolary essays, which were widely circulated and read in his day. He was one of the founding members of the Académie française.

entries.name: Francesco Borromini
entries.desc: Italian Baroque architect from Swiss Ticino who shaped Roman architecture alongside Bernini and Pietro da Cortona.
entries.tldr: Francesco Borromini, born Francesco Castelli in the Swiss canton of Ticino, was a leading figure in Roman Baroque architecture alongside Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Pietro da Cortona. His bold use of geometry and dynamic forms broke with Renaissance convention, producing masterpieces such as San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane and Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza in Rome.

entries.name: Alexander VII
entries.desc: Pope Alexander VII, born Fabio Chigi, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 7 April 1655 to his death, in May 1667.
entries.tldr: Pope from 1655 to 1667, born Fabio Chigi, who had earlier served as papal representative at the negotiations that produced the Peace of Westphalia, a settlement he formally protested as harmful to Catholic interests even as it ended the Thirty Years' War. As pope he became one of the great patrons of Baroque Rome, commissioning Gian Lorenzo Bernini to design the sweeping colonnade enclosing St Peter's Square. He also reorganized the Vatican Library and imposed strict quarantine measures that helped shield Rome from a plague then devastating southern Italy.

entries.name: Francesco Cavalli
entries.desc: Francesco Cavalli was a Venetian composer, organist, and singer of the early Baroque period. He succeeded his teacher Claudio Monteverdi as the leading opera composer of the mid-17th century.
entries.tldr: Francesco Cavalli was a Venetian composer, organist and singer of the early Baroque period. He succeeded his teacher Claudio Monteverdi as the dominant and leading opera composer of the mid 17th-century. A central figure of Venetian musical life, Cavalli wrote more than thirty operas, almost all of which premiered in the city's theaters.

entries.name: John IV of Portugal
entries.desc: First Braganza king, restored Portuguese independence from Spain in 1640; also a prolific composer and patron of music.
entries.tldr: A wealthy nobleman with a strong hereditary claim, John was proclaimed king in December 1640 when conspirators overthrew sixty years of Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal in a coup later celebrated as the Restoration. He spent much of his reign fighting the long Portuguese Restoration War to defend that independence, while rebuilding Portugal's overseas empire and navy. Away from politics he was a serious composer, amassing one of Europe's largest music libraries and writing several surviving sacred works. The library was destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake.

entries.name: Tianqi Emperor
entries.desc: 16th Ming emperor (1620–1627) who ceded court power to the eunuch Wei Zhongxian while pursuing carpentry.
entries.tldr: Enthroned as a teenager in 1620, Zhu Youjiao showed little aptitude for governing, reportedly struggling with literacy, and instead threw himself into elaborate carpentry and construction projects inside the palace. That neglect let the eunuch Wei Zhongxian, promoted to head the Directorate of Ceremonial, seize effective control of the court, purging rival officials and building a personal cult. Wei's dominance during this reign is often cited as a major accelerant of Ming decline. The emperor died childless in 1627 at twenty-one; Wei was soon forced to suicide.

entries.name: Christine of France
entries.desc: Christine of France was Duchess of Savoy from 26 July 1630 to 7 October 1637 as the consort of Duke Victor Amadeus I. She was the daughter of Henry IV of France and sister of Louis XIII.
entries.tldr: Christine of France was Duchess of Savoy from 26 July 1630 to 7 October 1637 as the consort of Duke Victor Amadeus I. She was the daughter of Henry IV of France and sister of Louis XIII. Following her husband's death in 1637, she acted as regent of Savoy between 1637 and 1648.

entries.name: Evangelista Torricelli
entries.desc: Italian physicist and mathematician, student of Galileo, best known for inventing the barometer.
entries.tldr: Italian physicist and mathematician who studied under Galileo in the last months of the older scientist's life and succeeded him as court mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany. In 1643 he built the first mercury barometer, demonstrating that the atmosphere exerts measurable pressure and that a vacuum could exist above the mercury column, a finding that overturned the Aristotelian belief that nature abhorred a vacuum. His experiments settled a long-running dispute over why suction pumps could not lift water more than about ten meters. The unit of pressure the torr is named in his honor.

entries.name: Thomas Fuller
entries.desc: Thomas Fuller was an English churchman and historian. He is now remembered for his writings, particularly his Worthies of England, published in 1662, after his death.
entries.tldr: Thomas Fuller was an English churchman and historian. He is now remembered for his writings, particularly his Worthies of England, published in 1662, after his death. He was a prolific author, and one of the first English writers able to live by his pen.

entries.name: Alexander VIII
entries.desc: Pope (1689–1691) known for nepotism and his condemnation of Jansenism during his brief pontificate.
entries.tldr: Venetian-born pope who reigned briefly from 1689 until his death in 1691, elected already in his late seventies after a long career as a canon lawyer and cardinal. His short pontificate was marked by conspicuous nepotism, including large grants of money and office to his relatives, alongside a formal condemnation of Jansenism and of the Gallican Articles that had asserted French royal authority over the church. He worked to mend relations with Louis XIV of France, strained under his predecessor, though a full reconciliation was left unfinished at his death.

entries.name: Chongzhen Emperor
entries.desc: Last emperor of the Ming dynasty (1627–1644), who hanged himself as rebel forces captured Beijing.
entries.tldr: Sixteenth and final emperor of China's Ming dynasty, who inherited a state crippled by factional court politics, a ruinous treasury, and rebellions provoked by famine and misrule. Despite personal industry and attempts at reform, he could not halt the empire's decline, and in 1644 the rebel leader Li Zicheng's forces breached Beijing. Rather than be captured, he hanged himself from a tree on Coal Hill overlooking the Forbidden City, reportedly leaving a note blaming his ministers. His death is conventionally taken to mark the end of Ming rule.

entries.name: Innocent XI
entries.desc: Pope (1676–1689) who led the Holy League against Ottoman expansion and championed Church reform.
entries.tldr: Pope from 1676 to 1689, Innocent XI pursued austere financial and moral reform within the Vatican while building and funding the Holy League, the coalition of Christian powers that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683 and began rolling back Ottoman power in central Europe. He clashed repeatedly with Louis XIV of France over the king's Gallican assertions of authority over the French church. Renowned for his personal piety, he was beatified in 1956.

entries.name: Saskia van Uylenburgh
entries.desc: Saskia van Uylenburgh was the wife of painter Rembrandt van Rijn. In the course of her life, she was his model for some of his paintings, drawings, and etchings.
entries.tldr: Orphaned young, Saskia was raised in Leeuwarden by an older sister after her father, the town's burgomaster, died, and she met Rembrandt in 1632 through her cousin, an Amsterdam art dealer. They married in 1634 and had four children, but only their son Titus, born in 1641, survived infancy; Saskia died the following year, probably of tuberculosis. Beyond providing Rembrandt financial security through her inheritance, she appears repeatedly across his paintings, drawings, and etchings, sometimes costumed as mythological figures such as Flora, leaving varied glimpses of her warmth and illness.

entries.name: Innocent XII
entries.desc: Pope Innocent XII, born Antonio Pignatelli, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 12 July 1691 until his death in September 1700.
entries.tldr: Pope from 1691 to 1700, Innocent XII is best remembered for the bull Romanum decet Pontificem, which banned popes from enriching their relatives with land, offices, or revenues and effectively ended the long-standing practice of papal nepotism. He also intervened in the Quietism controversy, ultimately siding against the mystic Madame Guyon and her defender Archbishop Fénelon, and worked to reform the Papal States' finances and charitable institutions during his relatively brief reign.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.desc: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer whose work spans projective geometry, probability theory, and Christian apologetics.
entries.tldr: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer. He made major contributions to projective geometry, probability theory, and the design of mechanical calculators. His Pensées remains a landmark of Christian apologetics.

entries.name: Empress Meishō
entries.desc: Empress Meishō was the 109th monarch of Japan. Her reign lasted from 1629 to 1643.
entries.tldr: 109th monarch of Japan and one of only a handful of women to have reigned as empress regnant, ascending the Chrysanthemum Throne in 1629 as a young child after her father, Emperor Go-Mizunoo, abdicated in protest at pressure from the shogunate. Because she was unmarried and a minor throughout her reign, real power lay with regents and the Tokugawa shogunate, which used her accession to assert authority over the imperial court. She abdicated in 1643 in favor of her half-brother, later Emperor Go-Kōmyō, and lived for decades afterward as a retired empress.

entries.name: John Bunyan
entries.desc: John Bunyan was an English writer and nonconformist preacher. He is best remembered as the author of the Christian allegory The Pilgrim's Progress, which also became an influential literary model.
entries.tldr: John Bunyan was an English writer and nonconformist preacher. He is best remembered as the author of the Christian allegory The Pilgrim's Progress, which also became an influential literary model. In addition to The Pilgrim's Progress, Bunyan wrote nearly sixty titles, many of them expanded sermons.

entries.name: Charles Perrault
entries.desc: Charles Perrault was a French author and member of the Académie Française who laid the foundations for the fairy tale genre with tales such as "Cinderella" and "Little Red Riding Hood".
entries.tldr: Charles Perrault was a French author and member of the Académie Française. He laid the foundations for a new literary genre, the fairy tale, with his works derived from earlier folk tales, published in his 1697 book Histoires ou contes du temps passé. The best known of his tales include "Little Red Riding Hood", "Cinderella", "Puss in Boots", "Sleeping Beauty", and "Bluebeard".

entries.name: Charles II of England
entries.desc: Charles II was King of Scotland from 1649 until 1651 and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from the 1660 Restoration of the monarchy until his death in 1685.
entries.tldr: King of England, Scotland, and Ireland whose restoration to the throne in 1660, after the execution of his father Charles I and the collapse of Oliver Cromwell's Commonwealth, ended eleven years of republican rule. Known as the 'Merry Monarch' for his lavish court and many mistresses, he presided over a cultural flowering that reopened the theatres and founded the Royal Society. His reign also weathered the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London in 1666. He fathered no legitimate heir, so the crown passed to his brother James.

entries.name: Jean-Baptiste Lully
entries.desc: Jean-Baptiste Lully was an Italian-French composer, dancer and instrumentalist, who is considered a master of the French Baroque music style. Best known for his operas, he spent most of his life working in the court of Louis XIV.
entries.tldr: An Italian-born composer who rose from kitchen servant to dominate the musical life of Louis XIV's court, Lully essentially invented French opera with his tragédies en musique, works combining spoken declamation, dance, and spectacle in a style distinct from Italian models. Granted a royal monopoly over musical theater in France, he controlled the field ruthlessly for two decades. He died in 1687 of gangrene after accidentally striking his own foot with a heavy conducting staff.

entries.name: Samuel Pepys
entries.desc: English naval administrator and MP whose candid diary, kept 1660–1669, is among the most vivid primary sources for the Stuart Restoration.
entries.tldr: Though he had no seafaring background, Pepys rose through patronage and administrative talent to become Chief Secretary to the Admiralty under Charles II and James II, helping professionalize the Royal Navy. His shorthand diary, running to roughly 1.25 million words, records grand events he witnessed firsthand, the coronation, the Great Plague, and the Fire of London, alongside frank confessions of his own weaknesses and infidelities. Deciphered and first published only in 1825, more than a century after his death, it remains a uniquely intimate window into everyday Restoration life.

entries.name: James II of England
entries.desc: King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1685 until deposed as the last Catholic monarch in the 1688 Glorious Revolution.
entries.tldr: James II and VII was King of England and Ireland as James II and King of Scotland as James VII from February 1685 until he was deposed in the 1688 Glorious Revolution. The last Catholic monarch of England, Scotland, and Ireland, his reign was marked by conflicts over religion, absolutism and the divine right of kings; his deposition ended a century of political and civil strife by confirming th…

entries.name: Isaac Newton
entries.desc: English physicist and mathematician who formulated the laws of motion and gravitation.
entries.tldr: An English physicist and mathematician at Cambridge, Newton laid out the laws of motion and universal gravitation in his 1687 Principia Mathematica, unifying terrestrial and celestial mechanics under a single mathematical framework for the first time. He independently developed calculus alongside Leibniz, conducted foundational experiments in optics showing that white light is composed of a spectrum of colors, and later served as Warden of the Royal Mint and president of the Royal Society.

entries.name: Denis Papin
entries.desc: French Huguenot physicist and inventor of the steam digester, forerunner of both the pressure cooker and the steam engine.
entries.tldr: French Huguenot physicist and inventor whose 'steam digester,' a sealed vessel that cooked food faster under pressure, was the ancestor of both the modern pressure cooker and, through its safety valve, mechanisms essential to later steam engines. Forced into exile in England and then Germany by the persecution of French Protestants, he worked alongside figures such as Robert Boyle and Gottfried Leibniz. He went on to design early experimental steam-powered pumps and a crude piston engine, anticipating key elements of the engines that would drive the Industrial Revolution.

entries.name: William III of England
entries.desc: William III, also known as William of Orange, was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1689 and Dutch stadtholder, who led the Glorious Revolution.
entries.tldr: William III and II, also known as William of Orange, was the sovereign Prince of Orange from birth, Stadtholder of Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Guelders, and Overijssel in the Dutch Republic from 1672, and King of England, Ireland, and Scotland from 1689 until his death in 1702. He ruled jointly with his wife, Queen Mary II, until her death in 1694. His Glorious Revolution reshaped the British constitutional monarchy.

entries.name: Jacob Bernoulli
entries.desc: Jacob Bernoulli was a Swiss mathematician and an early proponent of Leibnizian calculus. Along with his brother Johann, he was one of the founders of the calculus of variations.
entries.tldr: A Swiss mathematician and early champion of Leibniz's calculus, Jacob Bernoulli helped found the calculus of variations alongside his younger brother Johann, though the siblings' collaboration curdled into a bitter rivalry over priority and credit. His most influential work, Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, laid the foundations of probability theory, introducing the Law of Large Numbers and the sequence of Bernoulli numbers still used across mathematics today.

entries.name: George I of Great Britain
entries.desc: George I was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1714 and ruler of the Electorate of Hanover from 1698 until his death in 1727. He was the first British monarch of the House of Hanover.
entries.tldr: George I was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1 August 1714 and ruler of the Electorate of Hanover within the Holy Roman Empire from 23 January 1698 until his death in 1727. He was the first British monarch of the House of Hanover.

entries.name: Mary II of England
entries.desc: Mary II was Queen of England, Scotland, and Ireland alongside her husband William III from 1689 until her death in 1694. Their joint reign is known as that of William and Mary.
entries.tldr: Mary II was Queen of England, Scotland, and Ireland with her husband, King William III and II, from 1689 until her death in 1694. She was also Princess of Orange following her marriage on 4 November 1677. Her joint reign with William over Britain is known as that of William and Mary.

entries.name: Anne of Great Britain
entries.desc: Anne of Great Britain may refer to Anne, Queen of Great Britain (1665–1714), who ruled after William III and before the House of Hanover.
entries.tldr: Queen who reigned from 1702 to 1714, and under whose rule England and Scotland merged into the single Kingdom of Great Britain by the 1707 Act of Union. Her reign coincided with the War of the Spanish Succession, in which the Duke of Marlborough's victories, such as Blenheim, established Britain as a major continental power. Despite seventeen pregnancies, none of her children survived to adulthood, leaving the crown to pass to the German House of Hanover after her death. Her close friendship with Sarah Churchill shaped much of her reign.

entries.name: Benedict XIV
entries.desc: Pope Benedict XIV, born Prospero Lorenzo Lambertini, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 17 August 1740 to his death on 3 May 1758.
entries.tldr: Pope from 1740 to 1758, born Prospero Lambertini, widely regarded as one of the most scholarly and broadly respected popes of the eighteenth century, admired even by Enlightenment figures such as Voltaire, who dedicated a play to him. A canon lawyer by training, he had earlier written the standard procedural manual on beatification and canonization still influential in Vatican practice. As pope he reduced nepotism at the papal court, encouraged scientific study in Rome, and negotiated concordats with several states. He also issued the definitive ban on Chinese and Malabar rites.

entries.name: Robert Walpole
entries.desc: British Whig statesman regarded as the de facto first Prime Minister of Great Britain, serving 1721–1742.
entries.tldr: Walpole rose to dominance by skillfully managing the fallout of the 1720 South Sea Bubble crash, shielding allies from blame while restoring public finances as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721. Over two decades mocked by critics as the "Robinocracy," he used patronage and parliamentary majorities to run government in a way historians now recognize as the first British premiership. He championed peace and low taxes, becoming Britain's longest-serving prime minister before resigning in 1742 after a costly war eroded his support.

entries.name: Muhammad bin Saud
entries.desc: Muhammad bin Saud, also known as Ibn Saud, was the emir of Diriyah and is considered the founder of the First Saudi State and the Saud dynasty. His reign lasted from 1727 to 1765.
entries.tldr: Muhammad bin Saud Al Muqrin Al Saud, also known as Ibn Saud, was the emir of Diriyah and is considered the founder of the First Saudi State and the Saud dynasty, named after his father, Saud bin Muhammad Al Muqrin. His reign lasted between 1727 and 1765.

entries.name: Vitus Bering
entries.desc: Danish-born Russian cartographer and naval officer who led the First Kamchatka and Great Northern expeditions, exploring Asia's northeastern coast and beyond.
entries.tldr: Vitus Jonassen Bering, also known as Ivan Ivanovich Bering, was a Danish-born Russian cartographer, explorer, and officer in the Russian Navy. He is known as a leader of two Russian expeditions, the First Kamchatka Expedition and the Great Northern Expedition, exploring the northeastern coast of the Asian continent and from there the western coast of the North American continent. The Bering Str…

entries.name: Louis, Dauphin of France, Duke of Burgundy
entries.desc: Grandson of Louis XIV known as le Petit Dauphin, groomed by Fénelon to be an enlightened king but died of measles before acceding.
entries.tldr: Grandson of Louis XIV and heir to the French throne, the young Duke of Burgundy was notorious as a child for a violent temper before undergoing a widely noted transformation under the theologian Fénelon, who used the prince as inspiration for his didactic novel Télémaque. By adulthood he was known for piety and reforming ambitions that raised hopes he might correct his grandfather's excesses. Those hopes ended in 1712, when he died of measles within days of his wife, briefly leaving the succession resting on an infant, the future Louis XV.

entries.name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
entries.desc: French Baroque composer and music theorist who became the dominant figure in French opera.
entries.tldr: A French composer who did not achieve prominence until his forties, Rameau first made his name as a music theorist with the 1722 Traité de l'harmonie, which grounded harmonic analysis in the concept of a fundamental bass and shaped Western music theory for centuries afterward. He went on to become the dominant figure in French opera after Lully, composing works like Hippolyte et Aricie and Les Indes galantes that were prized for their harmonic daring and orchestral color.

entries.name: George II of Great Britain
entries.desc: George II was King of Great Britain and Ireland, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg (Hanover) and a prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 11 June 1727 (O.S.) until his death in 1760.
entries.tldr: Born in Hanover and the last British monarch not born in Britain, George II personally led his troops into combat at the Battle of Dettingen in 1743, the last time a reigning British monarch ever fought on a battlefield. His reign saw the decisive defeat of the Jacobite cause at Culloden in 1746, ending Stuart hopes of reclaiming the throne. Though often overshadowed by capable ministers like Robert Walpole, he presided over Britain's rise as a global colonial power. He died suddenly in 1760, reportedly while sitting on the toilet.

entries.name: Friedrich Wilhelm I of Prussia
entries.desc: King of Prussia (1713–1740) known as the ‘Soldier King’ who built a highly disciplined army and centralised the Prussian state.
entries.tldr: Frugal, militaristic, and famously bad-tempered, Friedrich Wilhelm I tripled the Prussian army's size while personally living with near-miserly austerity, funneling state wealth into his military machine. His most eccentric obsession was the Potsdam Giants, an elite regiment recruited, bribed, or sometimes kidnapped from across Europe purely for their exceptional height. He clashed bitterly with his artistic, French-speaking son and heir, the future Frederick the Great, once forcing the young prince to witness the execution of a close friend as punishment for trying to flee.

entries.name: Giuseppe Tartini
entries.desc: Giuseppe Tartini was an Italian composer and violinist of the Baroque era born in Pirano in the Republic of Venice. Tartini was a prolific composer, composing over a hundred pieces for the violin, the majority of them violin concertos. He is best remembered for his Violin Sonata in G Minor.
entries.tldr: Born in Pirano, he trained for the priesthood and law before a secret marriage forced him into hiding, where he spent years in solitary violin study reshaping his ideas on bowing. From age twenty-nine he led the orchestra of Padua's Basilica of St. Anthony for life and founded a violin school drawing students from across Europe. He claimed his best-known work, the Violin Sonata in G minor, came from a dream of the Devil playing astonishing music on his violin, hence its nickname, the Devil's Trill Sonata. He also studied acoustics, describing the combination tones now called Tartini tones.

entries.name: Clement XIII
entries.desc: Pope Clement XIII, born Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 6 July 1758 to his death in February 1769.
entries.tldr: Pope Clement XIII, born Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 6 July 1758 to his death in February 1769. He was installed on 16 July 1758.

entries.name: Nicolaus II Bernoulli
entries.desc: Nicolaus II Bernoulli was a Swiss mathematician as were his father Johann Bernoulli and one of his brothers, Daniel Bernoulli. He was one of the many prominent mathematicians in the Bernoulli family.
entries.tldr: A prodigy who earned a law doctorate at twenty while mastering advanced mathematics, Nicolaus worked on curves, differential equations, and probability; an exchange with cousin Daniel over a gambling puzzle helped seed the St. Petersburg paradox. He tutored in Venice, then held Padua's mathematics chair before switching to law in Bern. In 1725 Peter the Great lured him and brother Daniel to the new St. Petersburg Academy, but he died of appendicitis within a year. His death opened the post that in 1727 went to a young Leonhard Euler, recommended by the Bernoullis themselves.

entries.name: Pietro Locatelli
entries.desc: Pietro Antonio Locatelli was an Italian Baroque composer and violinist.
entries.tldr: Trained in Bergamo and possibly under Corelli in Rome, he toured German and Italian courts as a celebrated virtuoso through the 1720s before settling in Amsterdam in 1729. There he mostly stopped public performing, instead teaching wealthy amateurs and selling violin strings from his home, a sideline so profitable it reportedly made him the city's highest-earning musician. His 1733 collection L'arte del violino paired concertos with fiendishly difficult solo caprices that pushed violin technique to new extremes, anticipating Paganini.

entries.name: Pierre Bouguer
entries.desc: French mathematician, geophysicist, and astronomer known as “the father of naval architecture” and for pioneering photometry.
entries.tldr: A prodigy who succeeded his own father as royal hydrographer at fifteen, he later spent nearly a decade in the Andes with the French Geodesic Mission, measuring a degree of meridian arc to test whether the Earth bulges at the equator or the poles. His 1746 Traite du navire founded naval architecture as a science, introducing the metacenter to explain ship stability, while his light-comparing device pioneered photometry. Atop Mount Pambamarca in Ecuador, he and a colleague famously watched their own shadows ringed by a colored halo on the clouds below.

entries.name: Johann Jakob Bodmer
entries.desc: Johann Jakob Bodmer was a Swiss author, academic, critic and poet.
entries.tldr: A Zurich literary critic and professor, Bodmer became one of the most influential arbiters of German-language taste in the eighteenth century, championing imagination and feeling in poetry against the rigid classicism then dominant in Leipzig under Johann Christoph Gottsched. His 1757 edition of the medieval epic the Nibelungenlied helped revive interest in Germanic literary heritage decades before Romanticism made it fashionable. Working with his collaborator Johann Jakob Breitinger, he mentored younger writers and helped shape the Sturm und Drang movement that followed.

entries.name: Daniel Bernoulli
entries.desc: Daniel Bernoulli was a Swiss mathematician and physicist particularly remembered for his applications of mathematics to fluid mechanics and his pioneering work in probability and statistics.
entries.tldr: Swiss mathematician and physicist, member of the prolific Bernoulli family of scientists, best known for Bernoulli's principle, which relates the speed of a moving fluid to the pressure it exerts and underlies much of fluid mechanics and the physics of flight. His 1738 book Hydrodynamica was among the first works to apply calculus systematically to fluid flow. He also made foundational contributions to probability, including an early formulation of expected utility explaining why people value risk differently than pure expected value would predict.

entries.name: Jean-Étienne Liotard
entries.desc: Genevan painter and pastellist renowned for strikingly naturalistic portraits and Orientalist scenes painted across Europe and Istanbul.
entries.tldr: Jean-Étienne Liotard was a Genevan painter, pastellist, printmaker, art theorist, and art dealer born to exiled French Huguenots. He spent his career in Rome, Istanbul, Paris, Vienna, London, and Amsterdam, and is best known for his detailed, naturalistic portraits in pastel and Orientalist scenes of daily life. His Turkish dress and long beard made him one of the most recognizable artists of the 18th century.

entries.name: Gabriel Cramer
entries.desc: Gabriel Cramer was a Genevan mathematician.
entries.tldr: A professor of mathematics and philosophy in his native Geneva, Cramer spent much of his career editing and popularizing the work of earlier mathematicians, including the Bernoulli brothers and Christiaan Huygens, alongside his own research. He is remembered chiefly for Cramer's rule, a formula using determinants to solve systems of linear equations, though the idea did not originate entirely with him. Elected to the Royal Society and academies across Europe, he died in 1752 at just 47, having collapsed from exhaustion on a journey to southern France undertaken to recover his health.

entries.name: Clement XIV
entries.desc: Pope Clement XIV, born Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 1769 until his death in 1774.
entries.tldr: Pope Clement XIV, born Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 19 May 1769 to his death in September 1774. At the time of his election, he was the only Franciscan friar in the College of Cardinals, having been a member of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual. He is the most recent pope to take the pontifical name of "Clement" upon…

entries.name: Carl Linnaeus
entries.desc: Swedish biologist who formalised binomial nomenclature and is known as the father of modern taxonomy.
entries.tldr: Swedish botanist and physician who devised the binomial system of naming species still used today, pairing a genus and species name for every organism. His Systema Naturae classified plants, animals, and minerals into a nested hierarchy of kingdoms, classes, orders, genera, and species. He trained student 'apostles' who traveled the globe collecting specimens for him, and personally named or described thousands of species, including humans as Homo sapiens. He is remembered as the father of modern taxonomy.

entries.name: Albrecht von Haller
entries.desc: Swiss anatomist, physiologist, naturalist, and poet sometimes called “the father of modern physiology.”
entries.tldr: Albrecht von Haller was a Swiss anatomist, physiologist, naturalist, encyclopedist, bibliographer and poet, sometimes called “the father of modern physiology.” A pupil of Herman Boerhaave and Jacob Winslow, he made foundational contributions to understanding muscle irritability and nervous sensation. He also wrote celebrated poetry and compiled massive bibliographies of medical and botanical literature.

entries.name: Elizabeth I of Russia
entries.desc: Elizabeth, or Elizaveta Petrovna, was Empress of Russia from 1741 until her death in 1762. She is remembered for not executing a single person during her reign and for her building projects.
entries.tldr: Elizabeth or Elizaveta Petrovna was Empress of Russia from 1741 until her death in 1762. She remains one of the most popular Russian monarchs because of her decision not to execute a single person during her reign, her numerous construction projects, and her strong opposition to Prussian policies. She was the last person on the agnatic line of the Romanovs as her nephew ascended, thus creating …

entries.name: Wilhelm Friedemann Bach
entries.desc: Wilhelm Friedemann Bach was a German composer, organist and harpsichordist. He was the second child and eldest son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach.
entries.tldr: Wilhelm Friedemann Bach was a German composer, organist and harpsichordist. He was the second child and eldest son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach. Despite his acknowledged genius as an improviser and composer, his income and employment were unstable, and he died in poverty.

entries.name: José I of Portugal
entries.desc: Dom Joseph I, known as the Reformer, was King of Portugal from 1750 until his death in 1777, with his reign dominated by the Marquis of Pombal.
entries.tldr: Known to history chiefly through the man who ran his government, José I left the administration of Portugal almost entirely to his powerful chief minister, the Marquis of Pombal, while devoting himself to hunting, opera, and court entertainments. Pombal used this latitude to rebuild the capital on a modern grid plan after the catastrophic 1755 Lisbon earthquake and to curb the power of the Jesuits and old nobility. José survived an assassination attempt in 1758 that Pombal used as pretext to execute several rival nobles, the Távora family, in a brutal purge.

entries.name: Christoph Willibald von Gluck
entries.desc: Christoph Willibald von Gluck was a composer of Italian and French opera in the early classical period who reformed opera's dramaturgical practices at the Habsburg court in Vienna.
entries.tldr: Christoph Willibald Ritter von Gluck was a composer of Italian and French opera in the early classical period. Born in the Upper Palatinate and raised in Bohemia, both part of the Holy Roman Empire at the time, he gained prominence at the Habsburg court in Vienna. There he brought about the practical reform of opera's dramaturgical practices for which many intellectuals had been campaigning.

entries.name: Pius VI
entries.desc: Pope Pius VI was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 15 February 1775 to his death in August 1799.
entries.tldr: Born Giovanni Angelo Braschi, he presided over one of history's longest pontificates, nearly a quarter century, which ended in humiliation at the hands of revolutionary France. He condemned the Revolution's seizure of Church property, and when he refused to renounce his rule over the Papal States, French troops occupied Rome in 1798 and proclaimed a Roman Republic. Though eighty years old and ailing, he was taken prisoner and marched across the Alps into France, where he died at Valence eighteen months later, the first pope in centuries to die in captivity.

entries.name: Maria Theresa of Austria
entries.desc: Maria Theresa was ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1740 until her death in 1780, and the only woman to hold the position in her own right, reigning over Austria, Hungary, and Bohemia.
entries.tldr: Maria Theresa was the ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1740 until her death in 1780, and the only woman to hold the position in her own right. She was the sovereign of Austria, Hungary, Croatia, Bohemia, Transylvania, Slavonia, Mantua, Milan, Moravia, Galicia and Lodomeria, Dalmatia, Austrian Netherlands, Carinthia, Carniola, Gorizia and Gradisca, Austrian Silesia, Tyrol, Styria, and Parma. …

entries.name: Charles Bonnet
entries.desc: Genevan naturalist and philosophical writer who coined the term phyllotaxis and was among the first to document parthenogenesis in aphids.
entries.tldr: Charles Bonnet was a Genevan naturalist and philosophical writer who coined the term phyllotaxis to describe the arrangement of leaves on a plant. He was among the first to observe parthenogenetic reproduction in aphids and established that insects respired through their spiracles. He also wrote influential works on philosophy of nature and soul.

entries.name: Jean-André Deluc
entries.desc: Geologist, natural philosopher, and meteorologist from Geneva who coined the term ‘geology’ and invented precision instruments for measuring temperature and pressure.
entries.tldr: Jean-André Deluc was a geologist, natural philosopher, and meteorologist from the Republic of Geneva who is credited with coining the term ‘geology.’ He devised precision measuring instruments and made important contributions to meteorology and the theory of Earth’s history. He later served as reader to Queen Charlotte of Great Britain.

entries.name: Johann Heinrich Lambert
entries.desc: Johann Heinrich Lambert was a polymath who made important contributions to mathematics, physics, philosophy, astronomy and map projections.
entries.tldr: A largely self-taught polymath from Alsace, Lambert proved in 1761 that pi is an irrational number, the first rigorous demonstration of that fact, and made significant contributions to hyperbolic geometry, photometry, and cartography, including the Lambert conformal conic projection still used in mapmaking. He also invented the first practical hygrometer for measuring humidity and corresponded with Kant on the philosophical foundations of geometry and physical measurement.

entries.name: Louis, Dauphin of France
entries.desc: Son of Louis XV of France and father of three kings (Louis XVI, Louis XVIII, Charles X) who never himself ascended the throne.
entries.tldr: Eldest son of Louis XV, this Dauphin was raised to be king but never reigned, dying of tuberculosis at thirty-six, eleven years before his father. He was known for genuine piety and a conservative religious outlook that put him at odds with Enlightenment currents at Versailles, earning him quiet influence as leader of a conservative faction, the parti dévot. His true historical weight came through his children: three of his sons became kings of France in turn, as Louis XVI, Louis XVIII, and Charles X. He did not live to see any of them crowned.

entries.name: Salomon Gessner
entries.desc: Swiss painter, graphic artist, and poet best known for his Idylls; co-founder of the Helvetic Society and first publisher of the Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
entries.tldr: Salomon Gessner was a Swiss painter, graphic artist, government official, newspaper publisher, and poet, best known for his Idylls. He was a co-founder of the Helvetic Society and the first publisher and editor of the Neue Zürcher Zeitung. His pastoral poetry was widely translated across Europe and influenced the Romantic movement.

entries.name: Henry Cavendish
entries.desc: Henry Cavendish was an English experimental and theoretical chemist and physicist. He is noted for his discovery of hydrogen, which he termed "inflammable air".
entries.tldr: Henry Cavendish was an English experimental and theoretical chemist and physicist. He is noted for his discovery of hydrogen, which he termed "inflammable air". He described the density of inflammable air, which formed water on combustion, in a 1766 paper, On Factitious Airs.

entries.name: Jacques Necker
entries.desc: Jacques Necker was a Genevan banker, financier and statesman who served as finance minister of France for Louis XVI.
