entries.tldr: A Genevan banker who rose to serve as Louis XVI's finance minister, Necker gained huge popularity by publishing the Compte rendu au roi in 1781, an unprecedented public account of royal finances that concealed France's mounting debt behind an appearance of solvency. His dismissal in July 1789, seen as a blow against fiscal reform, helped spark the crowd unrest that culminated in the storming of the Bastille days later. He was the father of the writer Madame de Staël.

entries.name: Jean-Honoré Fragonard
entries.desc: French Rococo painter and printmaker who produced more than 550 paintings, known for intimate, playful genre scenes.
entries.tldr: Jean-Honoré Fragonard was a French painter and printmaker whose late Rococo manner was distinguished by remarkable facility, exuberance, and hedonism. One of the most prolific artists active in the last decades of the Ancien Régime, Fragonard produced more than 550 paintings, of which only five are dated. Among his most popular works are genre paintings conveying an atmosphere of intimacy and v…

entries.name: Johann Christian Bach
entries.desc: Youngest son of J.S. Bach, German-born Classical composer who settled in London and profoundly influenced the young Mozart.
entries.tldr: The youngest son of Johann Sebastian Bach, known as the “London Bach,” Johann Christian broke from his father's contrapuntal style after converting to Catholicism in Italy and settling in London, where he became music master to Queen Charlotte and a leading composer of the emerging galant, pre-Classical style. His warm friendship with the young Mozart during the boy's 1764-65 London visit left a lasting imprint on Mozart's piano concertos and symphonic writing.

entries.name: John Adams
entries.desc: John Adams was a Founding Father and the second president of the United States from 1797 to 1801. He was a leader of the American Revolution that achieved independence from Great Britain.
entries.tldr: A Massachusetts lawyer who first gained prominence defending the British soldiers accused in the Boston Massacre, insisting even unpopular defendants deserved a fair trial, Adams became one of the most forceful advocates for independence in the Continental Congress. He helped draft the Declaration of Independence and served as a wartime diplomat securing loans and recognition from the Dutch and French. As the first vice president and second president, he steered a fragile young republic through the divisive Quasi-War with France, at real cost to his own re-election.

entries.name: Thomas Paine
entries.desc: English-born American Founding Father and political philosopher whose pamphlets Common Sense and The American Crisis helped frame the case for independence.
entries.tldr: Thomas Paine was an English-born American Founding Father, inventor, political philosopher, and statesman. His pamphlets Common Sense (1776) and The American Crisis (1776–1783) framed the Patriot argument for independence from Great Britain at the outset of the American Revolution. Paine advanced Enlightenment-era arguments for human rights that shaped revolutionary discourse on both sides of t…

entries.name: George III of Great Britain
entries.desc: George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 until his death in 1820, and King of the United Kingdom from 1801. He was also concurrently Elector, then King, of Hanover.
entries.tldr: George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 25 October 1760 until his death in 1820. The Acts of Union 1800 unified Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with George as its king. He was concurrently duke and prince-elector of Hanover in the Holy Roman Empire before becoming King of Hanover on 12 October 1814.

entries.name: Horace Bénédict de Saussure
entries.desc: Horace Bénédict de Saussure was a Genevan geologist, meteorologist, physicist, mountaineer and Alpine explorer, often called the founder of alpinism and modern meteorology.
entries.tldr: A Genevan naturalist often called the founder of alpinism, Saussure spent decades studying the geology, botany, and weather of the Alps, inventing an improved hygrometer to measure atmospheric humidity along the way. In 1760 he offered a prize for the first ascent of Mont Blanc, finally claimed in 1786, and the following year he made the second ascent himself, hauling scientific instruments to the summit to take the first measurements of temperature and pressure at that altitude.

entries.name: Isabelle de Charrière
entries.desc: Dutch-Swiss Enlightenment writer and composer known for letters, novels, pamphlets, and music composed in Colombier, Neuchâtel.
entries.tldr: Isabelle de Charrière, also known as Belle van Zuylen, was a Dutch and Swiss writer of the Enlightenment who spent the latter half of her life in Colombier, Neuchâtel. She is best known for her letters and novels, but also wrote pamphlets, composed music, and authored plays. She engaged keenly with the society and politics of her time and corresponded with notable contemporaries including James Boswell and Benjamin Constant.

entries.name: Marquis de Sade
entries.desc: The Marquis de Sade, born Donatien Alphonse François, was a French writer, libertine, political activist, and nobleman known for his libertine novels and imprisonment for sex crimes.
entries.tldr: Donatien Alphonse François, Marquis de Sade was a French writer, libertine, political activist, and nobleman best known for his libertine novels and imprisonment for sex crimes, blasphemy, and pornography. His works include novels, short stories, plays, dialogues, and political tracts. Some of these were published under his own name during his lifetime, but most appeared anonymously or posthumo…

entries.name: Henry Fuseli
entries.desc: Henry Fuseli was a Swiss painter, draughtsman, and writer on art who spent much of his career in Britain.
entries.tldr: Trained as a Zwinglian minister in Zurich before turning to painting, Fuseli settled in London and became a central figure of Romantic art. He is best known for The Nightmare (1781), a startling image of a demon crouched on a sleeping woman that fixed the visual language of gothic horror. A close friend of William Blake, he taught as Professor of Painting at the Royal Academy and drew heavily on Shakespeare, Milton, and classical myth for his theatrical, unsettling compositions.

entries.name: Angelica Kauffmann
entries.desc: Maria Anna Angelika Kauffmann was a Swiss painter who had a successful career in London and Rome. She was one of two female painters among the founding members of the Royal Academy of Art in London in 1768.
entries.tldr: Swiss-born painter who achieved international success first in Rome and then in London, where in 1768 she became one of only two women among the founding members of the Royal Academy of Arts, a distinction no woman would match again for over a century. She specialized in history painting, a genre considered the most prestigious but largely closed to women artists, and her mythological scenes were also reproduced widely as decorative panels for Robert Adam's interiors. She later returned to Rome, remaining a leading figure in the international art world until her death.

entries.name: Johann Kaspar Lavater
entries.desc: Johann Kaspar Lavater was a Swiss poet, writer, philosopher, physiognomist and Reformed theologian.
entries.tldr: A Zurich pastor and prolific writer, Lavater is best remembered for popularizing physiognomy, the now-discredited theory that character could be read from the fixed features of the face, in his widely translated Physiognomic Fragments. The work made him a celebrity, corresponding with figures including Goethe, though critics like Georg Christoph Lichtenberg mocked its pseudoscientific claims. A public attempt to convert Moses Mendelssohn to Christianity embroiled him in controversy. He died from wounds tending the injured during the French occupation of Zurich in 1799.

entries.name: Jakob Friedrich Ehrhart
entries.desc: German botanist and pupil of Carl Linnaeus who directed Hannover's Botanical Garden and was among the first to use the rank of subspecies in botany.
entries.tldr: Jakob Friedrich Ehrhart was a German botanist, a pupil of Carl Linnaeus at Uppsala University, and later director of the Botanical Garden of Hannover, where he produced several major botanical works between 1780 and 1793. Ehrhart was the first author to use the rank of subspecies in botanical literature, and he published many subspecific names between 1780 and 1789. Ehrhart issued several exsic…

entries.name: Pius VII
entries.desc: Pope Pius VII was head of the Catholic Church from 14 March 1800 to his death in August 1823. He was the leader of the Papal States from June 1800 to 17 May 1809 and again from 1814 to his death.
entries.tldr: Pope Pius VII was head of the Catholic Church from 14 March 1800 to his death in August 1823. He was the leader of the Papal States from June 1800 to 17 May 1809 and again from 1814 to his death. Chiaramonti was also a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict in addition to being a well-known theologian and bishop.

entries.name: Thomas Jefferson
entries.desc: Thomas Jefferson was a Founding Father and the third president of the United States from 1801 to 1809. Jefferson was the primary author of the Declaration of Independence.
entries.tldr: A Virginia planter and lawyer, Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 as part of the Continental Congress's Committee of Five, articulating the natural-rights ideals that defined the new nation. He served as vice president under John Adams, then won the bitterly contested 1800 election and, as president from 1801 to 1809, doubled the country's size via the Louisiana Purchase. He founded the University of Virginia, yet enslaved more than 600 people despite writing eloquently against slavery. He died July 4, 1826, the Declaration's fiftieth anniversary.

entries.name: Jean-Paul Marat
entries.desc: Jean-Paul Marat was a French political theorist, physician, and scientist. A journalist and politician during the French Revolution, he was a vigorous defender of the sans-culottes.
entries.tldr: A physician and scientist before the French Revolution, Marat became one of its most radical journalistic voices through his newspaper L'Ami du Peuple, relentlessly denouncing counter-revolutionaries and demanding harsh measures against them. Suffering from a painful skin disease, he worked from a medicated bath for relief, and it was there in 1793 that the Girondin sympathizer Charlotte Corday stabbed him to death, an assassination immortalized in Jacques-Louis David's painting The Death of Marat.

entries.name: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi
entries.desc: Swiss educational reformer who pioneered child-centred learning methods emphasising hands-on experience, shaping the foundations of modern elementary education.
entries.tldr: A Swiss educational reformer often called the father of modern pedagogy, Pestalozzi ran schools for poor and orphaned children where he pioneered child-centered methods built on direct sensory observation, or Anschauung, rather than rote memorization and harsh discipline. His conviction that education should engage “head, heart, and hands” together influenced Friedrich Fröbel's invention of the kindergarten and shaped elementary education systems across Europe and North America.

entries.name: Tipu Sultan
entries.desc: Sultan of Mysore (1782–1799) who pioneered iron-cased rocket artillery and fiercely resisted British expansion.
entries.tldr: Known as the Tiger of Mysore, Tipu ruled from 1782 until he was killed defending his capital Srirangapatna in 1799, inheriting a kingdom his father Hyder Ali had already built into a regional power. He expanded the pioneering iron-cased Mysorean rockets, capable of striking targets up to two kilometers away, and commissioned a military manual, Fathul Mujahidin, to standardize his forces. These rockets damaged British and allied troops at battles like Pollilur, and captured examples directly inspired the British Congreve rocket later used in the Napoleonic Wars.

entries.name: James Madison
entries.desc: James Madison was an American statesman, diplomat, and Founding Father who served as the fourth president of the United States from 1809 to 1817. He was popularly acclaimed as the "Father of the Constitution".
entries.tldr: A Virginia statesman and principal architect of the United States Constitution, Madison earned the title Father of the Constitution for his role drafting its framework and later co-authoring the Federalist Papers defending its ratification. As the fourth president, from 1809 to 1817, he led the country through the War of 1812 against Britain, including the burning of Washington, before overseeing the postwar recovery. He also authored the Bill of Rights as a member of the first Congress.

entries.name: Pierre Joseph Bonnaterre
entries.desc: Abbé Pierre Joseph Bonnaterre was a French zoologist who contributed to the Tableau encyclopédique et méthodique and was the first scientist to study the feral child Victor of Aveyron.
entries.tldr: Abbé Pierre Joseph Bonnaterre was a French zoologist who contributed sections on cetaceans, mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and insects to the Tableau encyclopédique et méthodique. He is also notable as the first scientist to study the feral child Victor of Aveyron.

entries.name: James Monroe
entries.desc: James Monroe was an American Founding Father who served as the fifth president of the United States from 1817 to 1825. He was the last Founding Father to serve as president.
entries.tldr: The fifth president of the United States and the last of the Founding Fathers to hold the office, Monroe served from 1817 to 1825 during a period later called the Era of Good Feelings for its relative absence of partisan strife. His presidency is best remembered for the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, which warned European powers against further colonization or intervention in the Americas and became a cornerstone of American foreign policy for generations afterward.

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.desc: English writer and philosopher whose A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) is a founding text of feminism.
entries.tldr: Largely self-educated, she worked as a governess and translator before publishing A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792, arguing women seemed frivolous only because they were denied education, not from natural inferiority. She lived unconventionally, having a daughter out of wedlock with speculator Gilbert Imlay before marrying philosopher William Godwin. She died of complications eleven days after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary Shelley, future author of Frankenstein. Godwin's candid memoir scandalized her name for decades before feminists reclaimed her work.

entries.name: William Pitt the Younger
entries.desc: William Pitt was a British statesman who served as both the last prime minister of Great Britain and the first prime minister of the United Kingdom, holding office twice between 1783 and 1806.
entries.tldr: William Pitt was a British statesman who served as the last prime minister of Great Britain from 1783 until the Acts of Union 1800, and the first official prime minister of the United Kingdom from January 1801. He left office in March 1801, but served as prime minister again from 1804 until his death in 1806. He was also Chancellor of the Exchequer for all his time as prime minister.

entries.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
entries.desc: German philosopher and founding figure of German Idealism who extended Kant's ethics and epistemology into a systematic philosophy of the self.
entries.tldr: A German philosopher who studied under Kant, Fichte developed the Wissenschaftslehre, a systematic idealist philosophy grounding all reality and knowledge in the self-positing activity of the “I,” extending Kant's critical project into a more radically subject-centered system. During the Napoleonic occupation of Berlin he delivered his stirring Addresses to the German Nation, calling for national cultural renewal through education, and later became the first rector of the newly founded University of Berlin.

entries.name: George IV of the United Kingdom
entries.desc: George IV was King of the United Kingdom from 1820 to 1830, having previously served as Prince Regent during his father's mental illness from 1811.
entries.tldr: George IV was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and King of Hanover from 29 January 1820 until his death in 1830. At the time of his accession to the throne, he was acting as prince regent for his father, King George III, having done so since 5 February 1811 during his father's final mental illness. He was known for his extravagance and his patronage of the arts and architecture.

entries.name: William IV
entries.desc: King of the United Kingdom and Hanover from 1830 until his death in 1837, the third son of George III who succeeded his brother George IV.
entries.tldr: William IV was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and King of Hanover from 26 June 1830 until his death in 1837. The third son of George III, William succeeded his elder brother George IV, becoming the last king and penultimate monarch of the United Kingdom's House of Hanover.

entries.name: Germaine de Staël
entries.desc: Anne Louise Germaine de Staël-Holstein, commonly known as Madame de Staël, was a prominent French novelist, woman of letters, philosopher, and political theorist.
entries.tldr: Daughter of Louis XVI's finance minister Jacques Necker, Staël turned her Paris salon into a center of intellectual opposition to Napoleon, whose regime she criticized for crushing individual liberty. Napoleon, threatened by her influence, banished her from Paris in 1803; she spent much of the following decade in exile at her family's château at Coppet and traveling across Europe. That exile inspired her novel Corinne, or Italy and her influential study of German Romantic culture, De l'Allemagne, whose print run Napoleon's police seized and pulped.

entries.name: Andreas Hofer
entries.desc: Andreas Hofer was a Tyrolean innkeeper and drover who became the leader of the 1809 Tyrolean Rebellion during the War of the Fifth Coalition.
entries.tldr: Tyrolean innkeeper and cattle trader who led a popular uprising in 1809 against Bavarian and French rule after Austria ceded Tyrol to Bavaria under the Peace of Pressburg. His irregular militia defeated Bavarian and French forces three times at the Battle of Bergisel near Innsbruck and briefly restored Tyrolean self-government. When Austria made peace with Napoleon without securing Tyrol's return, Hofer fought on alone until betrayed, captured, and, on Napoleon's order, shot in Mantua in 1810. He remains Tyrol's most celebrated national hero.

entries.name: John Quincy Adams
entries.desc: John Quincy Adams was the sixth president of the United States, serving from 1825 to 1829. He previously served as the eighth United States secretary of state from 1817 to 1825.
entries.tldr: Son of the second president, Adams built an extraordinary diplomatic career before reaching the White House himself, serving as minister to the Netherlands, Prussia, Russia, and Britain, and as secretary of state negotiating the treaty that brought Florida into the United States. His single term as president, won in a contested 1824 election decided by the House, was hampered by opponents who denounced it as a “corrupt bargain.” He later returned to Congress, spending nearly two decades as a leading opponent of slavery, and died on the House floor in 1848.

entries.name: Andrew Jackson
entries.desc: Andrew Jackson was the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837. He rose to fame as a U.S. Army general.
entries.tldr: Seventh president of the United States, who first won national fame as a general for his decisive victory over the British at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815. As president from 1829 to 1837 he championed an expanded popular democracy for white male voters while signing the Indian Removal Act of 1830, forcing tens of thousands of Native Americans westward on marches that killed thousands, remembered as the Trail of Tears. He fought a fierce battle against the Second Bank of the United States, ultimately destroying it, giving rise to the term Jacksonian democracy.

entries.name: Benjamin Constant
entries.desc: Henri-Benjamin Constant de Rebecque, or simply Benjamin Constant, was a Swiss and French political thinker, activist and writer on political theory and religion.
entries.tldr: Swiss-French writer and political theorist regarded as one of the founding figures of European liberalism, best known for his 1819 essay distinguishing the "liberty of the ancients," rooted in collective political participation, from the "liberty of the moderns," centered on individual rights and private life. He also wrote Adolphe, a short psychological novel about a doomed love affair drawn partly from his own turbulent relationship with Madame de Staël. Though a longtime opponent of Napoleon, he briefly helped draft a liberal constitution for him during the Hundred Days in 1815.

entries.name: Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Francis II was the last Holy Roman Emperor, reigning from 1792 to 1806, and the first Emperor of Austria as Francis I from 1804 to 1835. He also served as first president of the German Confederation.
entries.tldr: Francis II and I was the last Holy Roman Emperor as Francis II from 1792 to 1806, and the first Emperor of Austria as Francis I from 1804 to 1835. He was also King of Germany, Hungary, Croatia and Bohemia, and served as the first president of the German Confederation following its establishment in 1815.

entries.name: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
entries.desc: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, was a British Army officer and statesman who twice served as Prime Minister and helped defeat Napoleon in the Napoleonic Wars.
entries.tldr: Field Marshal Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington was a British Army officer and statesman who was one of the leading military and political figures in Britain during the early 19th century, twice serving as Prime Minister. He was one of the British commanders who ended the Anglo-Mysore wars by defeating Tipu Sultan in 1799, and among those who ended the Napoleonic Wars in a Coalition vict…

entries.name: William Henry Harrison
entries.desc: William Henry Harrison was the ninth president of the United States from March to April 1841. He died 31 days into his term, making him the shortest serving president and the first president to die in office.
entries.tldr: A military hero of the War of 1812 and the Battle of Tippecanoe, Harrison rode that fame to the presidency in 1840 as the Whig candidate, campaigning with the slogan "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too." At 68 he was the oldest president elected up to that time, and he delivered the longest inaugural address in history, nearly two hours in cold weather without a coat. He fell ill soon after and died on his 31st day in office, the shortest presidency in U.S. history. His death triggered the first test of presidential succession, resolved when Vice President John Tyler claimed the full office.

entries.name: Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi
entries.desc: Swiss historian and political economist known for his writings on French and Italian history and an early liberal critique of political economy.
entries.tldr: Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi, also known as Jean Charles Leonard Simonde de Sismondi, whose real surname was Simonde, was a Swiss historian and political economist, who is best known for his works on French and Italian history, and his economic ideas. His Nouveaux principes d'économie politique, ou de la richesse dans ses rapports avec la population (1819) represents the first liberal criti…

entries.name: Caspar David Friedrich
entries.desc: German Romantic painter whose landscapes, including Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, express spiritual solitude and the sublime power of nature.
entries.tldr: German Romantic painter whose brooding landscapes of ruins, fog, and solitary figures gazing into vast nature became emblematic of Romanticism's search for the sublime. His best-known work, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, depicts a lone man surveying a mist-shrouded mountain range, a composition endlessly reproduced as shorthand for Romantic yearning. He often painted figures from behind, inviting the viewer to share their contemplative gaze. Neglected for decades after his death, his reputation was revived in the early 20th century.

entries.name: Giuseppe Caspar Mezzofanti
entries.desc: Giuseppe Gasparo Mezzofanti was an Italian cardinal known for being a hyperpolyglot. He spoke 38 to 50 languages.
entries.tldr: Born in Bologna to a carpenter, he showed a gift for languages from childhood and became a professor of Oriental languages at Bologna before serving as Vatican librarian and, from 1838, a cardinal. Sources disagree on how many languages he actually commanded, estimates ranging from about 38 spoken fluently to over 70 with some skill, and he reportedly conversed easily with foreign pilgrims in their native tongue. Lord Byron, no slouch at languages himself, once challenged him to a multilingual swearing match and lost. He learned nearly all his languages without ever leaving Italy.

entries.name: François Adrien Boieldieu
entries.desc: François-Adrien Boieldieu was a French composer, mainly of operas, often called “the French Mozart”.
entries.tldr: Born in Rouen, Boieldieu made his name young with comic operas before spending 1804 to 1811 as court composer to Tsar Alexander I in St Petersburg, later teaching composition at the Paris Conservatoire. He worked mainly in opéra-comique, favoring elegant melody and light drama over grand tragedy. His masterpiece, La Dame blanche, premiered in 1825 with a libretto based on Walter Scott and had racked up 1,700 performances by 1914, making it one of the most durable French operas of its era.

entries.name: Matthew Gregory Lewis
entries.desc: Matthew Gregory Lewis was an English novelist and dramatist whose writings are often classified as "Gothic horror". He was frequently referred to as "Monk" Lewis, because of his 1796 Gothic novel The Monk.
entries.tldr: He reportedly wrote The Monk in ten weeks at nineteen while a diplomat in the Netherlands, publishing it anonymously in 1796. Its lurid mix of demonic seduction, incest, and violence scandalized British readers and drew accusations of blasphemy serious enough to threaten prosecution, making its author notorious as 'Monk' Lewis. Elected to Parliament that year, he largely abandoned politics for literature and theater, and inherited sugar plantations and enslaved people in Jamaica from his father. He died of yellow fever at sea in 1818, returning from a voyage to improve his estates.

entries.name: Eugène François Vidocq
entries.desc: Eugène-François Vidocq was a French criminal turned criminalist. He was the founder and first director of France's Sûreté Nationale, and the head of the first known private detective agency.
entries.tldr: French adventurer and former criminal who, after years as a fugitive and prison escapee, offered his knowledge of the Parisian underworld to the police and in 1811 founded the Sûreté, a plainclothes unit largely staffed by ex-convicts like himself. His network of informants and use of undercover disguise were novel for their time and dramatically improved arrest rates, though his past also drew suspicion. After leaving the police, he opened what is considered the first private detective agency. His memoirs helped inspire fictional detectives from Vautrin to Sherlock Holmes.

entries.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
entries.desc: Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal Emperor and an Urdu poet, whose authority was limited to Delhi but who was declared Emperor of India during the 1857 rebellion.
entries.tldr: Bahadur Shah II, also known by his poetic title Bahadur Shah Zafar, was the twentieth and last Mughal Emperor and an Urdu poet. He was a titular Emperor with his authority limited to the Walled City of Delhi, but was declared the Emperor of India by the forces opposing East India Company forces across the Indian subcontinent during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Zafar was exiled to Yangon in Bri…

entries.name: Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle
entries.desc: Augustin Pyramus de Candolle was a Swiss botanist who documented hundreds of plant families and created a new natural plant classification system.
entries.tldr: Swiss botanist who devoted his career to reorganizing plant classification around natural relationships rather than the artificial sexual system of Linnaeus, work that led him to coin the term "taxonomy." His monumental Prodromus attempted to describe every known flowering plant species, eventually cataloguing more than 58,000, a project his son continued after his death. He also identified the principle of plant competition for resources, an idea Darwin later cited as an influence. He held professorships at Montpellier and Geneva.

entries.name: William Hazlitt
entries.desc: English essayist, drama and literary critic, painter, and philosopher, now considered among the greatest critics in the history of the English language.
entries.tldr: William Hazlitt was an English essayist, drama and literary critic, painter, social commentator, and philosopher. He is now considered one of the greatest critics and essayists in the history of the English language, placed in the company of Samuel Johnson and George Orwell. He is also acknowledged as the finest art critic of his age.

entries.name: Humphry Davy
entries.desc: British chemist and inventor who isolated several chemical elements using electrolysis and invented the Davy safety lamp for miners.
entries.tldr: Sir Humphry Davy, 1st Baronet was a British chemist and inventor who invented the Davy lamp and an early form of arc lamp. He is also remembered for isolating, by using electricity, several elements for the first time: potassium and sodium in 1807 and calcium, strontium, barium, magnesium and boron the following year, as well as for discovering the elemental nature of chlorine and iodine. Davy …

entries.name: Antoine-Henri Jomini
entries.desc: Baron Antoine-Henri Jomini was a Swiss-French military officer who served as a general in French and later in Russian service, and one of the most celebrated writers on the Napoleonic art of war.
entries.tldr: Swiss-born soldier and military theorist who served as a staff officer under Napoleon, including as chief of staff to Marshal Ney, before defecting to Russian service in 1813 after feeling passed over for promotion. He is remembered chiefly as a writer, whose Summary of the Art of War distilled Napoleonic strategy into geometric principles of lines of operation and decisive points that dominated European and American military education for much of the nineteenth century. His systematic approach was later contrasted with the more philosophical theories of his rival Carl von Clausewitz.

entries.name: Richard Mentor Johnson
entries.desc: Richard Mentor Johnson was an American lawyer, military officer and politician who served as the ninth vice president of the United States from 1837 to 1841 under President Martin Van Buren.
entries.tldr: A Kentucky lawyer turned War Hawk congressman, Johnson led mounted volunteers at the 1813 Battle of the Thames, where he was widely credited with personally killing Shawnee chief Tecumseh, a claim he rode to fame with the jingle "Rumpsey Dumpsey." As Van Buren's running mate in 1836 he fell one electoral vote short of a majority, becoming the only vice president elected by the Senate itself. His open relationship with Julia Chinn, an enslaved woman he treated as his common-law wife, scandalized Democrats and helped end his career by 1840.

entries.name: Thomas Stamford Raffles
entries.desc: Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles was a British colonial official and naturalist who founded modern Singapore and served as governor in the Dutch East Indies.
entries.tldr: Sir Thomas Stamford Bingley Raffles was a British colonial official who served as the governor of the Dutch East Indies between 1811 and 1816 and lieutenant-governor of Bencoolen between 1818 and 1824. He founded modern Singapore in 1819. Raffles was also a keen naturalist who co-founded the Zoological Society of London and had many species named after him.

entries.name: Daniel Webster
entries.desc: American lawyer and statesman who served as U.S. Senator and twice as Secretary of State, a dominant voice for Union and constitutional law.
entries.tldr: American lawyer and statesman who served as a U.S. senator from Massachusetts and twice as Secretary of State, and was renowned as the most formidable orator of his generation. He argued many landmark cases before the Supreme Court, including Dartmouth College v. Woodward, and negotiated the Webster-Ashburton Treaty settling the U.S.-Canada border dispute. His 1850 Senate speech supporting the Compromise of 1850, including a stronger fugitive slave law, aimed to preserve the Union but cost him support among Northern abolitionists who felt betrayed.

entries.name: Martin Van Buren
entries.desc: Martin Van Buren was the eighth president of the United States, serving from 1837 to 1841. He co-founded the Democratic Party with Andrew Jackson.
entries.tldr: A shrewd New York operator nicknamed 'the Little Magician,' he built the machine that became the Democratic Party and served as Andrew Jackson's vice president before winning the presidency in 1836. His single term was dominated by the Panic of 1837, which he refused to fight with federal relief, instead separating government funds from private banks in an independent treasury, a stance that cost him reelection. Raised speaking Dutch in Kinderhook, New York, he was the first president born a citizen of the new United States. He later ran again in 1848 on the antislavery Free Soil ticket.

entries.name: Ivan Paskevich
entries.desc: Count Ivan Fyodorovich Paskevich-Erevansky, Serene Prince of Warsaw was a Russian military leader who was the namiestnik of Poland.
entries.tldr: A Russian field marshal under three tsars, Paskevich built his reputation defeating Persian and Ottoman forces in the 1820s, capturing Erivan and earning the title Count of Erivan. He crushed the Polish uprising of 1830 to 1831 and was rewarded with the title Prince of Warsaw and appointment as the kingdom's viceroy, ruling it with an iron hand for over two decades. In 1849 he led Russian forces into Hungary at Austria's request, helping suppress its revolution.

entries.name: Zachary Taylor
entries.desc: Zachary Taylor was the 12th president of the United States, serving from 1849 until his death in 1850. He was a career officer in the United States Army, rising to major general.
entries.tldr: A career U.S. Army officer for four decades, Taylor rose to national fame commanding American forces to victory at the Battle of Buena Vista during the Mexican-American War, earning the nickname "Old Rough and Ready." He had never voted in a presidential election before the Whigs nominated him in 1848, largely on his war celebrity. As president he resisted extending slavery into the new western territories, angering many in his own Southern, slaveholding base. He died suddenly in July 1850, after sixteen months in office, following a Fourth of July illness.

entries.name: Alessandro Manzoni
entries.desc: Italian poet and novelist whose The Betrothed (1827) is considered the greatest Italian novel and a pillar of the Risorgimento.
entries.tldr: Italian novelist and poet whose 1827 novel The Betrothed, set during a seventeenth-century plague and famine in Spanish-ruled Lombardy, is widely regarded as the greatest work of Italian fiction. He rewrote the book's language after 1840 to match Florentine usage, a deliberate effort to forge a shared literary Italian ahead of national unification, and the novel became a set text that shaped the modern language itself. A committed Catholic and liberal, he was made a senator of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1860. When he died in 1873, Giuseppe Verdi composed his Requiem in tribute.

entries.name: Guillaume Henri Dufour
entries.desc: Swiss general, structural engineer, and topographer who led the Confederation to victory in 1847 and chaired the First Geneva Convention.
entries.tldr: Guillaume Henri Dufour was a Swiss military officer, structural engineer, and topographer who served under Napoleon I. He held the Swiss office of General four times, most notably leading Confederation forces to victory against the Sonderbund in 1847. In 1864 he presided over the First Geneva Convention, which established the International Red Cross.

entries.name: Louis Daguerre
entries.desc: Louis Daguerre was a French scientist, artist, and photographer recognized for inventing the daguerreotype photographic process, becoming known as one of the fathers of photography.
entries.tldr: Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre was a French scientist, artist and photographer recognized for his invention of the eponymous daguerreotype process of photography. He became known as one of the fathers of photography. Though he is most famous for his contributions to photography, he was also an accomplished painter, scenic designer, and a developer of the diorama theatre.

entries.name: James Barry
entries.desc: James Barry was a British military surgeon and Inspector General of Hospitals, one of the first women to practise medicine in Britain under a male identity.
entries.tldr: James Barry was a British military surgeon who rose to the rank of Inspector General of Hospitals. Born Margaret Ann Bulkley, Barry lived as a man for decades, becoming one of the first women to practise medicine in Britain. Barry performed one of the earliest successful caesarean sections and was renowned for improving conditions for soldiers and the poor in colonial postings across the British Empire.

entries.name: John Tyler
entries.desc: John Tyler was the tenth president of the United States, serving from 1841 to 1845. He succeeded to the presidency following Harrison's death 31 days after assuming office.
entries.tldr: Elected vice president in 1840 on a ticket meant to balance regional interests, Tyler became the first vice president to assume the presidency on a sitting president's death when William Henry Harrison died a month into office. He insisted, against considerable objection, that he had become president in full rather than a mere caretaker, establishing the ‘Tyler Precedent’ for succession, later codified in the 25th Amendment. His independence from party discipline led most of his cabinet to resign and the Whigs to expel him. He later sided with the Confederacy at the Civil War's outbreak.

entries.name: Leopold I of Belgium
entries.desc: Leopold I was the first king of the Belgians, reigning from 1831 until his death in 1865 after being chosen by the Belgian National Congress.
entries.tldr: Leopold I was the first king of the Belgians, reigning from 21 July 1831 until his death in 1865. He had previously served as a general in Russian service during the Napoleonic Wars. After declining the Greek throne, he accepted the Belgian crown and steered the new state through its early years with skill, strengthening its constitutional monarchy.

entries.name: Manuel Blanco Encalada
entries.desc: Manuel José Blanco y Calvo de Encalada was a vice-admiral in the Chilean Navy, a political figure, and Chile's first President (Provisional) (1826).
entries.tldr: Born in Buenos Aires and educated in the Spanish navy, Blanco Encalada joined the Chilean independence movement and became the founding commander of the Chilean Navy, leading its first ships against Spanish forces along the Pacific coast. He served briefly as Chile's first head of state, as Supreme Director in 1826, though internal conflict forced his resignation within months. He later commanded Chilean forces during the war against the Peru-Bolivia Confederation and held senior diplomatic posts, including ambassador to France and Britain, before his death in 1876.

entries.name: Giacomo Meyerbeer
entries.desc: German-Jewish opera composer whose grand operas—including Les Huguenots—dominated Parisian stages for decades and influenced later Romantic opera.
entries.tldr: Born Jakob Liebmann Meyer Beer near Berlin, a piano prodigy who debuted at eleven, he studied with Salieri and first made his name with Italian operas in Rossini's style. In Paris, Robert le Diable (1831) was a sensation that helped create the lavish "grand opera" genre. Les Huguenots, set amid the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre, followed in 1836 as his greatest triumph, admired even by rivals like Wagner and Verdi who publicly scorned him. For decades he was Europe's wealthiest, most-performed opera composer, bridging Mozart's era and Wagner's.

entries.name: James Buchanan
entries.desc: 15th president of the United States (1857–1861), the only president never to marry.
entries.tldr: James Buchanan Jr. was the 15th president of the United States, serving from 1857 to 1861. He also served as the 17th United States Secretary of State (1845–1849) and represented Pennsylvania in both houses of Congress. His presidency is largely remembered for failing to prevent the secession of Southern states on the eve of the Civil War.

entries.name: Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky
entries.desc: Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky was a Russian mathematician who pioneered hyperbolic geometry, challenging Euclidean axioms and laying groundwork for non-Euclidean mathematics.
entries.tldr: Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky was a Russian mathematician and geometer, known primarily for his work on hyperbolic geometry, otherwise known as Lobachevskian geometry, and also for his fundamental study on Dirichlet integrals, known as the Lobachevsky integral formula.

entries.name: Casimir Delavigne
entries.desc: Jean-François Casimir Delavigne was a French poet and dramatist.
entries.tldr: French poet and playwright whose patriotic verses, the Messéniennes, made him famous after France's 1815 defeat at Waterloo, capturing public grief while skirting censorship under the restored monarchy. He turned to the stage with historical dramas and comedies, including Les Vêpres siciliennes and Louis XI, that were hugely popular with Parisian audiences. Positioned between classical and Romantic drama, he softened classical form with more contemporary subject matter, and was elected to the Académie française in 1825.

entries.name: James K. Polk
entries.desc: James Knox Polk was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849. He was an advocate of American expansionism and Jacksonian democracy.
entries.tldr: The eleventh president of the United States, Polk took office in 1845 pledging to fulfill a single ambitious term focused on territorial expansion. He oversaw the annexation of Texas, negotiated a treaty with Britain fixing the Oregon boundary, and led the country into the Mexican-American War, which added California and the Southwest to the United States. True to his pledge, he declined to seek reelection and died just months after leaving office in 1849.

entries.name: Horace Mann
entries.desc: American educational reformer who championed public schooling, known as the Father of American Education.
entries.tldr: An American lawyer turned educational reformer, Mann became the first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education in 1837 and used the post to campaign nationally for free, tax-supported public schooling open to all children regardless of class. He professionalized teacher training through the first state normal schools and standardized curricula and school terms, work that earned him the title Father of the American Public School. He later served in Congress opposing the expansion of slavery.

entries.name: Jakob Steiner
entries.desc: Swiss mathematician who revolutionized synthetic geometry, developing projective methods without the use of coordinates.
entries.tldr: Jakob Steiner was a Swiss mathematician who worked primarily in geometry, revolutionizing synthetic geometry by developing projective methods without coordinates. His work on conic sections, algebraic curves, and inversive geometry earned him a professorship at Berlin and lasting influence in pure mathematics.

entries.name: Nicholas I of Russia
entries.desc: Nicholas I was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1825 to 1855. He was the third son of Paul I and younger brother of his predecessor, Alexander I.
entries.tldr: Nicholas I was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1825 to 1855. He was the third son of Paul I and younger brother of his predecessor, Alexander I. Nicholas's 29-year reign began with the failed Decembrist revolt.

entries.name: Princess Charlotte Augusta of Wales
entries.desc: Princess Charlotte of Wales was the only child of George, Prince of Wales, and Caroline of Brunswick, expected to ascend the British throne. She died in childbirth at the age of 21.
entries.tldr: Princess Charlotte of Wales was the only child of George, Prince of Wales, and Caroline of Brunswick. She was expected to ascend the British throne after the deaths of her grandfather, George III, and her father, but died in childbirth at the age of 21, predeceasing them both.

entries.name: Gaetano Donizetti
entries.desc: Italian composer of over 70 operas, a leading figure of the bel canto style alongside Rossini and Bellini.
entries.tldr: Born into a poor Bergamo family with no musical background, Donizetti composed at extraordinary speed, producing more than 70 operas, from comedies like Don Pasquale to tragedies. His 1835 masterpiece Lucia di Lammermoor, based on Walter Scott, became famous for its extended mad scene, still considered one of opera's great tests of a soprano. From the early 1840s he suffered from neurosyphilis, which progressively destroyed his mind; by 1846 he had to be institutionalized, and friends eventually brought him home to Bergamo, where he died paralyzed and largely unaware of his surroundings.

entries.name: Sojourner Truth
entries.desc: American abolitionist born into slavery who delivered the landmark ‘Ain’t I a Woman?’ speech at the 1851 Women’s Rights Convention.
entries.tldr: Born Isabella Bomefree into slavery in New York, she escaped with her infant daughter in 1826 and in 1828 sued successfully to recover her son, becoming the first Black woman to win such a case against a white man. In 1843 she renamed herself Sojourner Truth after a religious calling to travel and preach. At the 1851 Ohio women's rights convention she gave an extemporaneous speech, later popularized in a disputed dialect version as "Ain't I a Woman?" During the Civil War she recruited Black troops for the Union and afterward campaigned unsuccessfully for land grants to freed slaves.

entries.name: Mirza Ghalib
entries.desc: Mirza Ghalib was an Indian poet and letter writer of the Mughal Empire, writing in Persian and Urdu. His poetry addressed love, loss, philosophy, and socio-political upheaval.
entries.tldr: Mirza Asadullah Beg Khan, commonly known as Mirza Ghalib, was an Indian poet and letter writer of the Mughal Empire. Writing in Persian and Urdu during the final years of the Mughal Empire and the rise of British colonial rule, his poetry often addressed themes of love, loss, philosophy, the human condition, and socio-political disturbances with a depth and complexity that influenced the litera…

entries.name: Jeremias Gotthelf
entries.desc: Albert Bitzius was a Swiss novelist, best known by his pen name of Jeremias Gotthelf.
entries.tldr: The pen name of Albert Bitzius, a Swiss Reformed pastor who turned to fiction in his forties to reach his rural parishioners more effectively than sermons could. His novels and tales, most famously the eerie allegorical novella Die schwarze Spinne (The Black Spider), depicted Bernese peasant life with unsentimental realism while pressing moral and social reform, including temperance, thrift, and responsible farming, making him one of Switzerland's most distinctive nineteenth-century writers.

entries.name: Alexander Bestuzhev
entries.desc: Alexander Alexandrovich Bestuzhev was a Russian writer and Decembrist who, after the failed revolt, was exiled to the Caucasus where he wrote romantic fiction under the pseudonym Marlinsky.
entries.tldr: Alexander Alexandrovich Bestuzhev was a Russian writer and Decembrist. After the Decembrist revolt he was sent into exile to the Caucasus where the Russian Empire was waging war against the Circassians. There writing under the pseudonym Marlinsky he became known as a romantic poet, short story writer and novelist.

entries.name: Charles Wilkes
entries.desc: Charles Wilkes was an American naval officer, ship's captain, and explorer. He led the first United States Exploring Expedition (1838–1842).
entries.tldr: American naval officer who commanded the United States Exploring Expedition of 1838–1842, a four-year voyage of six ships that charted vast stretches of the Pacific and confirmed the existence of the Antarctic continent, later named Wilkes Land in his honor. The expedition's scientific collections helped found the Smithsonian Institution. His combative temperament led to a court-martial after the voyage, yet the survey stood as a landmark of American exploration. He later gained notoriety during the Civil War for the Trent Affair, seizing Confederate envoys from a British ship.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.desc: Auguste Comte was a French philosopher, mathematician and writer who formulated the doctrine of positivism and coined the term sociology.
entries.tldr: Isidore Auguste Marie François Xavier Comte was a French philosopher, mathematician and writer who formulated the doctrine of positivism. He is often regarded as the first philosopher of science in the modern sense of the term. Comte’s ideas were fundamental to the development of sociology, with him inventing the very term and treating the discipline as the crowning achievement of the sciences.

entries.name: William Lassell
entries.desc: English merchant-astronomer who improved the reflecting telescope and discovered Triton, Ariel, Umbriel, and Hyperion.
entries.tldr: Lassell was a self-taught English astronomer who made his fortune brewing beer and poured it into building some of the largest, most precise reflecting telescopes of his era. Working from his own private observatory, he discovered Neptune's moon Triton just weeks after Neptune itself was found in 1846, and later found Uranus's moons Ariel and Umbriel and Saturn's moon Hyperion. He pioneered an equatorial mounting that let telescopes track the sky's rotation. His work turned amateur wealth into lasting contributions to planetary astronomy.

entries.name: France Prešeren
entries.desc: Slovene Romantic poet whose sonnets and the poem Zdravljica established him as the national poet of Slovenia.
entries.tldr: Slovene Romantic poet whose sonnets and longer narrative poems established the modern Slovene literary language and are credited with shaping Slovene national identity in the 19th century. His best-known work, the Sonnet Wreath, is a technically demanding cycle of interlinked sonnets combining unrequited love with reflections on his people's history and fate. A stanza from his drinking song Zdravljica later became the lyrics of independent Slovenia's national anthem. Despite this later acclaim, his life was marked by unrequited love and struggles with alcohol and the Habsburg censors.

entries.name: Millard Fillmore
entries.desc: Millard Fillmore was the 13th president of the United States, serving from 1850 to 1853. He was the last president to be a member of the Whig Party while in the White House.
entries.tldr: Fillmore rose from a poor upstate New York upbringing to the presidency when Zachary Taylor died in office in 1850. He backed the Compromise of 1850 and signed the Fugitive Slave Act, forcing Northerners to help capture escaped slaves, which made him deeply unpopular even as it temporarily defused the sectional crisis over slavery. In 1852 he sent Commodore Perry's fleet to force open Japan's ports after two centuries of isolation, a move with far bigger consequences than most of his domestic record. Denied renomination, he ran again in 1856 as the nativist Know Nothing candidate.

entries.name: Niels Henrik Abel
entries.desc: Niels Henrik Abel was a Norwegian mathematician best known for the first complete proof that the general quintic equation cannot be solved in radicals, a problem unresolved for 250 years.
entries.tldr: Niels Henrik Abel was a Norwegian mathematician who made pioneering contributions in a variety of fields. His most famous single result is the first complete proof demonstrating the impossibility of solving the general quintic equation in radicals. This question was one of the outstanding open problems of his day, and had been unresolved for over 250 years.

entries.name: Hector Berlioz
entries.desc: French Romantic composer known for Symphonie fantastique and his influential innovations in orchestration.
entries.tldr: Berlioz fell into obsessive infatuation with Irish actress Harriet Smithson after seeing her play Ophelia, and channeled the heartbreak into the Symphonie fantastique, an autobiographical symphony depicting an opium-fueled artist's visions of love, execution, and a witches' sabbath. Smithson eventually heard the piece, met him, and the two married in 1833, though the marriage later collapsed. He also wrote the Treatise on Instrumentation and Modern Orchestration, a foundational text shaping how composers used the orchestra. He struggled for recognition at home, finding more acclaim abroad.

entries.name: Charles Sturm
entries.desc: French mathematician known for Sturm’s theorem, which counts the real roots of a polynomial within an interval.
entries.tldr: Jacques Charles François Sturm was a French mathematician who made a significant contribution to equation theory with Sturm’s theorem, an algorithm for counting the distinct real roots of a polynomial within a given interval. He also contributed to differential equations and mathematical physics.

entries.name: Charles-Augustin Sainte-Beuve
entries.desc: Foremost French literary critic of the 19th century, influential for his biographical method of contextualizing authors' lives and works.
entries.tldr: The dominant French literary critic of the 19th century, who argued that a work of literature could only be understood through close study of its author's biography, character, and milieu. His weekly essays, later collected as the Causeries du lundi, surveyed centuries of French letters with an authority that made or broke reputations in his own time. Marcel Proust later attacked this biographical method at length, arguing a book's true self is separate from its author's everyday self. He began his career as a Romantic poet before turning almost entirely to criticism.

entries.name: Franklin Pierce
entries.desc: Franklin Pierce was the 14th president of the United States, serving from 1853 to 1857. He signed the Kansas–Nebraska Act and enforced the Fugitive Slave Act.
entries.tldr: A New Hampshire lawyer and Mexican-American War general, Pierce was a Bowdoin College classmate of Nathaniel Hawthorne, who wrote his campaign biography. Weeks before his inauguration, his young son Benjamin was killed before his eyes in a train derailment, a tragedy that darkened his presidency and left his wife Jane in lasting seclusion. Sympathetic to Southern interests, he pushed through the Kansas-Nebraska Act, helping ignite the violent Bleeding Kansas crisis. He later drank heavily and is generally ranked among the least effective American presidents.

entries.name: William Rowan Hamilton
entries.desc: Sir William Rowan Hamilton was an Irish mathematician, physicist, and astronomer who made numerous major contributions to algebra, classical mechanics, and optics.
entries.tldr: An Irish child prodigy, Hamilton was appointed Royal Astronomer of Ireland while still an undergraduate at Trinity College Dublin. His reformulation of classical mechanics, Hamiltonian mechanics, became foundational to physics and later to quantum theory. His best-known breakthrough came in a flash of insight in 1843 while walking along Dublin's Royal Canal: he carved the defining equations of quaternions, a number system extending complex numbers, into the stone of Broom Bridge. Quaternions remain essential today for computer graphics and spacecraft orientation.

entries.name: Matthew Fontaine Maury
entries.desc: American oceanographer and naval officer who pioneered systematic charting of ocean winds and currents.
entries.tldr: A leg injury ended his active-duty Navy career, so he turned to studying the ocean itself, mining old ships' logbooks for wind and current data and persuading captains worldwide to record observations in a standardized format. His 1855 book The Physical Geography of the Sea is regarded as the first oceanography textbook, and his charts of winds and currents shortened Atlantic crossings by weeks. He also mapped the Atlantic seafloor, helping show a transatlantic cable was feasible. During the Civil War he resigned to serve the Confederacy, complicating his legacy.

entries.name: Alphonse Pyramus de Candolle
entries.desc: French-Swiss botanist who continued his father’s Prodromus and pioneered phytogeography and the study of plant origins.
entries.tldr: Alphonse Louis Pierre Pyramus de Candolle was a French-Swiss botanist, son of the Swiss botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle. He continued his father’s monumental Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis and made significant contributions to phytogeography and the scientific study of plant origins and distribution.

entries.name: Johan Vilhelm Snellman
entries.desc: Finland-Swedish philosopher and statesman regarded as one of the central figures who awakened Finnish national identity in the 19th century.
entries.tldr: Johan Vilhelm Snellman was a Finland-Swedish philosopher, journalist and statesman, and one of the leading figures of Fennoman nationalism in 19th-century Finland. A central exponent of Hegelian philosophy in the Nordic countries, he is regarded as one of the most important 'awakeners' of Finnish national identity, alongside Elias Lönnrot and J. L.

entries.name: Louis Agassiz
entries.desc: Jean Louis Rodolphe Agassiz was a Swiss-born American biologist and geologist who is recognized as a scholar of Earth's natural history.
entries.tldr: Trained in Switzerland and Germany, Agassiz first made his name studying fossil fish before turning to the glaciers of the Alps, where his fieldwork established that much of Europe had once been covered by ice sheets, founding the concept of past ice ages. After emigrating to the United States in 1846 to lecture at Harvard, he built one of the era's leading natural history museums. He was also a vocal proponent of polygenism, the now-discredited and racist theory that human races were separately created, an idea he used to support arguments controversial even among his contemporaries.

entries.name: Charles Darwin
entries.desc: English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed biology.
entries.tldr: English naturalist whose five-year voyage aboard HMS Beagle exposed him to the geology, fossils, and living species of South America and the Galápagos Islands that reshaped his understanding of life. In On the Origin of Species (1859) he laid out the theory of evolution by natural selection, arguing that species change over time as favorable variations are passed on and unfavorable ones are weeded out. The idea overturned centuries of belief in the fixity of species and provoked fierce controversy that continues in some quarters today.

entries.name: Frédéric Chopin
entries.desc: Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the early Romantic period who wrote almost exclusively for solo piano.
entries.tldr: Frédéric François Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the early Romantic period who wrote primarily for solo piano. He has maintained worldwide renown as a leading composer of his era whose “poetic genius was based on a professional technique that was without equal in his generation”.

entries.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
entries.desc: American author and abolitionist whose novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) galvanized the anti-slavery movement across the US and Britain.
entries.tldr: Daughter of the preacher Lyman Beecher, she was teaching in Cincinnati when exposure to fugitive slaves and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 drove her to write Uncle Tom's Cabin, serialized in 1851 before appearing as a book in 1852. It sold roughly 300,000 copies in the US within a year and over a million in Britain, becoming the century's best-selling novel after the Bible. Its depiction of families torn apart hardened Northern opinion and provoked rebuttals in the South. She is said to have been greeted by Lincoln in 1862 as "the little woman who made this great war," likely apocryphal.

entries.name: Urbain Le Verrier
entries.desc: French astronomer who predicted the existence and position of Neptune through mathematics alone, prompting its discovery in 1846.
entries.tldr: Le Verrier was a French mathematician-astronomer who in 1845-46 calculated that wobbles in Uranus's orbit must come from an undiscovered planet, working out its likely position using only Newtonian mechanics and pen and paper. He sent his coordinates to Berlin astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle, who found Neptune the first night he looked, within about a degree of the prediction. The feat was hailed as proof Newton's laws could reveal unseen worlds through calculation alone. He later ran the Paris Observatory and proposed a phantom planet "Vulcan" to explain Mercury's orbit.

entries.name: Samuel Smiles
entries.desc: Samuel Smiles was a British author and government reformer. His primary work, Self-Help (1859), promoted thrift and claimed that poverty was caused largely by irresponsible habits.
entries.tldr: Trained as a physician in Edinburgh, Smiles abandoned medicine for journalism, editing the reformist Leeds Times in the early 1840s while sympathizing with Chartist aims. By the 1850s he concluded that changed attitudes, not new laws, drove real progress, a philosophy crystallized in his 1859 bestseller Self-Help, which held up biographical examples of diligence and character. Dubbed "the bible of mid-Victorian liberalism," it shaped British political thought for generations. Smiles is now seen as a forerunner of the modern self-help and motivational genre.

entries.name: Empress Amélie of Brazil
entries.desc: Amélie of Leuchtenberg was Empress of Brazil as the wife of Pedro I, the first Emperor of Brazil.
entries.tldr: Amélie of Leuchtenberg was Empress of Brazil as the wife of Pedro I of Brazil. She was the daughter of Eugène de Beauharnais, stepson of Napoleon I. She accompanied Pedro I during his abdication and followed him to Portugal where he fought for his daughter Maria II's rights. She was noted for her charitable work and dignity during political upheaval.

entries.name: Ivar Andreas Aasen
entries.desc: Norwegian philologist and poet who assembled Nynorsk, one of Norway's two official written language forms, from regional dialects.
entries.tldr: Ivar Andreas Aasen was a Norwegian philologist, lexicographer, playwright, and poet. He is best known for having assembled one of the two official written versions of the Norwegian language, Nynorsk, from various dialects.

entries.name: Johann Jakob Bachofen
entries.desc: Johann Jakob Bachofen was a Swiss antiquarian, jurist, philologist, anthropologist, and professor of Roman law at the University of Basel from 1841 to 1844.
entries.tldr: A Swiss jurist and classical scholar who taught Roman law at the University of Basel, Bachofen is best remembered for Das Mutterrecht (1861), a sweeping study of ancient myth and law arguing that human societies had passed through an early matriarchal stage of “mother right” before patriarchy took hold. Though later anthropologists largely rejected its evidentiary basis, the theory profoundly influenced Friedrich Engels, Freud, and later feminist and anthropological thought.

entries.name: John A. Macdonald
entries.desc: Sir John Alexander Macdonald was the first prime minister of Canada, serving from 1867 to 1873 and from 1878 until his death in 1891. He was the dominant figure of Canadian Confederation.
entries.tldr: Sir John Alexander Macdonald was the first prime minister of Canada, serving from 1867 to 1873 and from 1878 until his death in 1891. He was the dominant figure of Canadian Confederation, and had a political career that spanned almost half a century.

entries.name: Charlotte Brontë
entries.desc: Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, the elder sister of Emily, Anne and Branwell Brontë, best known for her novel Jane Eyre.
entries.tldr: Charlotte Nicholls, commonly known by her maiden name Charlotte Brontë, was an English novelist and poet, and was the elder sister of Emily, Anne and Branwell Brontë. She is best known for her novel Jane Eyre, which was first published under the pseudonym Currer Bell. Jane Eyre was a great success on publication, and has since been acknowledged as a classic of English literature.

entries.name: Baháʼu'lláh
entries.desc: Iranian founder of the Baháʼí Faith who proclaimed a new divine revelation in 1863 after decades of exile.
entries.tldr: Iranian nobleman born Mirza Husayn-Ali who became the founder and central prophetic figure of the Baháʼí Faith. A follower of the Báb, he was imprisoned and exiled by the Persian and Ottoman authorities through a series of cities — Baghdad, Istanbul, Edirne, and finally the prison city of Acre — over four decades. In 1863, in a garden outside Baghdad remembered as Ridván, he declared himself the messianic figure the Báb had foretold, and went on to write the faith's central scripture. His teachings on the unity of religions spread despite his lifelong confinement.

entries.name: Albert von Kölliker
entries.desc: Swiss anatomist, physiologist, and histologist who co-founded modern histology and established that nerve fibers are extensions of nerve cells.
entries.tldr: Albert von Kölliker was a Swiss anatomist, physiologist, and histologist who co-founded modern histology and established that nerve fibers are extensions of nerve cells. He taught at Würzburg for decades and authored influential textbooks on microscopic anatomy that shaped the discipline through the 19th century.

entries.name: Carl Nägeli
entries.desc: Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli was a Swiss botanist. He studied cell division and pollination but became known as the man who discouraged Gregor Mendel from further work on genetics.
entries.tldr: Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli was a Swiss botanist. He studied cell division and pollination but became known as the man who discouraged Gregor Mendel from further work on genetics. He rejected natural selection as a mechanism of evolution, favouring orthogenesis, though the term was only coined in 1893, two years after his death, driven by a supposed "inner perfecting principle".

entries.name: William III of the Netherlands
entries.desc: King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg from 1849 until 1890, also Duke of Limburg until 1866, reigning for 41 years.
entries.tldr: William III was King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg from 1849 until his death in 1890, and was also the Duke of Limburg from 1849 until the abolition of the duchy in 1866. Having reigned for 41 years, he is the second-longest reigning Dutch monarch, only surpassed by his daughter, Wilhelmina.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.desc: American writer and philosopher known for Walden, on simple living, and the essay "Civil Disobedience."
entries.tldr: Henry David Thoreau was an American naturalist, essayist, poet, and philosopher. A leading transcendentalist, he is best known for his book Walden, a reflection upon simple living in natural surroundings, and his essay "Civil Disobedience", an argument in favor of citizen disobedience against an unjust state.

entries.name: Báb
entries.desc: Iranian religious leader who founded Bábism in 1844 and is revered as a central figure of the Baháʼí Faith.
entries.tldr: Iranian merchant born Siyyid Ali-Muhammad Shirazi, who in 1844 declared himself the Báb, or "Gate," to a promised messianic figure, launching the Bábí movement that broke from Twelver Shia Islam. His teachings attracted a fervent following that alarmed clerical and state authorities in Qajar Persia. After followers were implicated in uprisings and an attempt on the shah's life, he was executed by firing squad in Tabriz in 1850; a famous account holds the first volley severed his ropes without killing him. He is venerated in the Baháʼí Faith as herald of Baháʼu'lláh.

entries.name: Annibale de Gasparis
entries.desc: Italian astronomer who discovered nine asteroids and contributed to theoretical astronomy from the Naples Observatory.
entries.tldr: Italian astronomer who worked for decades at the Capodimonte Observatory in Naples, where he discovered nine asteroids between 1849 and 1865, beginning with 10 Hygiea, the first asteroid ever found by an Italian observer. His discoveries, made through painstaking visual comparison of star charts against the night sky, came during the mid-nineteenth-century boom in asteroid hunting that followed the identification of Ceres. Beyond observation, he contributed to the theoretical mathematics of orbit determination used to confirm and track newly found bodies.

entries.name: Gottfried Keller
entries.desc: Gottfried Keller was a Swiss poet and writer of German literature. Best known for his novel Green Henry, he became one of the most popular narrators of literary realism in the late 19th century.
entries.tldr: Expelled from school as a boy and raised by a struggling widowed mother, he trained as a landscape painter in Munich before abandoning art for literature in his thirties. He spent years in Berlin establishing himself as a writer, then returned to Zurich in 1861 to serve fifteen years as the canton's state secretary while still writing. His semi-autobiographical novel Green Henry, revised over decades, follows a young artist's failures and drew praise from Nietzsche, who reportedly called him the only living German writer worth reading. He also wrote the novella cycle The People of Seldwyla.

entries.name: George Eliot
entries.desc: Mary Ann Evans, known by her pen name George Eliot, was an English novelist, poet, journalist, and translator of the Victorian era. Her seven novels include Middlemarch and The Mill on the Floss.
entries.tldr: Mary Ann Evans, known by her pen name George Eliot, was an English novelist, poet, journalist, translator, and one of the leading writers of the Victorian era. She wrote seven novels: Adam Bede (1859), The Mill on the Floss (1860), Silas Marner (1861), Romola (1862–1863), Felix Holt, the Radical (1866), Middlemarch (1871–1872) and Daniel Deronda (1876). Her novels are known for their realism, p…

entries.name: Clara Schumann
entries.desc: Clara Schumann was a German virtuoso pianist, composer and piano teacher who had a 61-year concert career and reshaped the format of the piano recital.
entries.tldr: Clara Josephine Schumann was a German virtuoso pianist, composer, and piano teacher. Regarded as one of the most distinguished pianists of the Romantic era, she exerted her influence over the course of a 61-year concert career, changing the format and repertoire of the piano recital by lessening the importance of purely virtuosic works. She also composed solo piano pieces, a piano concerto, cha…

entries.name: Florence Nightingale
entries.desc: Founder of modern nursing and a pioneer of statistics in public health.
entries.tldr: English social reformer regarded as the founder of modern nursing, whose work organizing care for wounded soldiers during the Crimean War earned her the nickname 'the Lady with the Lamp' for her nighttime rounds of the wards. Appalled by unsanitary conditions that killed far more soldiers from disease than combat, she pushed through hygiene reforms that sharply cut mortality and used statistical charts, including an early pie chart, to make her case to policymakers. After the war she founded a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital, establishing nursing as a trained profession.

entries.name: Harriet Tubman
entries.desc: American abolitionist who escaped slavery and led some 70 people to freedom via the Underground Railroad, and later served as a Union spy.
entries.tldr: Born Araminta Ross into slavery in Maryland, she suffered a head injury from an overseer that caused lifelong seizures and visions she read as divine guidance. After escaping in 1849 she returned south some thirteen times as an Underground Railroad conductor despite a bounty on her head. In 1863 she became the first woman to lead an armed U.S. military raid, freeing nearly 700 enslaved people along the Combahee River in one night. She later scouted for the Union Army, championed women's suffrage, and died in a home for the elderly she herself had helped found.

entries.name: Pauline Viardot
entries.desc: Pauline Viardot was a French dramatic mezzo-soprano, composer and pedagogue of Spanish descent.
entries.tldr: Born into opera's first great dynasty, daughter of tenor Manuel García and sister of soprano Maria Malibran, Pauline trained as a pianist under Liszt before turning to singing after her sister's early death. She became one of Europe's leading mezzo-sopranos, creating the role of Fides in Meyerbeer's Le Prophete and inspiring Berlioz to revive Gluck's Orphee for her voice. Offstage she ran a salon for Brahms and Sand, and composed operettas. For forty years novelist Ivan Turgenev was infatuated with her, trailing the Viardots across Europe and living alongside her and her husband.

entries.name: Henri-Frédéric Amiel
entries.desc: Henri Frédéric Amiel was a Swiss moral philosopher, poet, and critic.
entries.tldr: A Swiss academic who taught aesthetics and later moral philosophy at Geneva, orphaned young by his mother's tuberculosis and his father's suicide, Amiel felt himself a failure despite his post. His real work was private: a diary kept almost daily from 1847 until 1881, filling thousands of pages with unsparing self-analysis on doubt, love, and the gap between thought and action. Published posthumously as Fragments d'un journal intime, it became a European sensation, translated by novelist Mary Augusta Ward. It remains the work by which he is remembered, more than anything he published in life.

entries.name: Richard Francis Burton
entries.desc: Richard Francis Burton was a British explorer, army officer, writer, and scholar, famed for his travels across Asia, Africa, and South America and his fluency in up to 29 languages.
entries.tldr: Sir Richard Francis Burton was a British explorer, army officer, writer and scholar. He was famed for his travels and explorations in Asia, Africa and South America, as well as his extensive knowledge of languages and cultures, speaking up to 29 different languages.

entries.name: Charles Tupper
entries.desc: Sir Charles Tupper, 1st Baronet, was a Canadian Father of Confederation who served as the sixth prime minister of Canada from May 1 to July 8, 1896.
entries.tldr: Sir Charles Tupper, 1st Baronet, was a Canadian Father of Confederation who served as the sixth prime minister of Canada from May 1 to July 8, 1896. As the premier of Nova Scotia from 1864 to 1867, he led Nova Scotia into Confederation.

entries.name: John Abbott
entries.desc: Sir John Joseph Caldwell Abbott was the third prime minister of Canada, serving from 1891 to 1892. He held office as the leader of the Conservative Party.
entries.tldr: A Montreal lawyer and longtime member of Canada's Parliament, Abbott became the country's third prime minister in 1891 almost by default, chosen as a compromise candidate after the sudden death of Sir John A. Macdonald left the Conservatives without an obvious successor. He led from the Senate rather than the Commons, the only Canadian prime minister ever to do so, and spent his brief eighteen months managing party divisions and his own declining health. Already suffering from the brain cancer that would kill him, he resigned in 1892 and died the following year.

entries.name: Nikolay Danilevsky
entries.desc: Nikolay Yakovlevich Danilevsky was a Russian naturalist, economist, ethnologist, philosopher, historian and ideologue of pan-Slavism and the Slavophile movement.
entries.tldr: A botanist turned Russian fisheries expert, Danilevsky is remembered for one book, Russia and Europe (1869), arguing civilizations behave like organisms with their own birth, flowering, and decline, not stages on one universal path. He cast the Slavic world as a distinct 'cultural-historical type' fated to clash with a declining West, and called for a Slavic federation centered on Constantinople. The book founded pan-Slavism and Eurasianism and anticipated Oswald Spengler's cyclical theory of civilizations. As a young man he was arrested alongside Dostoevsky in the Petrashevsky circle.

entries.name: Edmond de Goncourt
entries.desc: Edmond Louis Antoine Huot de Goncourt was a French writer, literary critic, art critic, book publisher and the founder of the Académie Goncourt.
entries.tldr: French writer who, with his brother Jules, pioneered a documentary, unsparingly detailed style of naturalist fiction, producing novels such as Germinie Lacerteux that influenced Émile Zola and the naturalist movement. Together the brothers also kept an extensive journal recording Parisian literary and artistic life, a vivid firsthand record of the era's salons and rivalries. After Jules's death in 1870, Edmond continued writing alone and used his estate to endow the Académie Goncourt, whose annual Prix Goncourt remains France's most prestigious literary award.

entries.name: Alexander Mackenzie
entries.desc: Alexander Mackenzie (1822–1892) was the second prime minister of Canada, serving from 1873 to 1878. A journalist and stonemason by trade, he was the first Liberal PM of Canada.
entries.tldr: Alexander Mackenzie (1822–1892) was the second prime minister of Canada. He began his career as a stonemason and journalist, entering politics in the 1860s and becoming Liberal Party leader. His government introduced the secret ballot and the Supreme Court of Canada.

entries.name: Étienne Lenoir
entries.desc: Jean Joseph Étienne Lenoir was a Belgian-French engineer who invented the internal combustion engine in 1858.
entries.tldr: Jean Joseph Étienne Lenoir was a Belgian-French engineer who invented the internal combustion engine in 1858. Prior designs for such engines were patented as early as 1807 and 1854. His engine used illuminating gas and was the first to be produced commercially, with several hundred built before 1865.

entries.name: Mackenzie Bowell
entries.desc: Sir Mackenzie Bowell was the fifth prime minister of Canada, serving from 1894 to 1896.
entries.tldr: An Ontario newspaper publisher and long-serving cabinet minister, Bowell became Canada's fifth prime minister in 1894, again largely by default after a previous succession arrangement collapsed.
