His seventeen months in office were dominated by the Manitoba Schools Question, a bitter dispute over funding for French Catholic schools that split his cabinet, seven of whose members resigned in revolt in early 1896. He was forced to step aside for Charles Tupper shortly before that year's election, which the Conservatives lost to Wilfrid Laurier's Liberals.

entries.name: William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin
entries.desc: William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin was a Scottish mathematician, mathematical physicist and engineer.
entries.tldr: Thomson was a Scottish mathematical physicist and engineer whose work spanned thermodynamics, electricity, and telecommunications. He developed the absolute temperature scale that bears his title, Kelvin, and helped formulate the second law of thermodynamics. As chief scientific consultant on the first transatlantic telegraph cable, he solved the signal-degradation problems that had doomed earlier attempts, making the project commercially viable. His prominence earned him a peerage as Baron Kelvin in 1892.

entries.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
entries.desc: Indian political leader, founding member of the Indian National Congress, and the first Indian elected to the British Parliament.
entries.tldr: Indian scholar and political leader known as the 'Grand Old Man of India' for his decades of work founding and leading the Indian National Congress. In 1892 he became the first Indian, and first person of Asian descent, elected to the British Parliament, sitting as a Liberal MP for a London constituency. His book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India developed the influential 'drain theory,' arguing that British colonial policy systematically transferred India's wealth to Britain. His writings and activism laid groundwork for the later independence movement.

entries.name: Johann Jakob Balmer
entries.desc: Johann Jakob Balmer was a Swiss mathematician best known for his work in physics, the Balmer series of the hydrogen atom.
entries.tldr: A Swiss schoolteacher with no formal training in physics, Balmer was in his sixties, teaching at a girls' school in Basel, when in 1885 he found a simple formula that precisely predicted the wavelengths of hydrogen's visible spectral lines. He had no explanation for why it worked, having derived it purely by pattern-matching against data supplied by a colleague. The Balmer series later proved crucial evidence for Niels Bohr's 1913 quantum model of the atom, which finally explained why hydrogen's electron produced exactly those wavelengths. He published little else of note.

entries.name: Conrad Ferdinand Meyer
entries.desc: Swiss poet and historical novelist, a master of literary realism best known for narrative ballads like “Die Füße im Feuer.”
entries.tldr: Conrad Ferdinand Meyer was a Swiss poet and historical novelist, a master of literary realism who is mainly remembered for stirring narrative ballads like “Die Füße im Feuer.” His novellas, set in the Italian Renaissance and Swiss history, combine psychological depth with precise, restrained prose.

entries.name: Stanislao Cannizzaro
entries.desc: Stanislao Cannizzaro was an Italian chemist. He is famous for the Cannizzaro reaction and for his influential role in the atomic-weight deliberations of the Karlsruhe Congress in 1860.
entries.tldr: Trained first in medicine before turning to chemistry, the Palermo-born Cannizzaro discovered in 1853 the reaction bearing his name, in which a non-enolizable aldehyde treated with base disproportionates into an alcohol and an acid, as he showed by converting benzaldehyde into benzyl alcohol and potassium benzoate. His lasting influence came at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress, called to resolve chaos over atomic weights. On the final day, reprints of his 1858 paper reviving Avogadro's hypothesis were distributed, swaying chemists toward a consistent system of atomic weights still used today.

entries.name: Johanna Spyri
entries.desc: Johanna Spyri was a Swiss author of novels, notably children's stories. She wrote the popular book Heidi.
entries.tldr: A Swiss pastor's wife who began writing relatively late in life to support charitable causes, Spyri achieved lasting fame with Heidi, published in two parts in 1880 and 1881, the story of an orphaned girl sent to live with her reclusive grandfather in the Swiss Alps. The novel's vivid depiction of alpine landscape, combined with its themes of homesickness and healing, made it an enduring international success, translated into dozens of languages and repeatedly adapted for film. She wrote roughly fifty other stories, though none matched Heidi's popularity, until her death in 1901.

entries.name: Arnold Böcklin
entries.desc: Arnold Böcklin was a Swiss Symbolist painter. His five versions of the Isle of the Dead inspired works by several late Romantic composers.
entries.tldr: Swiss Symbolist painter best known for Isle of the Dead, a haunting image of a boat approaching a rocky, tomb-studded island that he painted in five versions between 1880 and 1886 after a widow commissioned a "picture for dreaming." The painting became one of the most widely reproduced images of its era and directly inspired Sergei Rachmaninoff's tone poem of the same name. Böcklin's dreamlike, mythologically charged landscapes, populated with fauns, nymphs, and centaurs, anticipated the Surrealists, and painters such as Giorgio de Chirico and Salvador Dalí later acknowledged his influence.

entries.name: John Hanning Speke
entries.desc: John Hanning Speke was an English explorer and army officer known for his search for the source of the Nile. With Richard Burton, he was the first European to reach Lake Victoria.
entries.tldr: John Hanning Speke was an English explorer and army officer who made three exploratory expeditions to Africa. He is most associated with the search for the source of the Nile and, with Richard Burton, was the first European to reach Lake Victoria.

entries.name: Petko Slaveykov
entries.desc: Petko Rachov Slaveykov was a Bulgarian poet, publicist, politician and folklorist.
entries.tldr: Born in Tarnovo, he renamed himself after the nightingales he heard as a boy and became a chief architect of modern Bulgarian culture, founding its children's literature and collecting thousands of folk sayings and songs. He wrote revolutionary verse, was imprisoned after the 1876 April Uprising, and lost his manuscripts and folklore archive when Ottoman troops burned Stara Zagora. Freed by Russian forces in 1877-78, he later fought for a democratic constitution as a deputy in Bulgaria's first Grand National Assembly.

entries.name: Henry Dunant
entries.desc: Henry Dunant was a Swiss humanitarian, businessman, social activist, and co-founder of the Red Cross. His humanitarian efforts won him the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
entries.tldr: A Swiss businessman traveling on unrelated matters, Dunant stumbled onto the aftermath of the 1859 Battle of Solferino, where some 40,000 casualties lay largely unattended, and organized locals, regardless of nationality, to nurse the wounded. His book A Memory of Solferino proposed neutral relief societies in every nation, leading to the Red Cross's founding in 1863 and the first Geneva Convention. He later went bankrupt from an unrelated venture, resigned in disgrace, and spent decades in poverty in a Swiss hospice, where a journalist found him; in 1901 he won the first Nobel Peace Prize.

entries.name: Louise of the Netherlands
entries.desc: Louise of the Netherlands, also called Lovisa, was Queen of Sweden and Norway from 1859 until her death in 1871 as wife of King Charles XV & IV.
entries.tldr: Louise of the Netherlands, also called Lovisa, was Queen of Sweden and Norway from 8 July 1859 until her death in 1871 as the wife of King Charles XV & IV. She was born a Dutch princess and became one of the most beloved queens of Sweden, known for her charm and grace at court. Her early death at age 42 was mourned widely across Scandinavia.

entries.name: Asaph Hall
entries.desc: American astronomer who in 1877 discovered Phobos and Deimos, the two moons of Mars, and determined the orbital mechanics of planetary satellites.
entries.tldr: American astronomer at the United States Naval Observatory who in August 1877 discovered both moons of Mars, Phobos and Deimos, during a systematic search timed to a close opposition of the planet. He had nearly abandoned the search after repeated failed nights before his wife, Angelina Stickney, urged him to continue, and he found Deimos the following night. His subsequent orbital calculations for the two tiny, irregularly shaped moons became foundational data for later study of Mars's satellite system. The discovery made him one of the best-known American astronomers of his generation.

entries.name: Carl Schurz
entries.desc: Carl Schurz was a German-American revolutionary who became a prominent American statesman, journalist and reformer after emigrating following the 1848–1849 German revolutions.
entries.tldr: Carl Christian Schurz was a German-American revolutionary and an American statesman, journalist, and reformer. He migrated to the United States after the German revolutions of 1848–1849 and became a prominent member of the newly-forming Republican Party. After serving as a Union general in the American Civil War, he helped found the short-lived Liberal Republican Party and became a prominent ad…

entries.name: Mary Harris Jones
entries.desc: Mary G. Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones from 1897 onward, was an American labor organizer, schoolteacher, and dressmaker who became a prominent union organizer, community organizer, and activist.
entries.tldr: Mary G. Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones from 1897 onward, was an American labor organizer, schoolteacher, and dressmaker who became a prominent union organizer, community organizer, and activist. She helped coordinate major strikes, secure bans on child labor, and co-founded the trade union Industrial Workers of the World (IWW).

entries.name: Jules de Goncourt
entries.desc: French writer who co-authored novels and art criticism with his brother Edmond; died at 39 in Paris.
entries.tldr: Jules Alfred Huot de Goncourt was a French writer who published books together with his brother Edmond, including novels, art criticism, and journals of Parisian literary life. Born and dying in Paris, Jules died at the age of 39 from a stroke brought on by syphilis. The Goncourt Academy and its literary prize were established in his and his brother's honor.

entries.name: Leo von Caprivi
entries.desc: Georg Leo Graf von Caprivi de Caprara de Montecuccoli was a German general and statesman. He served as the imperial chancellor of the German Empire from March 1890 to October 1894, succeeding longtime chancellor Otto von Bismarck.
entries.tldr: A career Prussian army officer with no political experience, Caprivi was picked by Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1890 specifically because he was not Bismarck, whose long domination of policy the young emperor wanted to end. As chancellor, Caprivi pursued a ‘New Course’ that lowered protective tariffs to build a network of trade treaties across Europe and let Bismarck's anti-socialist laws lapse. He also concluded the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty with Britain, trading German colonial claims in East Africa for the North Sea island of Heligoland, before being dismissed in 1894.

entries.name: Johann Martin Schleyer
entries.desc: Johann Martin Schleyer was a German Catholic priest who invented the constructed language Volapük. His official name was “Martin Schleyer”; he added the name “Johann” unofficially.
entries.tldr: A German Catholic priest serving a rural parish, Schleyer conceived the constructed language Volapük in 1879, reportedly after a sleepless night in which the idea came to him as a kind of religious calling. Built from heavily altered English, German, and Romance vocabulary wrapped in an elaborate original grammar, Volapük spread rapidly in the 1880s, acquiring hundreds of thousands of speakers and dozens of dedicated journals across Europe and the Americas. Its complexity and Schleyer's insistence on personal control alienated speakers, most of whom defected to the simpler, newer Esperanto.

entries.name: Wilhelm Busch
entries.desc: Heinrich Christian Wilhelm Busch was a German humorist, poet, illustrator, and painter. He published wildly innovative illustrated tales that remain influential to this day.
entries.tldr: Busch was a German illustrator and poet whose verse tales paired comic drawings with rhymed narration depicting mischief and gruesome comeuppance. His most famous work, Max and Moritz (1865), follows two boys through cruel pranks that each end in brutal punishment, and its picture-story format proved hugely influential. It inspired Rudolph Dirks's 1897 strip The Katzenjammer Kids, which introduced conventions like speech balloons, earning Busch the title "forefather of comics." Translated into languages from Japanese to Latin in his lifetime, his dark humor still shapes German culture.

entries.name: Edwin Arnold
entries.desc: English poet and journalist best known for The Light of Asia, a verse biography of the Buddha.
entries.tldr: English poet and journalist who spent years teaching in colonial India before returning to London to work as a newspaper editor. His 1879 narrative poem The Light of Asia retold the life and teachings of the Buddha in verse for a Victorian English readership, becoming a surprise bestseller that introduced Buddhism to many Western readers for the first time. The poem's popularity contributed to a broader wave of European interest in Asian religion and philosophy in the late 19th century. He was knighted in 1888 in recognition of his literary and journalistic career.

entries.name: José Echegaray
entries.desc: José Echegaray y Eizaguirre was a Spanish civil engineer, mathematician, statesman, and dramatist. He was awarded the 1904 Nobel Prize in Literature.
entries.tldr: José Echegaray y Eizaguirre was a Spanish civil engineer, mathematician, statesman, and one of the leading Spanish dramatists of the last quarter of the 19th century. He was awarded the 1904 Nobel Prize in Literature “in recognition of the numerous and brilliant compositions which, in an individual and original manner, have revived the great traditions of the Spanish drama”.

entries.name: Ernesto Teodoro Moneta
entries.desc: Ernesto Teodoro Moneta was an Italian journalist, nationalist, revolutionary soldier and later a pacifist and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate. He adopted the motto In varietate unitas!
entries.tldr: Italian journalist and former soldier who fought in several wars of Italian unification before undergoing a conversion to pacifism later in life. As editor of the Milan newspaper Il Secolo, he campaigned for international arbitration and disarmament, arguing that lasting peace required binding agreements between states rather than a balance of military power. He co-founded the Lombard Union for Peace and International Arbitration and became a prominent voice of the European peace movement. In 1907 he won the Nobel Peace Prize, the first Italian laureate.

entries.name: Élie Ducommun
entries.desc: Élie Ducommun was a Swiss peace activist. He was a Nobel laureate, awarded the 1902 Nobel Peace Prize, which he shared with Charles Albert Gobat.
entries.tldr: Ducommun was a Swiss journalist and lifelong pacifist who spent decades editing newspapers and campaigning for arbitration between nations as an alternative to war. He served as the first honorary secretary of the International Peace Bureau in Bern, coordinating peace societies across Europe and helping organize international peace congresses. His tireless, unpaid organizational work was credited with holding the fragmented peace movement together amid rising nationalist tension. In 1902 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with fellow Swiss pacifist Charles Albert Gobat.

entries.name: Alexander Emanuel Agassiz
entries.desc: Alexander Emmanuel Rodolphe Agassiz was an American scientist and engineer. He was the son of Louis Agassiz and stepson of Elizabeth Cabot Agassiz.
entries.tldr: American zoologist and mining engineer, the son of the naturalist Louis Agassiz, who used a fortune made running the Calumet and Hecla copper mine in Michigan to fund a second career in science. He became a leading authority on marine invertebrates, particularly echinoderms and coral reefs, and led oceanographic expeditions through the Pacific and Caribbean. He directed and heavily funded Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology, founded by his father, greatly expanding its collections. His reef studies helped refine Darwin's theory of coral atoll formation.

entries.name: Leopold II of Belgium
entries.desc: Leopold II was the second king of the Belgians from 1865 to 1909, and the founder and sole owner of the Congo Free State, infamous for brutal exploitation of its people.
entries.tldr: Leopold II was the second king of the Belgians from 1865 to 1909, and the founder and sole owner of the Congo Free State from 1885 to 1908. His regime in the Congo was responsible for the deaths of millions through forced labour and atrocities. International pressure eventually forced him to cede the territory to Belgium in 1908.

entries.name: Wilhelm Steinitz
entries.desc: Bohemian-Austrian chess player who became the first official World Chess Champion (1886–1894) and revolutionized chess theory.
entries.tldr: Steinitz was a Bohemian-Austrian chess master who held the unofficial title of world's strongest player for two decades before becoming the first official World Chess Champion in 1886. He rejected the swashbuckling attacking style that dominated 19th-century chess, developing a scientific theory of small positional advantages and defense that underpins modern strategy. He held the title until 1894, when his student-turned-rival Emanuel Lasker beat him. He died in poverty in New York in 1900, his final years marked by mental illness.

entries.name: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
entries.desc: British Liberal Prime Minister 1905–1908 who granted self-government to the former Boer republics and was the first PM officially titled as such.
entries.tldr: As Liberal opposition leader during the Boer War, he broke with pro-war sentiment in 1901 by condemning British internment camps for Boer civilians as methods of barbarism, a remark that scandalized imperialists but proved prescient once camp death tolls emerged. As prime minister from 1905, he used an Order in Council to grant the former Boer republics self-government, bypassing a hostile House of Lords; South Africa's first premier credited this act with healing the war's wounds. Already ill, he resigned days before his 1908 death, the only PM to die at 10 Downing Street.

entries.name: Norman Lockyer
entries.desc: Sir Joseph Norman Lockyer was an English scientist and astronomer. Along with the French scientist Pierre Janssen, he is credited with discovering the gas helium.
entries.tldr: Sir Joseph Norman Lockyer was an English scientist and astronomer. Along with the French scientist Pierre Janssen, he is credited with discovering the gas helium. Lockyer also is remembered for being the founder and first editor of the influential journal Nature.

entries.name: Sophia of Nassau
entries.desc: Sophia of Nassau was Queen of Sweden and Norway as wife of King Oscar II, the longest-serving queen in Swedish history until 2011.
entries.tldr: Sophia of Nassau, also Sofia, was Queen of Sweden and Norway as the wife of King Oscar II. She was Queen of Sweden for 35 years, longer than anyone before her, and the longest-serving queen until 2011, when she was surpassed by Queen Silvia. She is also the most recent woman to have been officially Dowager Queen of Sweden.

entries.name: Paul Morphy
entries.desc: American chess prodigy who dominated world chess in the late 1850s, widely regarded as the first unofficial World Chess Champion before retiring from the game.
entries.tldr: A New Orleans prodigy who learned chess just by watching his family play, Morphy earned a law degree before he was old enough to practice it, then swept the First American Chess Congress in 1857. His 1858 European tour became legendary: he outplayed Adolf Anderssen and famously beat two aristocrats in a lightning game played from a box at the Paris Opera. His swift, attacking style anticipated ideas chess theory would not formalize for decades. He quit at 22 and spent his last years a recluse, tormented by delusions that relatives wanted to poison him.

entries.name: Henry Becque
entries.desc: French dramatist known for naturalistic plays depicting Parisian bourgeois life.
entries.tldr: Often called the father of French Naturalist drama, Becque wrote plays stripped of moralizing plots or tidy endings, presenting unvarnished slices of life instead. His 1882 Les Corbeaux, a bitter portrait of relatives circling an inheritance after a man's death, so unsettled audiences with its refusal to punish its selfish characters that it ran only three performances. His 1885 La Parisienne, following a married woman juggling two lovers, was similarly scandalous at first. Both went unappreciated until a decade later, when younger writers hailed him as a major influence on realist theatre.

entries.name: Henry Draper
entries.desc: Henry Draper was an American medical doctor and amateur astronomer. He is best known today as a pioneer of astrophotography.
entries.tldr: An American physician who treated astronomy as a serious sideline, Draper built his own observatory and, working with his wealthy wife Anna, achieved photographic firsts: the first photograph of a star's spectrum, Vega, in 1872, and, in 1880, the first photograph ever taken of a nebula, Orion. He intended a comprehensive photographic catalogue of stellar spectra but died suddenly at 45 with it unfinished. Anna then funded Harvard Observatory's continuation of the work in his memory, producing the Henry Draper Catalogue, still a reference in stellar classification today.

entries.name: Johannes Diderik van der Waals
entries.desc: Dutch physicist awarded the 1910 Nobel Prize in Physics for his equation of state describing the behavior of gases and liquids.
entries.tldr: Johannes Diderik van der Waals was a Dutch theoretical physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1910 "for his work on the equation of state for gases and liquids." Van der Waals started his career as a schoolteacher, before becoming the first physics professor of the University of Amsterdam when its status was upgraded to Municipal University in 1877.

entries.name: Max Bruch
entries.desc: German Romantic composer best known for his Violin Concerto No. 1 in G minor, a cornerstone of the violin repertoire.
entries.tldr: Though remembered today almost entirely for one piece, his 1866 Violin Concerto No. 1 in G minor, he was a prolific composer of operas, choral works, and symphonies, and conducted orchestras across Germany, England, and the United States. He revised the concerto extensively on the advice of virtuoso Joseph Joachim before it reached its standard form. His other enduring piece, Kol Nidrei, sets a traditional Jewish melody for cello and orchestra, though Bruch himself was Protestant and simply admired the tune. He sold the manuscript outright, earning little from the work that made him famous.

entries.name: Liliʻuokalani
entries.desc: Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from 1891 until its overthrow in 1893. She composed "Aloha ʻOe" and other works.
entries.tldr: Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and the last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from January 29, 1891, until the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom on January 17, 1893, in a coup that was led by the Committee of Safety, composed of seven foreign residents and six Hawaiian Kingdom subjects of American descent in Honolulu. The composer of "Aloha ʻOe" and numerous other work…

entries.name: John Hay
entries.desc: John Milton Hay was an American statesman and official whose career in government stretched over almost half a century. He served as United States Secretary of State under Presidents William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt.
entries.tldr: A former private secretary to Abraham Lincoln who co-authored a monumental ten-volume biography of him, Hay went on to a diplomatic career culminating in his appointment as secretary of state under both William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt. In that role he negotiated the Open Door Policy notes seeking equal trading access to China, and the treaties securing American rights to build the Panama Canal after Panama's engineered secession from Colombia. He had earlier served as ambassador to Britain, remaining in office until his death in 1905.

entries.name: Giovanni Losi
entries.desc: Giovanni Losi was an Italian Catholic priest and Comboni missionary who served in South Sudan, ministering under extreme hardship in Central Africa.
entries.tldr: Giovanni Losi M.C.C.I. was an Italian Catholic priest and member of the Comboni Missionaries of the Heart of Jesus. He spent the majority of his ministry in South Sudan, working in difficult conditions in Central Africa. He is venerated for his dedication to spreading Christianity and providing pastoral care in remote regions of Africa.

entries.name: Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky
entries.desc: Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five." He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period.
entries.tldr: Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian composer, one of the group known as "The Five." He was an innovator of Russian music in the Romantic period and strove to achieve a uniquely Russian musical identity, often in deliberate defiance of the established conventions of Western music.

entries.name: Victoria, Princess Royal
entries.desc: Victoria, Princess Royal was German Empress and Queen of Prussia as the wife of Frederick III, German Emperor. She was the eldest child of Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom.
entries.tldr: Victoria was Queen Victoria's eldest child, raised in liberal ideals before marrying Crown Prince Frederick of Prussia at seventeen, in hopes she would help liberalize Germany. She spent decades as crown princess clashing with Bismarck and the Prussian court over her Anglophile views, earning the nickname "die Engländerin." Frederick finally became emperor in 1888 already dying of throat cancer and reigned only 99 days before conservative son Wilhelm II succeeded him. Shut out of politics afterward, she left a huge correspondence with her mother, now a major historical source.

entries.name: José Manuel Balmaceda
entries.desc: José Manuel Balmaceda was a Chilean politician who served as the 11th President of Chile from 1886 to 1891. His disputes with Congress led to the 1891 Chilean Civil War.
entries.tldr: José Manuel Emiliano Balmaceda Fernández was a Chilean politician who served as the 11th President of Chile from 18 September 1886 to 29 August 1891. A controversial figure, Balmaceda’s political disagreements with the Chilean congress led to the 1891 Chilean Civil War. Following the government forces’ defeat at the Battle of Placilla, Balmaceda took refuge in the Argentine embassy where he lat…

entries.name: Thomas Hardy
entries.desc: Thomas Hardy was an English novelist and poet. A Victorian realist in the tradition of George Eliot, he was influenced both in his novels and in his poetry by Romanticism.
entries.tldr: Thomas Hardy was an English novelist and poet. A Victorian realist in the tradition of George Eliot, he was influenced both in his novels and in his poetry by Romanticism, including the poetry of William Wordsworth. He was highly critical of much in Victorian society, especially on the declining status of rural people in Britain such as those from his native South West England.

entries.name: Berthe Morisot
entries.desc: French Impressionist painter who exhibited at most Impressionist exhibitions and was known for intimate domestic scenes in a distinctive loose style.
entries.tldr: French painter and one of the founding members of the Impressionist movement, exhibiting in seven of the eight group shows held between 1874 and 1886, missing only one for the birth of her daughter. She specialized in intimate domestic and garden scenes rendered in the loose, light-filled brushwork characteristic of Impressionism, often depicting women and children in unposed moments. She was closely linked to Édouard Manet, who painted her repeatedly, and later married his brother Eugène. Long overshadowed by her male contemporaries, she is now seen as one of the movement's finest painters.

entries.name: Emil Theodor Kocher
entries.desc: Swiss surgeon who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physiology for pioneering work on thyroid surgery.
entries.tldr: Swiss surgeon who transformed thyroid surgery from a notoriously dangerous procedure into a routine one, developing meticulous techniques that sharply reduced surgical mortality and popularizing the sterile, careful operating methods of the era. His research also established that removing the entire thyroid gland caused a debilitating condition, now understood as hypothyroidism, clarifying the gland's essential role in metabolism. For this work he received the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the first Nobel awarded for surgery.

entries.name: Wilfrid Laurier
entries.desc: Seventh prime minister of Canada, serving 1896 to 1911, the first French Canadian to hold the office and known for compromises between English and French Canada.
entries.tldr: Sir Henri Charles Wilfrid Laurier was the seventh prime minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911. The first French Canadian prime minister, his 15-year tenure remains the longest uninterrupted term of office among Canadian prime ministers and his nearly 45 years of service in the House of Commons is a record for the House. Laurier is best known for his compromises between English and French Canada.

entries.name: Georg Ritter von Schönerer
entries.desc: Austrian politician and pan-German nationalist whose virulent antisemitism and rhetoric directly influenced the young Adolf Hitler.
entries.tldr: An Austrian landowner turned agitator, Schönerer led the pan-German nationalist movement seeking to detach German-speaking Austria from the multiethnic Habsburg Empire and unite it with the German Reich. His followers had to prove they had no Jewish or Slavic relatives before joining, and demonstrate Aryan ancestry before marrying, an early template for racial exclusion politics. His supporters addressed him as Führer and used the Heil greeting decades before the Nazis adopted the same practices, which the young Hitler later praised in Mein Kampf.

entries.name: Osman Hamdi Bey
entries.desc: Osman Hamdi Bey was an Ottoman Greek administrator, intellectual, art expert and also a prominent and pioneering painter. He was the Ottoman Empire's first archaeologist and first museologist.
entries.tldr: Trained in Paris under orientalist painters Gérôme and Boulanger, Osman Hamdi Bey returned to Istanbul and reshaped how the Ottoman state treated its own antiquities, pushing an 1884 law barring foreign excavators from taking artifacts abroad. As director of the Imperial Museum from 1881 he built the Istanbul Archaeology Museums and personally excavated Sidon's royal necropolis, bringing home its sarcophagi, including the famed Alexander Sarcophagus. He also founded the empire's first fine-arts academy in 1883, and kept painting, producing works like The Tortoise Trainer.

entries.name: William James
entries.desc: American philosopher and psychologist, the first educator to teach a psychology course in the United States, often called the father of American psychology.
entries.tldr: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist. The first educator to offer a psychology course in the United States, he is considered to be one of the leading thinkers of the late 19th century, one of the most influential philosophers and is often dubbed the "father of American psychology".

entries.name: Vasily Vereshchagin
entries.desc: Vasily Vasilyevich Vereshchagin was a Russian painter, war artist, and traveller. The graphic nature of his realist scenes led to many of them never being printed or exhibited to the public.
entries.tldr: Vereshchagin was a Russian painter and traveler who accompanied army campaigns in Central Asia and the Balkans to paint war with unflinching, unheroic realism rather than glorify it. His most famous painting, The Apotheosis of War (1871), shows a pyramid of skulls in a scorched landscape, dedicated "to all great conquerors, past, present and to come." Because his scenes exposed war's brutality, Russian authorities sometimes blocked his paintings from exhibition. He died in 1904 when the battleship Petropavlovsk struck a mine during the Russo-Japanese War, killing him and most of the crew.

entries.name: Friedrich Miescher
entries.desc: Johannes Friedrich Miescher was a Swiss physician and biologist. He was the first scientist to isolate nucleic acid in 1869.
entries.tldr: A Swiss physician working in a lab improvised in the kitchen of Tübingen Castle under Felix Hoppe-Seyler, Miescher extracted material from white blood cell nuclei he obtained by washing pus off used surgical bandages. In 1869 he identified a previously unknown, phosphorus-rich substance unlike any known protein, which he named nuclein; it is now recognized as DNA. He suspected it was linked to heredity but died decades before its structure and role were understood, so his discovery went largely unrecognized in his lifetime.

entries.name: Gabriel Fauré
entries.desc: French composer known for his Requiem, piano nocturnes, and chamber music who shaped the transition from Romanticism to modern French music.
entries.tldr: The son of a provincial schoolmaster, Fauré trained at the Niedermeyer School in Paris rather than the Conservatoire, studying under Camille Saint-Saëns, who became a lifelong mentor. He spent decades as organist at the Église de la Madeleine before becoming director of the Paris Conservatoire in 1905, where he taught Ravel and Boulanger. His gentle Requiem, composed without a fiery Dies Irae, broke from tradition and became his best-loved work. Progressive deafness set in around 1903, eventually forcing his retirement and leaving him largely unable to hear his own late music.

entries.name: Alexander III of Russia
entries.desc: Alexander III was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Finland from 13 March 1881 until his death in 1894. He was highly reactionary in domestic affairs.
entries.tldr: Emperor of Russia from 1881 to 1894, who came to the throne after his father was assassinated by revolutionaries and responded by abandoning liberal reform for autocracy. His government tightened press censorship, curtailed local self-government, and pursued Russification of national minorities, while restrictive laws worsened conditions for Jews and contributed to a wave of pogroms. Despite this domestic repression, he kept Russia out of any major war, earning the epithet "the Peacemaker." He began the Trans-Siberian Railway and was the father of the last tsar, Nicholas II.

entries.name: John Sparrow David Thompson
entries.desc: Sir John Sparrow David Thompson was the fourth prime minister of Canada, serving from 1892 until his death in 1894.
entries.tldr: Sir John Sparrow David Thompson was the fourth prime minister of Canada, serving from 1892 until his death in 1894. He had previously been fifth premier of Nova Scotia for a brief period in 1882. He is the only post-Confederation provincial premier to become prime minister, as of 2026.

entries.name: Gabriel Lippmann
entries.desc: Jonas Ferdinand Gabriel Lippmann was a French applied physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for his invention of a method of photographically reproducing colours.
entries.tldr: Jonas Ferdinand Gabriel Lippmann was a French applied physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for his invention of the Lippmann plate, a method of photographically reproducing colours based on the interference phenomenon.

entries.name: Vasily Surikov
entries.desc: Vasily Ivanovich Surikov was a Russian Realist painter, active in Moscow during Tsars Alexander III and Nicholas II's reigns, renowned for his large history pictures.
entries.tldr: Surikov was a Russian Realist painter from an old Siberian Cossack family whose massive canvases dramatized turning points in Russian history through crowds of individualized faces. His best-known work, Boyarina Morozova (1887), shows the noblewoman Feodosia Morozova dragged through Moscow in chains for refusing to renounce the Old Believer faith, a subject drawn from martyr stories he heard growing up among Siberian Old Believers. Other major histories include The Morning of the Streltsy Execution. Fellow artists praised his break from academic convention and rich, near-impressionistic color.

entries.name: Vilfredo Pareto
entries.desc: Italian polymath who formulated the Pareto principle (the 80/20 rule) and made foundational contributions to economics and sociology.
entries.tldr: Pareto was an Italian engineer-turned-economist who, after a career building railways, took a chair in political economy at Lausanne and pioneered mathematical economics. Studying Italian land ownership around 1906, he observed that roughly 80 percent of it belonged to about 20 percent of the population, a pattern later popularized as the 80/20 "Pareto principle." He also defined Pareto efficiency, a state where nobody's situation can improve without making someone else worse off. In later sociology he argued history is driven by a "circulation of elites," one ruling class replacing another.

entries.name: Édouard-Henri Avril
entries.desc: Édouard-Henri Avril was a French painter and commercial artist. Under the pseudonym Paul Avril, he was an illustrator of erotic literature.
entries.tldr: Avril was a 19th-century French painter trained in the academic tradition who built his public career illustrating adventure novels, including works by Jules Verne. Under the pseudonym Paul Avril, he became far better known for a separate body of work: finely detailed, technically accomplished erotic illustrations for clandestine editions of erotic literature. This dual career let him keep a respectable public reputation while his explicit work circulated privately among collectors. His erotic engravings remain the best-preserved examples of the genre from his era.

entries.name: John Ambrose Fleming
entries.desc: Sir John Ambrose Fleming was a British electrical engineer and physicist who invented the thermionic valve (vacuum tube) and established the right-hand rule in physics.
entries.tldr: Sir John Ambrose Fleming was a British electrical engineer and physicist. He is known for inventing the vacuum tube radio transmitter—with which the first transatlantic radio transmission was made—and establishing the right-hand rule used in physics.

entries.name: Henry Louis Le Châtelier
entries.desc: Henry Louis Le Chatelier was a French chemist who devised Le Chatelier’s principle, used by chemists to predict the effect a changing condition has on a system in chemical equilibrium.
entries.tldr: A French chemist and mining engineer, Le Chatelier formulated the principle bearing his name: a chemical system at equilibrium shifts to counteract any change imposed on its concentration, temperature, or pressure. He applied this and broader thermodynamic reasoning to industrial processes such as steelmaking and ammonia synthesis, and separately pioneered high-temperature thermocouples. His studies of mine explosions and combustion also helped found the field of industrial safety research.

entries.name: Henri Moissan
entries.desc: French chemist who won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for isolating fluorine and pioneering the electric arc furnace.
entries.tldr: This French chemist pursued hydrofluoric acid experiments that had maimed earlier researchers before he isolated elemental fluorine gas in 1886 by electrolyzing a potassium bifluoride solution at low temperature. He also invented the electric arc furnace to synthesize new compounds, work that earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside the fluorine research. He spent years trying to replicate diamond formation under intense heat and died believing he had succeeded, though he had actually made silicon carbide, later named moissanite in his honor.

entries.name: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff
entries.desc: Dutch physical chemist who won the inaugural Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1901) for discovering the laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure.
entries.tldr: A Dutch physical chemist, van 't Hoff won the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1901 for work establishing the laws governing chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure in solutions, effectively founding physical chemistry as a discipline. Earlier in his career he had proposed, controversially at the time, that carbon atoms bond in a three-dimensional tetrahedral arrangement, a stereochemical insight that explained why certain molecules exist as mirror-image forms.

entries.name: Albert Abraham Michelson
entries.desc: Albert Abraham Michelson was an American experimental physicist known for measuring the speed of light and for the Michelson–Morley experiment. In 1907 he won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
entries.tldr: Albert Abraham Michelson was an American experimental physicist known for his work on measuring the speed of light and especially for the Michelson–Morley experiment. In 1907, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first American to win the Nobel Prize in a science. He was the founder and the first head of the physics departments of the Case School of Applied Science and the Unive…

entries.name: José Martí
entries.desc: Cuban poet, journalist, and independence leader who organised the 1895 war against Spanish rule and died in its first skirmish.
entries.tldr: A Cuban poet and journalist exiled repeatedly by Spanish colonial authorities for his revolutionary writing, Martí spent most of his adult life organizing Cuban independence from abroad, principally in New York, where he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party. He was also a major figure in Spanish American letters, credited as a founder of the modernismo literary movement, and his poetry collection Versos Sencillos remains widely read across Latin America. In 1895 he returned to Cuba to help launch the war of independence he had planned, only to be killed weeks after landing.

entries.name: Wilhelm Ostwald
entries.desc: Baltic German chemist and philosopher, a founder of physical chemistry, who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on catalysis and reaction rates.
entries.tldr: Wilhelm Friedrich Ostwald was a Baltic German chemist and philosopher. Ostwald is credited with being one of the founders of the field of physical chemistry, with Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff, Walther Nernst and Svante Arrhenius. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1909 for his scientific contributions to the fields of catalysis, chemical equilibria and reaction velocities.

entries.name: Hussein bin Ali
entries.desc: Hussein bin Ali was Sharif and Emir of Mecca and King of the Hejaz, who launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire in 1916 during World War I.
entries.tldr: Hussein bin Ali was the Sharif of Mecca from 1908 and King of the Hejaz from 1916 to 1924. He launched the Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule during World War I, with British backing. He sought to establish a unified Arab state but was eventually driven from Arabia by Ibn Saud in 1924.

entries.name: Paul Sabatier
entries.desc: French chemist who developed a method for hydrogenating organic compounds using metal catalysts, awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1912.
entries.tldr: Working at Toulouse rather than Paris, Sabatier found around 1897, with student Jean-Baptiste Senderens, that nickel could catalyze hydrogen's addition to carbon compounds, a reaction now called hydrogenation. It became industrially vital almost overnight, underpinning mass production of margarine and hardened oils, and shared the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Victor Grignard. A devout Catholic in an anticlerical era of French science, he stayed at Toulouse his whole career. His namesake reaction later turned carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane aboard the space station.

entries.name: Robert Borden
entries.desc: Sir Robert Laird Borden was a Canadian lawyer and politician who served as the eighth prime minister of Canada from 1911 to 1920. He is best known for his leadership of Canada during World War I.
entries.tldr: Borden led Canada through the First World War, raising the Canadian Expeditionary Force to fight alongside Britain from the war's outset. In 1917 he forced through conscription over fierce opposition in Quebec, a fight so divisive it split his own party and forced him into a wartime Unionist coalition to survive. He also insisted Canada's nearly 60,000 war dead earned it a seat separate from Britain's at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, winning Ottawa its own signature on the Treaty of Versailles and a place in the League of Nations.

entries.name: Maria Zankovetska
entries.desc: Maria Zankovetska was a pioneering Ukrainian theater actress regarded as one of the greatest performers in Ukrainian theatrical history.
entries.tldr: Maria Kostiantynivna Adasovska, better known under her pseudonym Maria Zankovetska, was a Ukrainian theater actress. Some sources date her birth to 3 August 1860. She is regarded as the greatest actress in the history of Ukrainian theater and played leading roles in many Ukrainian dramatic productions during a period when Ukrainian culture faced significant suppression.

entries.name: Ronald Ross
entries.desc: British physician who proved mosquitoes transmit malaria, earning the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
entries.tldr: Ross was a British Army physician in India who, on 20 August 1897, dissected an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a malaria patient named Husein Khan and found the parasite developing in its gut, proving mosquitoes transmit the disease. He went on to trace the parasite's full life cycle using birds infected with avian malaria, work that opened the door to mosquito-control strategies still used today. The breakthrough won him the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, though a bitter priority dispute with Italian researcher Giovanni Battista Grassi shadowed the award.

entries.name: Eugen Bleuler
entries.desc: Paul Eugen Bleuler was a Swiss psychiatrist and eugenicist most notable for his influence on modern concepts of mental illness. He coined several psychiatric terms including schizophrenia, schizoid, autism, and depth psychology.
entries.tldr: Swiss psychiatrist who in 1908 coined the term 'schizophrenia' to replace 'dementia praecox,' arguing the disorder was defined less by inevitable mental decline than by a characteristic splitting of psychic functions such as thought, emotion, and behavior. He also introduced the terms 'schizoid' and 'autism,' the latter originally describing a symptom within schizophrenia rather than the distinct condition it denotes today. As director of the Burghölzli psychiatric hospital in Zurich, he brought Freud's psychoanalytic ideas into mainstream psychiatry and mentored Carl Jung early on.

entries.name: Antoni Grabowski
entries.desc: Antoni Grabowski was a Polish chemical engineer, and an activist of the early Esperanto movement. His translations had an influential impact on the development of Esperanto into a language of literature.
entries.tldr: Polish chemical engineer who became one of the most important early contributors to Esperanto literature after adopting the newly invented language in the 1880s. He translated major works into Esperanto, including Adam Mickiewicz's epic Pan Tadeusz and an anthology of poetry drawn from thirty languages, demonstrating the young language's literary capacity. As a chemist he also compiled much of Esperanto's technical vocabulary, helping the language function beyond everyday conversation. He is often called the father of Esperanto poetry.

entries.name: Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell
entries.desc: Robert Baden-Powell was a British Army officer and writer who founded The Boy Scouts Association, becoming its first Chief Scout, and co-founded The Girl Guides Association with his sister.
entries.tldr: Lieutenant-General Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell, was a British Army officer, writer, founder of The Boy Scouts Association and its first Chief Scout, and founder, with his sister Agnes, of The Girl Guides Association. Baden-Powell wrote Scouting for Boys, which with his previous books – such as his 1884 Reconnaissance and Scouting and his 1899 Aids to Scouting fo…

entries.name: Paul Doumer
entries.desc: Paul Doumer was a French politician who served as President of France from June 1931 until his assassination in May 1932, and was earlier a governor general of Indochina.
entries.tldr: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul Doumer, was a French politician who served as the President of France from June 1931 until his assassination in May 1932. He is described as “the Father of French Indochina”, and was seen as one of the most active and effective governors general of Indochina.

entries.name: Karl Adolph Gjellerup
entries.desc: Karl Adolph Gjellerup was a Danish poet and novelist who shared the 1917 Nobel Prize in Literature with Henrik Pontoppidan. He is associated with Scandinavia's Modern Breakthrough.
entries.tldr: Karl Adolph Gjellerup was a Danish poet and novelist who together with his compatriot Henrik Pontoppidan won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1917. He is associated with the Modern Breakthrough period of Scandinavian literature. He occasionally used the pseudonym Epigonos.

entries.name: Ferdinand de Saussure
entries.desc: Ferdinand Mongin de Saussure was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher. His ideas laid a foundation for many significant developments in both linguistics and semiotics in the 20th century.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand Mongin de Saussure was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher. His ideas laid a foundation for many significant developments in both linguistics and semiotics in the 20th century. He is widely considered one of the founders of 20th-century linguistics and one of two major founders of semiotics, or semiology, as Saussure called it.

entries.name: Christiaan Eijkman
entries.desc: Christiaan Eijkman was a Dutch physician and physiology professor whose demonstration that beriberi is caused by poor diet led to the discovery of vitamins, earning him the 1929 Nobel Prize.
entries.tldr: Christiaan Eijkman was a Dutch physician and professor of physiology whose demonstration that beriberi is caused by poor diet led to the discovery of antineuritic vitamins (thiamine). Together with Sir Frederick Hopkins, he received the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1929 for the discovery of vitamins.

entries.name: Rudolf Diesel
entries.desc: Rudolf Christian Karl Diesel was a German inventor and mechanical engineer, best known for inventing the diesel engine, which burns diesel fuel; both are named after him.
entries.tldr: After publishing his theory of a more efficient "rational heat motor" in 1893, Diesel developed the compression-ignition engine that still bears his name and now powers trucks, ships, and generators worldwide. His fortune grew rapidly, but on 29 September 1913, while crossing the English Channel aboard the SS Dresden to meet the Royal Navy about powering submarines with his engines, he vanished without a trace. A corpse recovered by a Dutch pilot boat ten days later was too decomposed to identify, and with his bank accounts found nearly empty, theories still range from suicide to murder.

entries.name: L. L. Zamenhof
entries.desc: L. L. Zamenhof (1859–1917) was the creator of Esperanto, the most widely used constructed international auxiliary language.
entries.tldr: An ophthalmologist practicing in Warsaw, then part of the Russian Empire, Zamenhof grew up amid the ethnic and linguistic tensions of his multilingual hometown, Białystok, an experience he credited with inspiring his lifelong project of a universal second language. He published the first Esperanto textbook in 1887 under the pseudonym ‘Doktoro Esperanto,’ meaning ‘one who hopes,’ a name that came to designate the language itself. Built with simple, regular grammar drawn mainly from Romance and Germanic roots, Esperanto grew a genuine international speaking community that persists today.

entries.name: Jean Jaurès
entries.desc: French socialist leader who became head of the French Socialist Party in 1902 and later led the unified French Section of the Workers' International.
entries.tldr: Auguste Marie Joseph Jean Léon Jaurès, commonly referred to as Jean Jaurès, was a French socialist leader. Initially a Moderate Republican, he later became a social democrat and one of the first possibilists and in 1902 the leader of the French Socialist Party, which opposed Jules Guesde’s revolutionary Socialist Party of France. The two parties merged in 1905 into the French Section of the Wor…

entries.name: Verner von Heidenstam
entries.desc: Carl Gustaf Verner von Heidenstam was a Swedish poet and novelist who won the 1916 Nobel Prize in Literature, celebrated for his lyrical evocations of Swedish history and landscape.
entries.tldr: Carl Gustaf Verner von Heidenstam was a Swedish poet, novelist and laureate of the 1916 Nobel Prize in Literature. He was a member of the Swedish Academy from 1912. His poems and prose work are filled with a great joy of life, sometimes imbued with a love of Swedish history and scenery, particularly its physical aspects.

entries.name: Charles Édouard Guillaume
entries.desc: Charles-Édouard Guillaume was a Swiss physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1920 for his discovery of anomalies in nickel steel alloys.
entries.tldr: Swiss physicist at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures who discovered invar, a nickel-steel alloy with an almost zero coefficient of thermal expansion, and elinvar, whose elasticity likewise barely changes with temperature. Invar transformed the precision of scientific instruments and clocks, since it no longer expanded or contracted with heat the way ordinary metals did. For this discovery he received the 1920 Nobel Prize in Physics. He spent his career refining international standards of measurement, work that depended directly on the alloys he invented.

entries.name: Jurji Zaydan
entries.desc: Jurji Zaydan was a prolific Lebanese novelist, journalist, editor and teacher, most noted for his creation of the magazine Al-Hilal, which he used to serialize his twenty three historical novels.
entries.tldr: A Beirut-born Christian intellectual who settled in Cairo, Zaydan became one of the most influential figures of the Nahda, the Arab cultural and literary revival of the late nineteenth century. In 1892 he founded the magazine Al-Hilal, using it both as a vehicle for popular education across the Arab world and to serialize his own sequence of twenty-three historical novels dramatizing episodes of Islamic and Arab history. He also wrote widely used scholarly histories of Arabic literature, aiming to present a modern, secular account of the Arab past accessible to general readers.

entries.name: Fatma Aliye Topuz
entries.desc: Ottoman Turkish novelist and feminist considered the first female novelist in Turkish literature.
entries.tldr: Ottoman Turkish novelist widely credited as the first female novelist in Turkish literature, publishing her debut novel Muhadarat in 1892 under conditions where women's authorship was still viewed with suspicion. Daughter of a prominent Ottoman historian, she was largely self-taught in a household that initially tried to discourage her from writing, and she used pseudonyms and family connections to get her early work published. Her fiction and essays argued for women's education and rights within an Islamic framework, and she was active in Ottoman feminist and charitable circles.

entries.name: Nitobe Inazō
entries.desc: Nitobe Inazō  was a Japanese agronomist, diplomat, political scientist, politician, and writer. He studied at Sapporo Agricultural College under the influence of its first president William S.
entries.tldr: Nitobe Inazō  was a Japanese agronomist, diplomat, political scientist, politician, and writer. He studied at Sapporo Agricultural College under the influence of its first president William S. Clark and later went to the United States to study agricultural policy.

entries.name: Sergei Prokudin-Gorskii
entries.desc: Russian chemist and photographer who pioneered colour photography and documented early 20th-century Russia.
entries.tldr: Trained as a chemist under Dmitri Mendeleev, Prokudin-Gorsky refined a three-color technique, photographing scenes through red, green, and blue filters so recombined images rendered lifelike color decades before commercial color film existed. Backed by Tsar Nicholas II with a railway darkroom car, he crisscrossed the Russian Empire around 1909 to 1915, producing over 2,600 images of villages, churches, and people before war and revolution changed that world. His glass negatives later reached the Library of Congress, which reassembled them into color photographs now widely reproduced.

entries.name: Alexandre Yersin
entries.desc: Alexandre Émile John Yersin was a Swiss-French physician and bacteriologist. He is remembered for his work as a pioneer in microbiology and immunology.
entries.tldr: Alexandre Émile John Yersin was a Swiss-French physician and bacteriologist. He is remembered for his work as a pioneer in microbiology and immunology. Yersin is the co-discoverer of both the Diphtheria and Tetanus toxins and of the bacillus responsible for the bubonic plague.

entries.name: Israel Zangwill
entries.desc: British Jewish author and Zionist leader known for novels exploring immigrant life and the play The Melting Pot.
entries.tldr: A British-born son of Jewish immigrants, Zangwill won acclaim for novels such as Children of the Ghetto depicting the crowded immigrant life of London's East End, and coined the enduring phrase “melting pot” with his 1908 play of that name, popularizing the idea of America absorbing and blending its newcomers. A committed Zionist, he broke with the mainstream movement over the rejected British offer of land in East Africa and founded the Jewish Territorial Organization to seek a homeland elsewhere.

entries.name: Camille Claudel
entries.desc: Camille Rosalie Claudel was a French sculptor known for her figurative works in bronze and marble.
entries.tldr: A gifted French sculptor whose sinuous, expressive bronzes and marbles rivaled the work of her mentor and lover Auguste Rodin, though she long struggled for recognition in her own right. Works like The Waltz and The Mature Age channel her tempestuous private life into startling physical drama. After her final break with Rodin she grew isolated and paranoid, and in 1913, following her father's death, her family committed her to an asylum, where she remained for the rest of her life.

entries.name: Heinrich Wölfflin
entries.desc: Swiss art historian whose formal principles of style — linear vs. painterly, plane vs. recession — shaped 20th-century art history.
entries.tldr: Heinrich Wölfflin was a Swiss art historian, aesthetician, and educator whose objective classifying principles were influential in the development of formal analysis in art history in the early 20th century. He taught at Basel, Berlin, and Munich and formulated paired concepts (e.g. linear vs. painterly, closed vs. open form) that became foundational tools in stylistic analysis.

entries.name: Nikolai Marr
entries.desc: Nikolai Yakovlevich Marr was a Georgian-born historian and linguist who gained a reputation as a scholar of the Caucasus.
entries.tldr: Marr began as a respected specialist in Caucasian languages before advancing a speculative theory that Georgian was a relic of a 'Japhetic' family, eventually claiming all languages descended from four primal exclamations: sal, ber, yon, and rosh. After 1917 he rebranded this as 'proletarian linguistics' against bourgeois philology and used Party favor to dominate Soviet language science. His followers enforced 'Marrism' as orthodoxy for over a decade after his death, until Stalin published a 1950 repudiation that dismantled it almost overnight.

entries.name: Sofia Okunevska
entries.desc: Sofia Okunevska was a Ukrainian physician, educator, feminist, and scholar. She was the first female Doctor of Medicine and the first female physician in Austria-Hungary.
entries.tldr: Barred from Austro-Hungarian universities, Okunevska studied medicine in Zurich, graduating in 1896 with a dissertation on blood changes in anemia, becoming Galicia's first university-educated Ukrainian woman and the empire's first female doctor. She practiced gynecology at a Ukrainian-run clinic, trained nurses and midwives, compiled Ukrainian medical terminology, and pioneered radiation therapy for cancer locally. She also helped found the region's first doctors' union and edited an early Galician women's almanac, First Wreath.

entries.name: Alfred Werner
entries.desc: Alfred Werner was a Swiss chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1913 for proposing the octahedral configuration of transition metal complexes.
entries.tldr: Swiss chemist who in 1893 proposed the coordination theory of transition metal complexes, explaining how a central metal atom bonds to a fixed number of surrounding ions or molecules in defined geometric arrangements. His model, including the octahedral configuration for many six-coordinate complexes, resolved decades of confusion over compounds whose formulas defied ordinary valence rules. He confirmed the theory by resolving optically active isomers that only made sense under his three-dimensional geometry. In 1913 he became the first inorganic chemist to win a Nobel Prize.

entries.name: Marie Curie
entries.desc: Physicist and chemist, pioneer of radioactivity and the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
entries.tldr: Born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw, she moved to Paris to study physics and worked with her husband Pierre to investigate the mysterious rays given off by uranium, a phenomenon she named radioactivity. Processing tons of pitchblende by hand, the couple isolated two new elements, polonium and radium, launching nuclear physics and radiation medicine. In World War I she built mobile X-ray units, nicknamed 'petites Curies,' and drove them to the front. She died of aplastic anemia from radiation exposure, and her lab notebooks are still too radioactive to handle safely.

entries.name: Władysław Reymont
entries.desc: Władysław Stanisław Reymont was a Polish novelist and the laureate of the 1924 Nobel Prize in Literature.
entries.tldr: Reymont was a Polish novelist who worked as a railway clerk, monk, and traveling actor before turning to writing full time. His masterwork, the four-volume novel The Peasants, portrays a year in a Polish village through the changing seasons and was praised for its vivid depiction of rural life and folk speech. He survived a serious train accident early in his career, using the compensation payout to fund his literary work. In 1924 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, narrowly beating his countryman and rival Stefan Żeromski.

entries.name: Robert Falcon Scott
entries.desc: British Royal Navy officer and Antarctic explorer who led two polar expeditions, perishing on the return from his 1910–13 attempt to reach the South Pole.
entries.tldr: Scott commanded two Antarctic expeditions, the Discovery voyage of 1901-04 and the fateful Terra Nova expedition of 1910-13. Racing Norway's Roald Amundsen to the South Pole, his five-man party reached it on 17 January 1912 only to find Amundsen's tent already there, beaten by 34 days. Exhausted and battling brutal cold on the return march, all five died; Scott's final diary entries, found months later beside his body, turned the doomed expedition into a lasting symbol of heroic sacrifice.

entries.name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
entries.desc: Henrietta Swan Leavitt was an American astronomer. Her discovery of how to effectively measure vast astronomical distances led to a shift in the understanding of the scale and nature of the universe.
entries.tldr: Working as one of Harvard Observatory's poorly paid female computers measuring star brightness on photographic plates, Leavitt studied variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds and in 1908 found a striking pattern: Cepheid variables with longer pulsation periods were reliably more luminous. That period-luminosity relation gave astronomers a standard candle for measuring cosmic distances, later used by Edwin Hubble to show some nebulae were separate galaxies and the universe is expanding. Leavitt lost most of her hearing young and received no Nobel recognition in her lifetime.

entries.name: Maxim Gorky
entries.desc: Alexei Maximovich Peshkov, popularly known as Maxim Gorky, was a Russian and Soviet writer, journalist, and proponent of socialism. He was nominated five times for the Nobel Prize in Literature.
entries.tldr: Alexei Maximovich Peshkov, popularly known as Maxim Gorky, was a Russian and Soviet writer, journalist, and proponent of socialism. He was nominated five times for the Nobel Prize in Literature. Before his success as an author, he travelled widely across the Russian Empire, changing jobs frequently; these experiences would later influence his writing.

entries.name: Mahatma Gandhi
entries.desc: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement against British rule.
entries.tldr: Trained as a lawyer in London, Gandhi first developed his philosophy of nonviolent civil resistance, satyagraha, while campaigning for the rights of the Indian community in South Africa over two decades before returning to India in 1915. He then took leadership of the Indian National Congress and transformed it into a mass movement, organizing nationwide campaigns of noncooperation, most famously the 1930 Salt March protesting the British salt tax. India achieved independence in 1947, accompanied by a violent partition that devastated him; he was assassinated months later, in January 1948.

entries.name: Neville Chamberlain
entries.desc: British Prime Minister 1937–1940, defined by his appeasement policy and the Munich Agreement ceding the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany.
entries.tldr: A former businessman known for competent domestic reform, Chamberlain became prime minister in 1937 convinced that firm, personal diplomacy could satisfy Hitler's demands and avert another war. He flew to Munich in September 1938 and agreed to let Germany annex the Sudetenland, returning to London waving the agreement and declaring he had secured peace for our time, a phrase that would haunt him within a year. When Hitler seized the rest of Czechoslovakia and then invaded Poland, his policy collapsed and Britain declared war; he resigned in May 1940, replaced by Churchill.

entries.name: Johannes Linnankoski
entries.desc: Johannes Linnankoski was a Finnish author and playwright. His most famous work is the romance novel, The Song of the Blood-Red Flower (1905). His primary themes were guilt, punishment, and redemption as moral questions.
entries.tldr: Born Johannes Vihtori Peltonen to a poor farming family, Linnankoski worked as a journalist and printer before achieving literary fame with his 1905 novel The Song of the Blood-Red Flower, a romance following a restless woodsman through love affairs across the Finnish countryside. The book's frank treatment of sexuality and lush nature writing made it popular in Finland and, in translation, abroad, and it was adapted into several films. His other major novel, The Fugitives, dealt with religious dissenters fleeing persecution. He died young, in 1913, at the height of his fame.

entries.name: Richard Bedford Bennett
entries.desc: Richard Bedford Bennett, 1st Viscount Bennett was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, philanthropist, and politician who served as the 11th prime minister of Canada from 1930 to 1935.
entries.tldr: A wealthy Calgary lawyer, Bennett won the 1930 election just as the Great Depression struck, then spent his term battling mass unemployment. He set up federal relief camps paying single men twenty cents a day for hard labour, provoking the 1935 On-to-Ottawa Trek, which his government suppressed in Regina, leaving two dead. Facing collapse, he unveiled an interventionist "Bennett New Deal" copying Roosevelt's reforms, but voters punished him anyway, crushing the Tories that October; he later retired to England as Viscount Bennett.

entries.name: Victor Grignard
entries.desc: French chemist who discovered the Grignard reagent, an essential tool in organic synthesis, earning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1912.
entries.tldr: Grignard was a French organic chemist who in 1900, at the University of Lyon, found that magnesium reacting with an alkyl halide in dry ether produces a highly reactive organomagnesium compound that readily adds to aldehydes and ketones. This Grignard reagent gave chemists a reliable general method for forming carbon-carbon bonds, and within a decade thousands of papers applied it. He shared the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Paul Sabatier for the discovery, later becoming a professor at Nancy and then Lyon. In the First World War he also worked on detecting poison gases.

entries.name: Anton Denikin
entries.desc: Anton Denikin was a Russian military officer and lieutenant general in the Imperial Russian Army who led the anti-Bolshevik White movement during the Russian Civil War.
entries.tldr: Anton Ivanovich Denikin was a Russian military officer who served as a lieutenant general in the Imperial Russian Army and as a leading commander of the anti-Bolshevik White movement during the Russian Civil War.

entries.name: Radoje Domanović
entries.desc: Radoje Domanović was a Serbian journalist, writer and teacher, most famous for his satirical short stories. His adult years were a constant fight against tuberculosis.
entries.tldr: Radoje Domanović was a Serbian journalist, writer and teacher, most famous for his satirical short stories. His adult years were a constant fight against tuberculosis. This circumstance of his life, and the affection which he inspired in all who knew him, created an aura of romanticism and sentimentality which stand in contrast to his literary accomplishments as a satirist and a powerful critic…

entries.name: Sergei Rachmaninoff
entries.desc: Russian composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor, widely regarded as one of the finest pianists of his day and among the last great Romantic composers.
entries.tldr: Sergei Vasilyevich Rachmaninoff was a Russian composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor. Rachmaninoff is widely considered one of the finest pianists of his day and, as a composer, one of the last great representatives of Romanticism in Russian classical music. Early influences of Tchaikovsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, and other Russian composers gave way to a thoroughly personal idiom notable for its s…

entries.name: Harry Houdini
entries.desc: Erik Weisz, known professionally as Harry Houdini, was an American escapologist, illusionist, and stunt performer noted for his escape acts.
entries.tldr: Born Erik Weisz in Budapest, he built his fame on death-defying escapes: chained jumps into icy rivers, a sealed milk can, and the Chinese Water Torture Cell, performed upside down in a straitjacket. Later he spent much time exposing fraudulent spirit mediums, even forging a fake photo of Lincoln's ghost to show how such tricks worked. He died on Halloween 1926 of peritonitis from a ruptured appendix, possibly worsened by a student's punch to his stomach. His widow held annual séances trying to reach him for a decade before giving up.

entries.name: Maurice Ravel
entries.desc: Joseph Maurice Ravel was a French composer, pianist and conductor. In the 1920s and 1930s Ravel was internationally regarded as France's greatest living composer.
entries.tldr: A meticulous craftsman of Basque and Swiss descent, he trained at the Paris Conservatoire and developed an orchestral palette so precise that Stravinsky reportedly nicknamed him 'the Swiss watchmaker.' His 1928 ballet score Bolero, built from one melody repeated over an unchanging rhythm as the orchestration steadily swells, became his most famous work almost by accident, since he considered it a minor experiment. His orchestration of Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition is now the standard concert version. A 1932 taxi accident left him unable to write or speak fluently in his final years.

entries.name: Francis William Aston
entries.desc: British physicist and chemist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering isotopes in non-radioactive elements via his mass spectrograph.
entries.tldr: British chemist and physicist who built the mass spectrograph, an instrument that separates atoms by the ratio of their mass to electric charge, letting him identify and measure the masses of dozens of isotopes. His measurements proved that many elements thought pure were actually mixtures of isotopes with the same chemical properties but different atomic weights, resolving longstanding puzzles in atomic weight measurements. He formulated the 'whole number rule,' showing isotope masses are close to whole-number multiples of hydrogen's mass, a clue supporting the model of atomic nuclei.

entries.name: Viktor Dyk
entries.desc: Viktor Dyk was a nationalist Czech poet, prose writer, playwright, politician and political writer. He was sent to jail during the First World War for opposing the Austro-Hungarian empire.
entries.tldr: Viktor Dyk was a nationalist Czech poet, prose writer, playwright, politician and political writer. He was sent to jail during the First World War for opposing the Austro-Hungarian empire. He was one of the signatories of the Manifesto of Czech writers.

entries.name: Joan Gamper
entries.desc: Hans Max Gamper-Haessig, commonly known as Joan Gamper, was a Swiss-born football executive and versatile athlete. He founded football clubs in Switzerland and Spain, most notably Barcelona.
entries.tldr: A Swiss-born accountant and versatile amateur athlete, Gamper moved to Barcelona for work and in 1899 placed a newspaper advertisement seeking fellow football enthusiasts, leading directly to the founding of FC Barcelona, which he served as player, coach, and president across several terms. He also helped found clubs in Switzerland and elsewhere in Spain. Financial ruin and depression, worsened by the dictatorship-era closure of the club he had built, led him to take his own life in 1930.

entries.name: Gustav Stresemann
entries.desc: German statesman who as chancellor and foreign minister steered Weimar Germany toward international reconciliation, sharing the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize.
entries.tldr: Son of a Berlin beer bottler, he earned a doctorate in economics before entering politics as a pragmatic liberal, briefly serving as chancellor in 1923 during hyperinflation, when he ended resistance in the Ruhr and introduced the Rentenmark currency. As foreign minister from 1923 until his death, he negotiated the 1925 Locarno treaties guaranteeing Germany's western borders, secured League of Nations entry in 1926, and pursued reparations relief via the Dawes Plan. For this diplomacy he shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with Aristide Briand. Worn down by overwork, he died of a stroke in 1929.

entries.name: Pyotr Wrangel
entries.desc: Pyotr Wrangel, nicknamed the Black Baron, was a Russian military officer who led the anti-Bolshevik Volunteer Army in the Russian Civil War and, from 1920, the White forces in Southern Russia.
entries.tldr: Baron Pyotr Nikolayevich Wrangel, nicknamed the "Black Baron", was a Russian military officer who served as a commanding general in the anti-Bolshevik Volunteer Army during the Russian Civil War. In 1920, he became the last commander-in-chief of the White forces in Southern Russia, which he reorganized as the Russian Army.

entries.name: Franz Reichelt
entries.desc: Austro-Hungarian tailor and inventor known as “the Flying Tailor” who died testing his parachute suit by jumping from the Eiffel Tower.
entries.tldr: A Paris tailor originally from Austria-Hungary, Reichelt spent years designing a wearable parachute suit of silk meant to save falling aviators. After dummy drops from his apartment window kept failing, he got police permission to test the suit from the Eiffel Tower using a mannequin, but arrived intending to jump himself. On 4 February 1912, before a crowd and film cameras, he hesitated on the platform, said a few words, then leapt; the suit failed to open and he died instantly, his fall captured on newsreel footage.

entries.name: Egon Friedell
entries.desc: Austrian cultural historian, playwright, and actor whose three-volume Cultural History of the Modern Age remains a landmark of popular historiography.
entries.tldr: Austrian cultural historian, essayist, playwright, and cabaret performer whose three-volume Cultural History of the Modern Age traced European civilization from the Black Death to the First World War with unusual wit and breadth for a work of popular scholarship. A fixture of Vienna's coffeehouse intellectual scene, he was as well known for his stage performances and aphorisms as for his historical writing. When German troops entered Austria in the 1938 Anschluss, he took his own life by jumping from his apartment window rather than be arrested for his Jewish ancestry.

entries.name: Marcel Grossmann
entries.desc: Marcel Grossmann was a Swiss mathematician who was a friend and classmate of Albert Einstein.
entries.tldr: A Swiss mathematician who befriended Einstein as a fellow student at Zurich's Federal Polytechnic, Grossmann lent Einstein his meticulous lecture notes so he could pass exams for classes he had skipped. Years later, when Einstein needed mathematics equal to his physical intuition about gravity, he turned back to Grossmann, who introduced him to the tensor calculus of Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita. Their joint 1913 papers on a gravitation theory supplied crucial scaffolding for what became general relativity in 1915. Grossmann remained a working geometer, outside his friend's later spotlight.

entries.name: Charles Ferdinand Ramuz
entries.desc: French-speaking Swiss novelist and poet whose works depict rural Vaud peasant life with austere, rhythmic prose.
entries.tldr: Charles Ferdinand Ramuz was a French-speaking Swiss writer whose novels and poems drew on the landscape and peasant life of the Vaud region. His austere, rhythmic prose and focus on collective experience set him apart from Parisian literary trends. He collaborated with Igor Stravinsky on L’Histoire du soldat (1918).

entries.name: Kazimir Malevich
entries.desc: Kazimir Malevich was a Russian avant-garde artist and art theorist who pioneered abstract painting in the 20th century. He founded Suprematism, a non-objective style, in 1915.
entries.tldr: Kazimir Severinovich Malevich was a Russian avant-garde artist and art theorist, whose work and writings pioneered the development of abstract painting in the 20th century.
