He is best known as the founder of Suprematism, a radically non-objective form of painting he introduced in 1915.

entries.name: María de las Mercedes, Princess of Asturias
entries.desc: María de las Mercedes was the eldest child of King Alfonso XII of Spain and heiress presumptive to the Spanish throne, holding the title Princess of Asturias for all 24 years of her life.
entries.tldr: María de las Mercedes, Princess of Asturias was the eldest child of King Alfonso XII of Spain and his second wife, Maria Christina of Austria. She was Princess of Asturias, the heiress presumptive to the Crown of Spain, for all 24 years of her life.

entries.name: Otto Bauer
entries.desc: Otto Bauer was an Austrian politician who was one of the founders and leading thinkers of the Austromarxists. He served as Foreign Minister of the Republic of German-Austria.
entries.tldr: A leading theorist of Austromarxism, Bauer charted a course between Bolshevik revolution and reformist social democracy, arguing socialists could win power gradually while preparing to defend it by force. At twenty-six he published a study proposing 'national-cultural autonomy' to defuse the nationality conflicts tearing at Austria-Hungary. As Austria's first foreign minister in 1918–19 he pushed for union with Germany, a plan the Allies vetoed. He shaped the 1926 Linz Program, then fled into exile in 1934 when Austrofascists banned the party, dying in Paris weeks after the Nazi Anschluss.

entries.name: Lili Elbe
entries.desc: Danish painter and one of the earliest known recipients of gender reassignment surgery.
entries.tldr: Born Einar Wegener, Lili Elbe trained as a painter in Copenhagen and worked professionally alongside her wife, the artist Gerda Gottlieb, who often used her as a model under the name Lili. In the late 1920s, after years of gender dysphoria initially treated by doctors as illness, she underwent a pioneering series of surgeries in Germany, becoming one of the first documented recipients of what would later be called gender-affirming surgery. She adopted the legal name Lili Elbe and died in 1931 from complications following a later, experimental operation intended to allow her to have children.

entries.name: Inayat Khan
entries.desc: Inayat Khan Rehmat Khan was an Indian professor of musicology, singer, poet, philosopher, writer, and pioneer of the transmission of Sufism to the West.
entries.tldr: An accomplished singer and vina player from a distinguished Indian musical family, Inayat Khan left India in 1910 to bring Sufi mysticism to the West, founding what became the Sufi Order International. He taught a Universal Sufism that drew on Vedanta as well as Islamic mysticism, emphasizing the unity underlying all religions and treating music as a path to spiritual awakening. His daughter Noor Inayat Khan later became a celebrated Allied secret agent killed by the Nazis in the Second World War.

entries.name: Douglas Fairbanks
entries.desc: American actor famed for swashbuckling silent-film roles including Zorro and Robin Hood, and co-founder of United Artists.
entries.tldr: American silent-film star whose swashbuckling roles in The Mark of Zorro, The Three Musketeers, Robin Hood, and The Thief of Bagdad made him Hollywood's leading action hero of the 1920s, celebrated for performing his own athletic stunts. In 1919 he co-founded United Artists with Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, and D. W. Griffith, giving major stars control over the distribution of their own films. His marriage to Pickford made the couple Hollywood's first celebrity power pair. His career declined with the arrival of sound film, which suited his flamboyant silent-era style less well.

entries.name: Amedeo Modigliani
entries.desc: Amedeo Clemente Modigliani was an Italian painter and sculptor of the École de Paris who worked mainly in France. He is known for portraits and nudes in a modern style.
entries.tldr: Italian painter and sculptor who moved to Paris in 1906 and became a central figure of the bohemian École de Paris, developing an instantly recognizable style of elongated faces and figures influenced by African and Cycladic sculpture. Chronic poverty, tuberculosis contracted in childhood, and heavy drinking marked most of his working life, bringing little recognition before his death. His nude paintings caused a scandal when exhibited in 1917 and were briefly shut down by police. He died in 1920 at thirty-five, and his pregnant partner took her own life the next day.

entries.name: Hermann Rorschach
entries.desc: Hermann Rorschach was a Swiss psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who developed the famous inkblot test that bears his name.
entries.tldr: A Swiss psychiatrist trained under Eugen Bleuler, Rorschach developed the inkblot test that bears his name, asking patients to describe what they saw in ten symmetrical ink patterns to reveal underlying personality and thought patterns. Published in 1921 as Psychodiagnostik, the method drew on his own boyhood fascination with klecksography, the parlour game of making pictures from blots. He died of complications from appendicitis the following year, just as the test began attracting clinical attention.

entries.name: Jacques Feyder
entries.desc: Jacques Feyder was a Belgian film director, screenwriter and actor who worked principally in France. He was associated with the style of poetic realism in French cinema.
entries.tldr: A Belgian-born filmmaker who worked mainly in France, Feyder became one of the leading directors of poetic realism, a style blending naturalistic settings with romantic, fatalistic storytelling that shaped French cinema of the 1930s. His 1934 film Le Grand Jeu and 1935 La Kermesse héroïque, made after a spell directing in Hollywood, are considered high points of the movement and influenced later directors including his own assistant, Marcel Carné.

entries.name: Engelbert Dollfuss
entries.desc: Engelbert Dollfuss was an Austrian politician and dictator who served as chancellor of Austria between 1932 and 1934.
entries.tldr: Austrian politician who became chancellor in 1932 and, facing a fractured parliament and rising Nazi and socialist paramilitaries, suspended the constitution the following year to rule by decree. In February 1934 he crushed an armed socialist uprising in Vienna, then established an authoritarian, corporatist one-party state modeled partly on fascist Italy, banning both the Social Democratic and Nazi parties. His government aimed to keep Austria out of Nazi Germany's orbit. In July 1934 he was shot during a failed Nazi coup attempt and left to bleed to death.

entries.name: Alexander Alekhine
entries.desc: Alexander Aleksandrovich Alekhine was a Russian and French chess player and the fourth World Chess Champion, a title he held for two reigns.
entries.tldr: Russian-born chess grandmaster who became the fourth World Chess Champion in 1927 by defeating the long-reigning José Raúl Capablanca in Buenos Aires, a result many considered an upset. He lost the title to Max Euwe in 1935 but won it back two years later, becoming the only world champion to die while still holding the crown, in 1946. Renowned for a sharp, combinative attacking style built on deep calculation, he emigrated from Soviet Russia and took French citizenship. Articles on chess and race attributed to him during the wartime occupation of France remain disputed.

entries.name: Joachim von Ribbentrop
entries.desc: German politician and diplomat who served as Nazi Germany's Foreign Minister 1938–1945; executed at Nuremberg as a war criminal.
entries.tldr: A former champagne salesman who cultivated ties to the Nazi elite, Ribbentrop became Hitler's foreign minister in 1938 and negotiated the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, a nonaggression treaty with the Soviet Union that secretly carved up Poland and the Baltic states between the two powers and cleared the way for Germany's invasion. He oversaw Axis diplomacy throughout the war, was convicted of war crimes at Nuremberg, and became the first defendant hanged following the trials in 1946.

entries.name: Vicente Huidobro
entries.desc: Vicente García-Huidobro Fernández, known by the pseudonym Vicente Huidobro, was a Chilean poet, writer, editor and literary critic. He was the founder of Creationism.
entries.tldr: Huidobro was a Chilean avant-garde poet who around 1912 founded Creationism, a movement holding that a poem should be an entirely new thing invented by the poet, not an imitation of nature. Moving between Paris and Madrid, he mingled with figures like Apollinaire and Juan Gris, spreading avant-garde ideas into Spanish-language poetry through journals he edited. His magnum opus, Altazor (1931), follows a parachuting poet-hero through seven cantos that dissolve language into pure invented sound. He also ran for the Chilean presidency in 1925 and later worked as a war correspondent.

entries.name: Vladimir Mayakovsky
entries.desc: Vladimir Vladimirovich Mayakovsky was a Russian poet, playwright, artist, and actor, renowned as a prominent figure of the Russian Futurist movement.
entries.tldr: Vladimir Vladimirovich Mayakovsky was a Russian poet, playwright, artist, and actor. During his early, pre-Revolution period leading into 1917, Mayakovsky became renowned as a prominent figure of the Russian Futurist movement. He co-signed the Futurist manifesto, A Slap in the Face of Public Taste (1913), and wrote such poems as A Cloud in Trousers (1915) and Backbone Flute (1916).

entries.name: Grand Duchess Olga Nikolaevna of Russia
entries.desc: Eldest daughter of Russia's last tsar Nicholas II, executed with her family by Bolsheviks in 1918.
entries.tldr: The eldest of Nicholas II's five children, tutors noted her strong memory and love of literature, music, and riding, and she was considered more independent-minded than her sisters. During the First World War she trained and worked as a nurse in a military hospital, tending wounded soldiers directly, though poor health eventually forced her to stop. Proposed marriages to European royalty fell through, leaving her unmarried when the 1917 revolution swept away the monarchy. She was shot alongside her parents and siblings by Bolshevik guards in Yekaterinburg in July 1918, at age twenty-two.

entries.name: Shote Galica
entries.desc: Shote Galica was a Kachak Albanian insurgent. She has been declared a People's Heroine of Albania.
entries.tldr: Born Qerime Halil Radisheva in Kosovo's Drenica region under Ottoman rule, she took the name Shote Galica after marrying kachak (outlaw-rebel) leader Azem Galica in 1915 and fighting alongside him against Serbian and later Yugoslav control. She took part in the Dukagjin and Junik uprisings of the early 1920s, and after Azem's death assumed command of his band herself, joining fellow insurgent Bajram Curri in the Has and Lumë regions. She is remembered for capturing a Serbian military commander and his soldiers at Çikatova. She died in Albania in 1927.

entries.name: Italo Balbo
entries.desc: Italian fascist politician and aviator who led pioneering transatlantic air expeditions in the 1930s and served as Governor-General of Libya until his death.
entries.tldr: An early and prominent Italian fascist, Balbo organized the Blackshirt squads that helped bring Mussolini to power before turning to aviation, where he led two spectacular mass transatlantic flights, including a 1933 formation crossing to Chicago that made him an international celebrity and gave Chicago's Balbo Drive its name. His growing popularity unsettled Mussolini, who sidelined him as Governor-General of Libya. Balbo died in 1940 when Italian anti-aircraft gunners mistakenly shot down his own aircraft over Tobruk.

entries.name: George Gershwin
entries.desc: George Gershwin was an American composer and pianist whose works spanned jazz, popular, and classical music. His best-known compositions include Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess.
entries.tldr: George Gershwin was an American composer and pianist whose compositions spanned jazz, popular and classical music. Among his best-known works are the songs "Swanee" (1919) and "Fascinating Rhythm" (1924), the orchestral compositions Rhapsody in Blue (1924) and An American in Paris (1928), the jazz standards "Embraceable You" (1928) and "I Got Rhythm" (1930) and the opera Porgy and Bess (1935), …

entries.name: Glenn Miller
entries.desc: American big band conductor and trombonist whose Orchestra was one of the most popular ensembles of the Swing era before he disappeared over the English Channel in 1944.
entries.tldr: A trombonist and arranger, he formed his own big band in 1938 after earlier failed ventures, and hits like In the Mood made it America's best-selling recording act by 1940. At the height of his fame in 1942 he gave up his career to join the Army Air Forces, leading an orchestra that toured bases to boost troop morale. On 15 December 1944 he boarded a small plane bound for Paris to arrange a Christmas concert for troops, and it vanished over the English Channel; no wreckage was ever recovered. A frozen carburetor likely caused the crash, but the disappearance was never conclusively solved.

entries.name: Annemarie Schwarzenbach
entries.desc: Swiss writer, journalist, and photographer whose anti-fascist activism drove her into exile and whose restless travels shaped her literary output.
entries.tldr: Annemarie Schwarzenbach was a Swiss writer, journalist, and photographer whose androgynous image suited bohemian Berlin society of the 1930s. Her anti-fascist campaigning forced her into exile, where she became close to the family of Thomas Mann. Her travel writing and novels reflect a life of perpetual movement across Europe, Asia, and the Americas.

entries.name: Jean Harlow
entries.desc: American actress and 1930s sex symbol dubbed the ‘Platinum Blonde’ whose comedic roles at MGM made her one of Hollywood’s biggest stars before her early death at 26.
entries.tldr: An American actress who became MGM's biggest star of the early 1930s, Harlow was marketed as the “Platinum Blonde” and built her fame on a string of brassy comedic performances in films including Red-Headed Woman and Bombshell that made her a defining sex symbol of the pre-Code Hollywood era. Beneath the glamour she suffered chronic illness, and she died suddenly in 1937 at age 26 from kidney failure, cutting short a career still at its peak.

entries.name: Manshuk Mametova
entries.desc: Kazakh machine-gunner in the Red Army who single-handedly held off a German assault near Nevel in 1943, posthumously awarded Hero of the Soviet Union.
entries.tldr: A Kazakh student in Alma-Ata when the Soviet Union entered the Second World War, Mametova volunteered for the Red Army and, after initially being assigned clerical duties, insisted on retraining as a machine gunner. Serving with the 21st Guards Rifle Division, she was killed in October 1943 defending a position near Nevel in western Russia, reportedly continuing to fire after her crew was wiped out and covering her unit's retreat. She was posthumously awarded Hero of the Soviet Union in 1944 and remains a celebrated national figure in Kazakhstan.

entries.name: Charles VII of France
entries.desc: Charles VII, called the Victorious, was King of France from 1422 until his death in 1461; his reign saw the end of the Hundred Years' War and of English claims to the French throne.
entries.tldr: Charles VII, called the Victorious or the Well-Served, was King of France from 1422 to his death in 1461. His reign saw the end of the Hundred Years' War and a de facto end of the English claims to the French throne.

entries.name: John Logie Baird
entries.desc: John Logie Baird was a Scottish inventor and electrical engineer who demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system on 26 January 1926.
entries.tldr: John Logie Baird was a Scottish inventor, electrical engineer and innovator who demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system on 26 January 1926. He went on to invent the first publicly demonstrated colour television system and the first viable purely electronic colour television picture tube.

entries.name: George Stinney
entries.desc: George Stinney was a 14-year-old African American boy wrongfully executed in 1944 after an unfair one-day trial convicted him of murdering two white girls in Alcolu, South Carolina.
entries.tldr: George Junius Stinney Jr. was an African American boy who was wrongfully executed at the age of 14 after being convicted, during an unfair trial, for the murders of two white girls – 11-year-old Betty June Binnicker and 8-year-old Mary Emma Thames – in his hometown of Alcolu, South Carolina. He was tried, convicted, and sentenced to death on a single day in April 1944 and then executed by elect…

entries.name: George Stephenson
entries.desc: George Stephenson was an English civil and mechanical engineer known as the Father of Railways. His chosen rail gauge became the basis for the standard gauge used by most of the world's railways.
entries.tldr: George Stephenson was an English civil engineer and mechanical engineer. Renowned as the "Father of Railways", Stephenson was considered by the Victorians as a great example of diligent application and thirst for improvement. His chosen rail gauge, sometimes called "Stephenson gauge", was the basis for the 4-foot-8+1⁄2-inch (1.435 m) standard gauge used by most of the world's railways.

entries.name: Howard Carter
entries.desc: British archaeologist and Egyptologist who discovered the intact tomb of Pharaoh Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.
entries.tldr: Howard Carter was a British archaeologist and Egyptologist who became known for discovering the intact tomb of the 18th Dynasty Pharaoh Tutankhamun in November 1922, the best-preserved pharaonic tomb ever found in the Valley of the Kings.

entries.name: Martin of Tours
entries.desc: Martin of Tours was the third bishop of Tours. He is the patron saint of many communities and organizations across Europe, including of the former French Third Republic.
entries.tldr: Martin of Tours was the third bishop of Tours. He is the patron saint of many communities and organizations across Europe, including of the former French Third Republic. A native of Pannonia, he converted to Christianity at a young age.

entries.name: William Henry Bragg
entries.desc: British X-ray crystallographer who shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics with his son Lawrence Bragg for their work on crystal structure analysis.
entries.tldr: Sir William Henry Bragg was a British X-ray crystallographer who uniquely shared a Nobel Prize with his son Lawrence Bragg – the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics "for their services in the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays," an important step in the development of X-ray crystallography.

entries.name: Agustín I of Mexico
entries.desc: Agustín Cosme Damián de Iturbide y Arámburu, commonly known as Agustín de Iturbide and later by his regnal name Agustín I, was the first Emperor of Mexico from 1822 until his abdication in 1823.
entries.tldr: Mexican general who, after fighting for Spain against the independence insurgency, switched sides in 1821 and issued the Plan of Iguala, uniting royalists and rebels behind independence, a Catholic state church, and equal citizenship. The resulting Army of the Three Guarantees swept Spanish forces from Mexico within months. Proclaimed Emperor Agustín I in 1822, he ruled barely a year before a republican revolt forced his abdication and exile. He returned to Mexico in 1824 unaware Congress had sentenced him to death, and was captured and executed on landing.

entries.name: Guillaume Apollinaire
entries.desc: Guillaume Apollinaire was a Polish-French poet, playwright, short story writer, novelist and art critic of Polish, Swiss and Italian descent.
entries.tldr: Born Wilhelm Albert Włodzimierz Apolinary Kostrowicki in Rome to a Polish noblewoman, he settled in Paris in 1902 and became a central figure of the avant-garde, closely befriending Picasso and Braque. He coined the term Cubism in 1911, writing some of the first essays defending the movement, and also coined the word Surrealism in 1917. His 1918 collection Calligrammes arranged poems' printed words into the visual shapes of their subjects. Wounded by shrapnel in the trenches in 1916, he died two days before the armistice, weakened by the injury and the influenza pandemic.

entries.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
entries.desc: German composer of the late Baroque period known for the Brandenburg Concertos, the Cello Suites, and The Well-Tempered Clavier.
entries.tldr: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and musician of the late Baroque period. He is known for his prolific output across a variety of instruments and forms, including the orchestral Brandenburg Concertos; solo instrumental works such as the Cello Suites and Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin; keyboard works such as the Goldberg Variations and The Well-Tempered Clavier; organ works such…

entries.name: Antonio Vivaldi
entries.desc: Antonio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist and impresario of Baroque music, whose influence spread widely across Europe during his lifetime.
entries.tldr: Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was an Italian composer, virtuoso violinist and impresario of Baroque music. Regarded as one of the greatest Baroque composers, Vivaldi's influence during his lifetime was widespread across Europe, giving origin to many imitators and admirers. He pioneered many developments in orchestration, violin technique and programmatic music.

entries.name: Jean-Baptiste Perrin
entries.desc: French physicist who verified Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion, confirming the atomic nature of matter, and won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics.
entries.tldr: Jean Baptiste Perrin was a French physicist who, in his studies of the Brownian motion of minute particles suspended in liquids, verified Albert Einstein's explanation of this phenomenon and thereby confirmed the atomic nature of matter. For this work, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926.

entries.name: Cnut the Great
entries.desc: Cnut the Great was King of England from 1016, King of Denmark from 1018, and King of Norway from 1028 until his death in 1035, ruling the North Sea Empire.
entries.tldr: Cnut, also known as Canute and with the epithet the Great, was King of England from 1016, King of Denmark from 1018, and King of Norway from 1028 until his death in 1035. The three kingdoms united under Cnut's rule are referred to together as the North Sea Empire by historians.

entries.name: José de San Martín
entries.desc: José de San Martín, nicknamed the Liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru, was an Argentine general who led much of South America's independence struggle against Spain.
entries.tldr: José Francisco de San Martín y Matorras, nicknamed "the Liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru", was an Argentine general and the primary leader of the southern and central parts of South America's successful struggle for independence from the Spanish Empire who served as the Protector of Peru. Born in Yapeyú, Corrientes, in modern-day Argentina, he left the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata a…

entries.name: Plotinus
entries.desc: Plotinus was an ancient Greek philosopher, born and raised in Roman Egypt. He is widely regarded by modern scholars as the founder of Neoplatonism.
entries.tldr: After eleven years in Alexandria under the teacher Ammonius Saccas, he opened a school in Rome around 245 that drew senators and interested Emperor Gallienus in a planned philosophers' city, Platonopolis. His system traces reality's emanation from a single source, the One, through Intellect and Soul into matter, with mystical return to that source as philosophy's goal, shaping later Christian, Islamic, and Jewish thought. He refused to sit for a portrait, saying it was humiliation enough to be trapped in a body. His notes were organized by his student Porphyry into the Enneads.

entries.name: Louis VII of France
entries.desc: Louis VII, was King of France from 1137 to 1180. His first marriage was to Duchess Eleanor of Aquitaine, one of the wealthiest and most powerful women in western Europe.
entries.tldr: Louis VII, was King of France from 1137 to 1180. His first marriage was to Duchess Eleanor of Aquitaine, one of the wealthiest and most powerful women in western Europe. The marriage temporarily extended the Capetian lands to the Pyrenees.

entries.name: Charles IX of France
entries.desc: Charles IX was King of France from 1560 until his death in 1574, ascending the throne on the death of his brother Francis II as the penultimate Valois monarch.
entries.tldr: Charles IX was King of France from 1560 until his death in 1574. He ascended the French throne upon the death of his brother Francis II in 1560, and as such was the penultimate monarch of the House of Valois.

entries.name: Charles VIII of France
entries.desc: Charles VIII, called the Affable, was King of France from 1483 to his death in 1498. He succeeded his father Louis XI at the age of 13.
entries.tldr: Charles VIII, called the Affable, was King of France from 1483 to his death in 1498. He succeeded his father Louis XI at the age of 13. His elder sister Anne acted as regent jointly with her husband Peter II, Duke of Bourbon until 1491, when the young king turned 21 years of age.

entries.name: Josephus
entries.desc: Flavius Josephus was a Roman–Jewish historian and military leader, best known for writing The Jewish War. He was born in Jerusalem to a father of priestly descent.
entries.tldr: Flavius Josephus was a Roman–Jewish historian and military leader. Best known for writing The Jewish War, he was born in Jerusalem—then part of the Roman province of Judea—to a father of priestly descent and a mother who claimed Hasmonean royal ancestry.

entries.name: Harry Carey
entries.desc:
Harry Carey may refer to:Harry Carey (actor) (1878–1947), American actor
Harry Carey Jr. (1921–2012), American actor
Harry Carey (footballer) (1916–1991), Australian rules footballer
entries.tldr: This entry's dates and roles point to Harry Carey, an American actor who became one of silent cinema's first Western stars, often playing the good-hearted outlaw Cheyenne Harry. He starred in Straight Shooting, the first feature directed by John Ford, and their partnership helped launch Ford's career until a rift split them in 1921. Carey later moved into character roles, earning a Best Supporting Actor nomination for playing the President of the Senate in Mr. Smith Goes to Washington. He died in 1947 of lung cancer and emphysema after decades of smoking.

entries.name: Khalil Sultan
entries.desc: Khalil Sultan was the Timurid ruler of Transoxiana from 18 February 1405 to 1409. He was a son of Miran Shah and a grandson of Timur.
entries.tldr: A grandson of Timur through his son Miran Shah, Khalil Sultan seized control of Transoxiana and the Timurid capital Samarkand in 1405 immediately after his grandfather's death, outmaneuvering rival claimants in the succession struggle that followed. His four-year rule was undermined by a controversial marriage to a former slave woman, widely blamed by chroniclers for depleting the treasury and alienating the Timurid nobility. He was overthrown in 1409 by his uncle Shah Rukh, another son of Timur, who reunified most of the empire; Khalil Sultan died two years later, still in his twenties.

entries.name: Ivane Javakhishvili
entries.desc: Georgian historian and linguist whose scholarship shaped modern study of Georgian history and culture; a founder of Tbilisi State University.
entries.tldr: Ivane Alexandres dze Javakhishvili was a Georgian historian and linguist whose works heavily influenced the modern scholarship of the history and culture of Georgia. He was one of the founding fathers of the Tbilisi State University (1918) and its rector from 1919 to 1926.

entries.name: Kartini
entries.desc: Raden Adjeng Kartini, also known as Raden Ayu Kartini, was a prominent Indonesian advocate of women's rights and female education.
entries.tldr: Born into Javanese aristocracy under Dutch colonial rule, Kartini received a Dutch-language education unusual for girls of her era before being confined, per local custom, to the family home from age twelve until her arranged marriage. During this seclusion she corresponded extensively with Dutch friends about the position of Indonesian women, arguing for access to education and against polygamy and forced early marriage. She died at twenty-five, days after giving birth; her letters, published posthumously as Through Darkness to Light, made her a founding figure of Indonesian feminism.

entries.name: Sakichi Toyoda
entries.desc: Sakichi Toyoda  was a Japanese inventor and industrialist who founded Toyoda Automatic Loom Works. The son of a farmer and sought-after carpenter, he started the Toyoda family companies.
entries.tldr: Sakichi Toyoda  was a Japanese inventor and industrialist who founded Toyoda Automatic Loom Works. The son of a farmer and sought-after carpenter, he started the Toyoda family companies. His son, Kiichiro Toyoda, would later establish Japan's largest automaker, Toyota.

entries.name: Thorfinn Karlsefni
entries.desc: Icelandic explorer who around 1010 followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland in a short-lived attempt to found a permanent settlement there.
entries.tldr: Thorfinn Karlsefni Thórdarson was an Icelandic explorer. Around the year 1010, he followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland in a short-lived attempt to establish a permanent settlement there with his wife Gudrid Thorbjarnardóttir and their followers.

entries.name: Grigory Potanin
entries.desc: Grigory Nikolayevich Potanin was a Russian botanist, ethnographer, and natural historian. He was an explorer of Inner Asia and was the first to catalogue many of the area's native plants.
entries.tldr: Grigory Nikolayevich Potanin was a Russian botanist, ethnographer, and natural historian. He was an explorer of Inner Asia and was the first to catalogue many of the area's native plants. Potanin was also an author and a political activist who aligned himself with the Siberian regionalist movement.

entries.name: James V of Scotland
entries.desc: James V was King of Scotland from 9 September 1513 until his death in 1542. He was crowned on 21 September 1513 at the age of seventeen months.
entries.tldr: James V was King of Scotland from 9 September 1513 until his death in 1542. He was crowned on 21 September 1513 at the age of seventeen months. James was the son of King James IV and Margaret Tudor, daughter of Henry VII of England.

entries.name: James IV of Scotland
entries.desc: King of Scotland from 1488, regarded as the most successful Stewart monarch, killed at the Battle of Flodden in 1513.
entries.tldr: James IV was King of Scotland from 11 June 1488 until his death at the Battle of Flodden in 1513. He inherited the throne at the age of fifteen on the death of his father, James III, at the Battle of Sauchieburn, following a rebellion in which the younger James was the figurehead of the rebels. James IV is generally regarded as the most successful of the Stewart monarchs of Scotland.

entries.name: Abbot Suger
entries.desc: Suger was a French abbot and statesman. He was a key advisor to King Louis VI and his son Louis VII, acting as the latter's regent during the Second Crusade.
entries.tldr: Suger was a French abbot and statesman. He was a key advisor to King Louis VI and his son Louis VII, acting as the latter's regent during the Second Crusade. His writings are seminal texts for early 12th-century Capetian history, and his reconstruction of the Basilica of Saint-Denis, where he was abbot, was instrumental in creating the Gothic architecture style.

entries.name: Francis Walsingham
entries.desc: Sir Francis Walsingham was principal secretary to Queen Elizabeth I of England from 20 December 1573 until his death and is popularly remembered as her "spymaster".
entries.tldr: English statesman who served as Elizabeth I's principal secretary and built one of early modern Europe's most sophisticated intelligence networks, earning his lasting reputation as her 'spymaster.' His agents decoded correspondence that implicated Mary, Queen of Scots, in the Babington Plot, providing evidence used to convict and execute her in 1587. A committed Protestant, he saw Catholic Spain as an existential threat and used espionage to uncover plots against the queen and gather intelligence ahead of the 1588 Spanish Armada. He died in debt, having funded his own operations.

entries.name: Saint Sava
entries.desc: Serbian prince and Eastern Orthodox monk known as the Enlightener, who became the first Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian Church, and also served as a writer and diplomat.
entries.tldr: Saint Sava, known as the Enlightener or the Illuminator, was a Serbian prince and Eastern Orthodox monk who became the first Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian Church. He was also a writer, diplomat, and the founder of Serbian law.

entries.name: Pyotr Stolypin
entries.desc: Pyotr Stolypin was a Russian statesman who served as prime minister and interior minister of the Russian Empire from 1906 until his assassination in 1911. His reforms were halted by his death.
entries.tldr: Pyotr Arkadyevich Stolypin was a Russian statesman who served as the third prime minister and the interior minister of the Russian Empire from 1906 until his assassination in 1911. Known as a reformer of Russian society and the economy, he initiated reforms which were halted by his assassination.

entries.name: Inge I of Norway
entries.desc: Inge Haraldsson was king of Norway from 1136 to 1161. Inge’s reign fell within the start of the period known in Norwegian history as the civil war era, and he was never the sole ruler of the country.
entries.tldr: Inge Haraldsson was king of Norway from 1136 to 1161. Inge’s reign fell within the start of the period known in Norwegian history as the civil war era, and he was never the sole ruler of the country. He is often known as Inge the Hunchback, because of his physical disability.

entries.name: Richard Strauss
entries.desc: Richard Strauss was a German composer and conductor known for his tone poems and operas, a leading figure of the late Romantic and early Modern era and successor to Wagner and Liszt.
entries.tldr: Richard Georg Strauss was a German composer and conductor known for his tone poems and operas. A leading figure of the late Romantic and early Modern era, and a successor to Richard Wagner and Franz Liszt, he combined, along with his friend Gustav Mahler, subtleties of orchestration with an advanced harmonic style.

entries.name: Guy Fawkes
entries.desc: English Catholic conspirator caught guarding explosives beneath the House of Lords in the 1605 Gunpowder Plot to kill King James I.
entries.tldr: Guy Fawkes, also known as Guido Fawkes while fighting for the Spanish, was a member of a group of provincial English Catholics involved in the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605. He was born and educated in York; his father died when Fawkes was eight years old, after which his mother married a recusant Catholic.

entries.name: Nuno Gonçalves
entries.desc: Nuno Gonçalves was court painter to Afonso V of Portugal from 1450 to 1471. Gonçalves is widely considered the most accomplished Portuguese painter of the 15th century.
entries.tldr: Nuno Gonçalves was court painter to Afonso V of Portugal from 1450 to 1471. Gonçalves is widely considered the most accomplished Portuguese painter of the 15th century. His surviving masterpiece is the polyptych known as the Saint Vincent Panels.

entries.name: Ferdynand Antoni Ossendowski
entries.desc: Ferdynand Antoni Ossendowski was a Polish writer, explorer, professor, and anticommunist activist, known for his books about Lenin and the Russian Civil War, in which he took part.
entries.tldr: Ferdynand Antoni Ossendowski was a Polish writer, explorer, university professor, and anticommunist political activist. He is known for his books about Lenin and the Russian Civil War in which he participated.

entries.name: Eva Ekeblad
entries.desc: Eva Ekeblad was a Swedish agriculturist and salon hostess. She discovered a method to make alcohol and flour from potatoes, significantly reducing Sweden's incidence of famine.
entries.tldr: Eva Ekeblad was a Swedish agriculturist and salon hostess. She discovered a method to make alcohol and flour from potatoes, significantly reducing Sweden's incidence of famine. She became the first female member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Uwais Qarni
entries.desc: Muslim military commander among the tabi'in who served the Rashidun Caliphate; a loyal companion of Ali, he was martyred at the Battle of Siffin in 657.
entries.tldr: ʾUways ibn ʿĀmir al-Qaranī was Muslim military commander and one of the tabi'in who served in the Rashidun Caliphate. As a tabi'i, he never met the Islamic prophet Muhammad, though was sometimes honorarily counted as among the companions. He was a loyal companion of Ali, and was a commander in Ali's army at the Battle of Siffin, where he was martyred in 657.

entries.name: Vladimir Lenin
entries.desc: Russian revolutionary and political theorist who led the October Revolution and served as first head of government of Soviet Russia, then the Soviet Union.
entries.tldr: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, better known as Vladimir Lenin, was a Russian revolutionary, politician and political theorist. He was the first head of government of Soviet Russia from 1917 to 1922, and then of the Soviet Union from 1922 until his death in 1924. As the Bolsheviks' founder, Lenin led the October Revolution, which established the world's first communist state.

entries.name: James Hargreaves
entries.desc: James Hargreaves was an English weaver, carpenter and inventor who lived and worked in Lancashire, England. Hargreaves is credited with inventing the spinning jenny in 1764.
entries.tldr: An English weaver and carpenter in Lancashire, Hargreaves is credited with inventing the spinning jenny around 1764, a hand-powered machine that let a single worker spin multiple threads of yarn at once. The device dramatically boosted textile output and became one of the pivotal innovations of the early Industrial Revolution, though it also provoked fear among hand-spinners for displacing their labor, and a mob reportedly destroyed his early machines before he patented an improved version in 1770.

entries.name: Tiberius
entries.desc: Second Roman emperor, reigning from AD 14 until his death, succeeding his stepfather Augustus as ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.
entries.tldr: Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor from AD 14 until his death, reigning as the second ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. He succeeded his stepfather Augustus, the first Roman emperor. Tiberius was born in Rome in 42 BC to politician Tiberius Claudius Nero and his wife, Livia Drusilla.

entries.name: Caligula
entries.desc: Caligula, born Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from AD 37 until his assassination in AD 41.
entries.tldr: Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, also called Gaius and Caligula, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from AD 37 until his assassination in AD 41. He was the son of the Roman general Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, Augustus' granddaughter, members of the first ruling family of the Roman Empire. He was born two years before Tiberius became emperor.

entries.name: Edward Burnett Tylor
entries.desc: Sir Edward Burnett Tylor was an English anthropologist, and professor of anthropology.
entries.tldr: English anthropologist widely regarded as a founder of cultural anthropology, whose 1871 book Primitive Culture proposed one of the discipline's first influential definitions of culture, as the complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, and custom acquired by people as members of society. He developed the theory of animism, arguing that belief in spirits and souls formed the earliest stage of religious thought. In 1896 he became Oxford's first professor of anthropology, helping establish the field as an academic discipline in Britain.

entries.name: Claudius
entries.desc: Claudius, born Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, was a Roman emperor who ruled from AD 41 until his death in AD 54, the first to be born outside Italy.
entries.tldr: Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, or Claudius, was a Roman emperor, ruling from AD 41 until his death in AD 54. The fourth ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, Claudius was born to Drusus the Elder, the brother of Emperor Tiberius, and Antonia Minor at Lugdunum in Roman Gaul, where his father was stationed as a military legate. He was the first Roman emperor to be born outside Italy.

entries.name: Nero
entries.desc: Nero was Roman emperor from 54 AD until his suicide in 68 AD, as the final emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.
entries.tldr: The last Julio-Claudian emperor, Nero began as a young ruler guided by advisors like Seneca but grew into one of history's most notorious tyrants, murdering his own mother Agrippina after a failed attempt to stage her death as a shipwreck accident. He blamed Rome's Great Fire of 64 AD on the city's Christians, launching the empire's first organized persecution of the new faith, and built a huge new palace on the cleared land. He also styled himself a performing artist, competing on stage as a singer, scandalizing the elite. He took his own life in 68 AD, lamenting what an artist dies in me.

entries.name: Galba
entries.desc: Servius Sulpicius Galba was a Roman emperor who ruled for seven months from June 68 to January 69 AD. He was the first emperor in the Year of the Four Emperors, succeeding Nero after his suicide.
entries.tldr: Servius Sulpicius Galba was a Roman emperor, ruling for 7 months from 8 June AD 68 to 15 January 69. He was the first emperor in the Year of the Four Emperors and assumed the throne following Emperor Nero's suicide.

entries.name: Otho
entries.desc: Marcus Salvius Otho was Roman emperor, ruling for three months from 15 January to 16 April 69. He was the second emperor of the Year of the Four Emperors.
entries.tldr: Once one of Nero's closest companions, Otho was banished to govern remote Lusitania after Nero took his wife Poppaea Sabina for himself. A decade later he backed Galba's revolt against Nero, then, feeling snubbed when Galba adopted a different heir, had Galba murdered in the Roman Forum and seized the throne in January 69. His reign lasted barely three months: facing Vitellius's rival army at the bloody Battle of Bedriacum, Otho chose to stab himself to death rather than prolong a civil war. He was the second of four men to wear the purple during the chaotic Year of the Four Emperors.

entries.name: Vitellius
entries.desc: Roman emperor for eight months in AD 69, one of the rulers of the Year of the Four Emperors, who took the title Germanicus instead of Caesar.
entries.tldr: Aulus Vitellius was Roman emperor, ruling for eight months from 19 April to 20 December AD 69. Vitellius became emperor following the quick succession of the previous emperors Galba and Otho, in a year of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Vitellius added the honorific title Germanicus to his name instead of Caesar upon his accession.

entries.name: Moctezuma II
entries.desc: Moctezuma II, often called Montezuma, was the ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, reigning from 1502 or 1503 until 1520.
entries.tldr: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, retroactively referred to in European sources as Moctezuma II, and often called Montezuma, was the ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, reigning from 1502 or 1503 to 1520. Through his marriage with Queen Tlapalizquixochtzin of Ecatepec, one of his two wives, he was also the king consort of the altepetl.

entries.name: Nikolai Yezhov
entries.desc: Nikolai Yezhov was a Soviet secret police official who headed the NKVD from 1936 to 1938 during the Great Purge, organizing mass arrests before his own arrest and execution.
entries.tldr: Nikolai Ivanovich Yezhov, also spelt Ezhov, was a Soviet secret police official under Joseph Stalin who was head of the NKVD from 1936 to 1938, at the height of the Great Purge. Yezhov organized mass arrests, torture, and executions during the Great Purge, but he fell out of favor with Joseph Stalin and was arrested, subsequently admitting in a confession to a range of anti-Soviet activity incl…

entries.name: Genrikh Yagoda
entries.desc: Genrikh Yagoda was a Soviet secret police official who directed the NKVD from 1934 to 1936. Appointed by Joseph Stalin, he oversaw arrests, show trials, and executions during the Great Purge.
entries.tldr: Genrikh Grigoryevich Yagoda was a Soviet secret police official who served as director of the NKVD, the Soviet Union's security and intelligence agency, from 1934 to 1936. Appointed by Joseph Stalin, Yagoda supervised arrests, show trials, and executions of the Old Bolsheviks Lev Kamenev and Grigory Zinoviev, climactic events of the Great Purge. Yagoda also supervised the construction of the Wh…

entries.name: Vespasian
entries.desc: Vespasian was Roman emperor from 69 to 79. The last emperor to reign in the Year of the Four Emperors, he founded the Flavian dynasty, which ruled the empire for 27 years.
entries.tldr: Vespasian was Roman emperor from 69 to 79. The last emperor to reign in the Year of the Four Emperors, he founded the Flavian dynasty, which ruled the empire for 27 years. His fiscal reforms and consolidation of the empire brought political stability and an extensive building program.

entries.name: Julius Fučík
entries.desc:
Julius Fučík may refer to:Julius Fučík (composer) (1872–1916), Czech composer and conductor
Julius Fučík (journalist) (1903–1943), Czech journalist and writer
entries.tldr: A Czech literary critic and committed Communist journalist, Fučík wrote for party newspapers through the 1920s and 1930s and traveled to the Soviet Union, producing enthusiastic reportage on Soviet life. After the Nazi occupation he went underground to lead the banned Communist Party's resistance, until his arrest by the Gestapo in Prague in 1942. While imprisoned and awaiting execution, he secretly wrote Notes from the Gallows on smuggled paper, a memoir that became a defining text of wartime resistance literature after its 1945 publication. He was executed in Berlin in 1943.

entries.name: Titus
entries.desc: Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD, a member of the Flavian dynasty who succeeded his father Vespasian, the first emperor ever to succeed his biological father.
entries.tldr: Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD. A member of the Flavian dynasty, Titus succeeded his father Vespasian upon his death, becoming the first Roman emperor ever to succeed his biological father.

entries.name: Mikhail Tukhachevsky
entries.desc: Mikhail Tukhachevsky, nicknamed the Red Napoleon, was a Soviet general prominent from 1918 to 1937 as a military officer and theoretician. He was executed during the Moscow trials.
entries.tldr: Mikhail Nikolayevich Tukhachevsky, nicknamed the Red Napoleon, was a Soviet general who was prominent between 1918 and 1937 as a military officer and theoretician. He was later executed during the Moscow trials of 1936–1938.

entries.name: Domitian
entries.desc: Domitian was Roman emperor from 81 to 96. The son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, he was the last member of the Flavian dynasty to rule.
entries.tldr: Domitian ( də-MISH-ən, -ee-ən; Latin: Domitianus was Roman emperor from 81 to 96. The son of Vespasian and the younger brother of Titus, his two predecessors on the throne, he was the last member of the Flavian dynasty. Described by the historian Brian W.

entries.name: Nerva
entries.desc: Nerva was a Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98. Nerva became emperor when aged almost 66, after a lifetime of imperial service under Nero and the succeeding rulers of the Flavian dynasty.
entries.tldr: A veteran senator with decades of service under earlier emperors, Nerva was installed by the Senate within a day of Domitian's assassination in 96, largely because he was elderly, childless, and unthreatening to rival factions. His reign was shaky: lacking a military base, he was forced by a Praetorian Guard mutiny to hand over Domitian's killers for execution. But one decision proved momentous. With no heir, he adopted the popular general Trajan as successor, starting a run of adoptions that produced the Five Good Emperors and Rome's most stable century.

entries.name: Edmund Blair Leighton
entries.desc: Edmund Blair Leighton was an English painter of historical genre scenes, specializing in Regency and medieval subjects. His work is linked to the Pre-Raphaelite movement of the late 19th century.
entries.tldr: Edmund Blair Leighton was an English painter of historical genre scenes, specialising in Regency and medieval subjects. His art is associated with the Pre-Raphaelite movement of the mid-to-late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, though his artwork is less stylised and much more naturalistic.

entries.name: Käthe Kollwitz
entries.desc: Käthe Kollwitz was a German artist who worked in painting, printmaking, and sculpture. Her art cycles, such as The Weavers, depict the effects of poverty, hunger, and war on the working class.
entries.tldr: Käthe Kollwitz was a German artist who worked with painting, printmaking and sculpture. Her most famous art cycles, including The Weavers and The Peasant War, depict the effects of poverty, hunger and war on the working class. Despite the realism of her early works, her art is now more closely associated with Expressionism.

entries.name: Trajan
entries.desc: Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117, remembered as the second of the Five Good Emperors, under whom the Roman Empire reached its greatest territorial extent.
entries.tldr: Trajan was a Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117, remembered as the second of the Five Good Emperors of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty. He was a philanthropic ruler and a successful soldier-emperor who presided over one of the greatest military expansions in Roman history, during which, by the time of his death, the Roman Empire reached its maximum territorial extent. He was given the title of optimus …

entries.name: Hadrian
entries.desc: Hadrian was Roman emperor from 117 to 138. His form of address as Roman emperor was Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus.
entries.tldr: Hadrian was Roman emperor from 117 to 138. His form of address as Roman emperor was Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus. Hadrian was born in Italica, in the present-day Andalusian province of Seville in southern Spain, an Italic settlement in Hispania Baetica; his gens Aelia came from the town of Hadria in eastern Italy.

entries.name: William Herschel
entries.desc: Frederick William Herschel was a German–British astronomer and composer. He frequently collaborated with his younger sister and fellow astronomer Caroline Herschel.
entries.tldr: Frederick William Herschel was a German–British astronomer and composer. He frequently collaborated with his younger sister and fellow astronomer Caroline Herschel. Born in the Electorate of Hanover, he followed his father into the military band of Hanover, before emigrating to Britain in 1757 at the age of 19.

entries.name: John Frederick William Herschel
entries.desc: English polymath — mathematician, astronomer, and chemist — who invented the blueprint process and pioneered experimental photography.
entries.tldr: Sir John Frederick William Herschel, 1st Baronet was an English polymath active as a mathematician, astronomer, chemist, inventor and experimental photographer who invented the blueprint and did botanical work.

entries.name: Giovanni Schiaparelli
entries.desc: Italian astronomer who mapped Mars and named its surface features, work later associated with the "canali" controversy.
entries.tldr: Giovanni Virginio Schiaparelli was an Italian astronomer and science historian. Schiaparelli established the Martian system of nomenclature still in use today; before him, features of the planet bore the names of contemporary astronomers, similar to the lunar map of van Langren that preceded that of Hevelius.

entries.name: Antoninus Pius
entries.desc: Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from AD 138 to 161, the fourth of the Five Good Emperors of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty.
entries.tldr: Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from AD 138 to 161. He was the fourth of the Five Good Emperors from the Nerva–Antonine dynasty and also the fourth of the six adoptive emperors.

entries.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
entries.desc: Eusebius of Caesarea was a historian of Christianity, exegete, and Christian polemicist from Syria Palaestina. Around AD 314 he became bishop of Caesarea Palaestina.
entries.tldr: Eusebius of Caesarea, also known as Eusebius Pamphilius, was a historian of Christianity, exegete, and Christian polemicist from the Roman province of Syria Palaestina. In about AD 314 he became the bishop of Caesarea Palaestina.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.desc: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher. A member of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty, he was the last of the rulers known as the Five Good Emperors.
entries.tldr: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher. He was a member of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty, the last of the rulers later known as the Five Good Emperors and the last emperor of the Pax Romana, an age of relative peace, calm, and stability for the Roman Empire lasting from 27 BC to 180 AD. He served as Roman consul in 140, 145, and 161.

entries.name: Taejong of Joseon
entries.desc: Third monarch of Korea's Joseon dynasty and father of Sejong the Great, a major contributor to establishing the regime founded by his father, King Taejo.
entries.tldr: Taejong, personal name Yi Pangwŏn, was the third monarch of Joseon and the father of Sejong the Great. The fifth son of King Taejo, the founder of the dynasty, he was himself a major contributor toward the establishment of the new regime. He ascended to the throne upon the abdication of his elder brother, King Jeongjong.

entries.name: Johannes Ockeghem
entries.desc: Franco-Flemish composer and singer of early Renaissance music, a leading European composer between Guillaume Du Fay and Josquin des Prez.
entries.tldr: Johannes Ockeghem was a Franco-Flemish composer and singer of early Renaissance music. Ockeghem was a significant European composer in the period between Guillaume Du Fay and Josquin des Prez, and he was—with his colleague Antoine Busnois—a prominent European composer in the second half of the 15th century. He was an important proponent of the early Franco-Flemish School.

entries.name: Sviatopolk II of Kiev
entries.desc: Sviatopolk II Iziaslavich was Grand Prince of Kiev from 1093 to 1113. He was not a popular prince, and his reign was marked by incessant rivalry with his cousin Vladimir Monomakh.
entries.tldr: Sviatopolk II Iziaslavich, who had earlier ruled Novgorod for a decade, took the Kievan throne in 1093 as senior prince, beginning a reign defined by rivalry with his cousin Vladimir Monomakh. He suffered a heavy defeat by Cuman nomads at the Stugna River in 1093 but later joined Monomakh in a victory over the Cumans at the Salnitsa in 1111. Widely disliked for his harsh rule, his death in 1113 triggered a Kiev uprising against officials, the wealthy, and Jewish moneylenders tied to his regime, forcing the boyars to invite the more popular Monomakh to the throne.

entries.name: Josquin des Prez
entries.desc: Josquin des Prez was a composer of Renaissance music, described as French or Franco-Flemish, and considered one of the greatest composers of the Renaissance.
entries.tldr: Josquin Lebloitte dit des Prez was a composer of Renaissance music, who is variously described as French or Franco-Flemish. Considered one of the greatest composers of the Renaissance, he was a central figure of the Franco-Flemish School and had a profound influence on the music of 16th-century Europe. Building on the work of his predecessors like Johannes Ockeghem, he developed a complex style…

entries.name: Lucius Verus
entries.desc: Lucius Aurelius Verus was Roman emperor from 161 until his death in 169, alongside his adoptive brother Marcus Aurelius. He was a member of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty.
entries.tldr: Lucius Aurelius Verus was Roman emperor from 161 until his death in 169, alongside his adoptive brother Marcus Aurelius. He was a member of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty. Verus' succession together with Marcus Aurelius marked the first time that the Roman Empire was ruled by more than one emperor simultaneously, an increasingly common occurrence in the later history of the Empire.

entries.name: Commodus
entries.desc: Commodus was Roman emperor from 177 to 192, ruling first as co-emperor with his father Marcus Aurelius, then alone from 180. His reign is often seen as marking the end of the Pax Romana.
entries.tldr: Commodus was Roman emperor from 177 to 192, first serving as nominal co-emperor under his father Marcus Aurelius and then ruling alone from 180. Commodus's sole reign is commonly thought to mark the end of the Pax Romana, a golden age of peace and prosperity in the history of the Roman Empire.

entries.name: Lysander
entries.desc: Lysander was a Spartan commander and statesman, one of the leading military and political leaders of Sparta during the Peloponnesian War. He destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC.
entries.tldr: Lysander was a Spartan commander and statesman who was one of the leading military and political leaders of Sparta during the Peloponnesian Wars. He destroyed the Athenian fleet at the Battle of Aegospotami in 405 BC, forcing Athens to capitulate and bringing the Peloponnesian Wars to an end. He then played a key role in Sparta's domination of Greece for the next decade until his death at the B…

entries.name: Pertinax
entries.desc: Publius Helvius Pertinax was Roman emperor for the first three months of 193, succeeding Commodus and becoming the first ruler of the turbulent Year of the Five Emperors.
entries.tldr: Son of a freed slave turned wool merchant, Pertinax rose from schoolteacher to army officer, distinguishing himself in the Parthian War before climbing through provincial commands to a consulship. When the Praetorian Guard's officers killed the tyrannical Commodus in late 192, they installed elderly Pertinax in his place, and he auctioned off Commodus's exotic animals to refill the treasury. His push for frugality on a Guard used to lavish bribes backfired fast: on 28 March 193 Praetorians stormed the palace, killed him, and paraded his head on a spear, opening the Year of the Five Emperors.

entries.name: Didius Julianus
entries.desc: Marcus Didius Julianus was Roman emperor from March to June 193, during the Year of the Five Emperors. He is known for having purchased the title of emperor in an auction run by the Praetorian Guard.
entries.tldr: Marcus Didius Julianus was Roman emperor from March to June 193, during the Year of the Five Emperors. He is known for having purchased the title of emperor in an auction run by the Praetorian Guard. His reign is a common delineation in the decline and fall of the Roman Empire.

entries.name: Septimius Severus
entries.desc: Lucius Septimius Severus was Roman emperor from 193 to 211. He was born in Leptis Magna, Libya, in the Roman province of Africa.
entries.tldr: Lucius Septimius Severus was Roman emperor from 193 to 211. He was born in Leptis Magna, Libya, in the Roman province of Africa. As a young man, he advanced through the customary succession of offices under the reigns of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus.

entries.name: Zayd ibn Ali
entries.desc: Son of Ali ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-Abidin and great-grandson of Ali ibn Abi Talib; his failed revolt against the Umayyad Caliphate gave rise to the Zaydi Shia sect.
entries.tldr: Zayd ibn ʿAlī, also spelled Zaid, was the son of Ali ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-Abidin, and great-grandson of Ali ibn Abi Talib. He led an unsuccessful revolt against the Umayyad Caliphate, in which he died. The event gave rise to the Zaydiyya sect of Shia Islam, which holds him as the next Imam after his father Ali ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-Abidin.

entries.name: Bolesław Prus
entries.desc: Bolesław Prus, pen name of Aleksander Głowacki, was a Polish journalist and novelist, a leading figure in the history of Polish literature.
entries.tldr: Aleksander Głowacki, better known by his pen name Bolesław Prus, was a Polish journalist, novelist, a leading figure in the history of Polish literature and philosophy, and a distinctive voice in world literature.

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.desc: English philosopher, biologist, and sociologist who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest" in his writings on evolution and society.
entries.tldr: Herbert Spencer was an English polymath active as a philosopher, psychologist, biologist, sociologist, and anthropologist. Spencer originated the expression "survival of the fittest", which he coined in Principles of Biology (1864) after reading Charles Darwin's 1859 book On the Origin of Species. The term strongly suggests natural selection, yet Spencer saw evolution as extending into realms o…

entries.name: Tughril I
entries.desc: Abu Talib Muhammad Tughril ibn Mika'il, better known as Tughril, was a Turkoman chieftain, who founded the Seljuk Empire, ruling from 1037 to 1063.
entries.tldr: A Turkoman chieftain, Tughril welded scattered nomadic warriors of the Central Asian steppe into a unified confederacy and led them in conquering Khorasan and much of Persia during the eleventh century. In 1055 he seized Baghdad from the Buyid dynasty, keeping the Abbasid caliph on as a figurehead while taking personal command of the caliphate's armies against the Byzantines and Fatimids. Ruling in the caliph's name while wielding real military power became the founding template for the Seljuk Empire. He endowed many mosques and madrasas before dying heirless in 1063.

entries.name: Caracalla
entries.desc: Caracalla, born Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was Roman emperor from 198 to 217 AD, first as co-emperor under his father Septimius Severus and then ruling alone after 211.
entries.tldr: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, better known by his nickname Caracalla, was Roman emperor from 198 to 217 AD, first serving as nominal co-emperor under his father and then ruling alone after 211 AD. He was a member of the Severan dynasty, the elder son of Emperor Septimius Severus and Empress Julia Domna. Severus proclaimed Caracalla co-ruler in 198, doing the same with his other son Geta in 209.

entries.name: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier
entries.desc: French gem merchant and traveler who made six voyages to Persia and India, publishing an account of his travels in 1675.
entries.tldr: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605–1689) was a 17th-century French gem merchant and traveler. Tavernier, a private individual and merchant traveling at his own expense, covered, by his own account, 60,000 leagues in making six voyages to Persia and India between the years 1630 and 1668. In 1675, Tavernier, at the behest of his patron Louis XIV, known as the Sun King, published Les Six Voyages de Jea…

entries.name: Charles Messier
entries.desc: Charles Messier was a French astronomer who published a catalogue of 110 nebulae and star clusters, known as the Messier objects, to help observers identify transient objects in the sky.
entries.tldr: Charles Messier was a French astronomer. He published an astronomical catalogue consisting of 110 nebulae and star clusters, which came to be known as the Messier objects, referred to with the letter M and their number between 1 and 110. Messier's purpose for the catalogue was to help astronomical observers distinguish between permanent and transient visually diffuse objects in the sky.

entries.name: Tanaka Giichi
entries.desc: Baron Tanaka Giichi was a Japanese general and politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 1927 to 1929.
entries.tldr: Born to a samurai family in Chōshū, Tanaka rose through the Imperial Japanese Army to become War Minister before entering politics as president of the conservative Rikken Seiyūkai party. As prime minister from 1927 to 1929 he pursued an aggressive China policy while cracking down on communists and socialists at home. His government sent troops into Shandong, clashing with Chinese forces near Jinan, and he was blamed for the unauthorized 1928 assassination of warlord Zhang Zuolin by a rogue Kwantung Army officer. That scandal forced his resignation in 1929; he died months later.

entries.name: Jamasp
entries.desc: Jamasp was Sasanian King of Kings of Iran from 496 to 498/9. He was a son of Peroz I and younger brother of Kavad I.
entries.tldr: Jamasp was Sasanian King of Kings of Iran from 496 to 498/9. He was a son of Peroz I and younger brother of Kavad I. Jamasp was installed on the Sasanian throne upon the deposition of the latter by the nobility and clergy.

entries.name: Albert VI, Archduke of Austria
entries.desc: Albert VI, a member of the House of Habsburg, was Duke of Austria from 1424 and Archduke from 1453, ruling the Inner Austrian duchies of Styria, Carinthia and Carniola.
entries.tldr: Albert VI, a member of the House of Habsburg, was Duke of Austria from 1424, elevated to Archduke in 1453. As a scion of the Leopoldian line, he ruled over the Inner Austrian duchies of Styria, Carinthia and Carniola from 1424, from 1457 also over the Archduchy of Austria until his death, rivalling with his elder brother Emperor Frederick III. According to tradition, Albert, later known as the …

entries.name: Anne, Duchess of York
entries.desc: Anne Hyde was the first wife of James, Duke of York, who later became King James II and VII, in 1685.
entries.tldr: English noblewoman, the daughter of the statesman Edward Hyde, who secretly married James, Duke of York — the future King James II — in 1660 while already pregnant with his child, a scandal at the Restoration court. Two of their daughters, Mary and Anne, both later became queens of England in their own right, making her the mother of two reigning monarchs despite dying more than a decade before her husband took the throne. She converted privately to Catholicism shortly before her death in 1671, a decision she reportedly kept hidden from most of the court.

entries.name: Ay
entries.desc: Ay, AY or variants, may refer to:
entries.tldr: Ancient Egyptian pharaoh who rose from courtier and vizier under Akhenaten to king in his own right around 1327 BCE, succeeding the young Tutankhamun. He secured the throne partly by marrying Tutankhamun's widow, Ankhesenamun, and organized his predecessor's elaborate burial in the Valley of the Kings. His own reign lasted only about four years and left few major monuments, reflecting his advanced age at accession. His successor, the general Horemheb, later tried to erase Ay from official king lists alongside the other rulers of the Amarna period.

entries.name: John Bosco
entries.desc: Italian Catholic priest and educator, known as Don Bosco, who founded schools and teaching methods to help disadvantaged and street children in Turin.
entries.tldr: John Melchior Bosco, SDB, popularly known as Don Bosco, was an Italian Catholic priest, educator, and writer. While working in Turin, where the population suffered many of the ill effects of industrialization and urbanization, he dedicated his life to the betterment and education of street children, juvenile delinquents, and other disadvantaged youth. He developed teaching methods based on love…

entries.name: Baldwin III of Jerusalem
entries.desc: Baldwin III was the king of Jerusalem from 1143 until his death. Although he only took up sole rule in 1152 and died young, he was the longest-reigning of the 12th-century kings of Jerusalem.
entries.tldr: Baldwin III was the king of Jerusalem from 1143 until his death. Although he only took up sole rule in 1152 and died young, he was the longest-reigning of the 12th-century kings of Jerusalem. He expanded the borders of the kingdom, paved the way for the later kings' attempts to conquer Egypt, and acted as the defender of the other crusader states in the Levant.

entries.name: Pelagius
entries.desc: Pelagius was a Christian theologian and ascetic monk whose doctrines emphasized human choice in salvation and denied original sin. He was accused of heresy at the Synod of Diospolis in 415.
entries.tldr: Pelagius was a Christian theologian known as an ascetic monk and promoting a system of doctrines which emphasized human choice in salvation and denied original sin. Pelagius was accused of heresy at the Synod of Diospolis in 415 and his doctrines were harshly criticized by Augustine of Hippo, especially the Pelagian views about mankind's good nature and individual responsibility for choosing as…

entries.name: Louis Antoine, Duke of Angoulême
entries.desc: Louis Antoine of France, Duke of Angoulême was the elder son of Charles X of France and the last Dauphin of France from 1824 to 1830.
entries.tldr: The elder son of the future Charles X, Angoulême grew up in exile during the French Revolution and later commanded royalist forces sent into Spain in 1823 to help restore the absolutist rule of Ferdinand VII, a campaign that succeeded but did little to help the reactionary Bourbon regime's popularity at home. When his father was overthrown in the July Revolution of 1830, Angoulême briefly held the title of King Louis XIX for perhaps twenty minutes before both he and Charles X signed abdication documents. He spent the rest of his life in exile, dying in Austria in 1844.

entries.name: Alphonse Mucha
entries.desc: Alphonse Mucha was a Czech painter, illustrator and graphic artist known for the distinctly stylised Art Nouveau theatrical posters he made in Paris, particularly for Sarah Bernhardt.
entries.tldr: Alfons Maria Mucha, known in English as Alphonse Mucha, was a Czech painter, illustrator, and graphic artist. Living in Paris during the Art Nouveau period, he was widely known for his distinctly stylised and decorative theatrical posters, particularly those of Sarah Bernhardt. He produced illustrations, advertisements, decorative panels, as well as designs, which became among the best-known im…

entries.name: Zane Grey
entries.desc: Zane Grey was an American author. He is known for his popular adventure novels and stories associated with the Western genre in literature and the arts; he idealized the American frontier.
entries.tldr: Zane Grey was an American author. He is known for his popular adventure novels and stories associated with the Western genre in literature and the arts; he idealized the American frontier. Riders of the Purple Sage (1912) was his best-selling book.

entries.name: Yuan Mei
entries.desc: Yuan Mei was a Chinese poet and artist. He was often mentioned with Ji Yun as the "Nan Yuan Bei Ji".
entries.tldr: Yuan Mei was an 18th-century Chinese poet, essayist, and gastronome of the Qing dynasty who retired early from a modest official career to live as a private literary man in a garden estate he called the Sui Yuan. He championed a poetics of natural feeling over rigid classical imitation, and unusually for his era, mentored numerous women poets and published their work. He also wrote a celebrated cookbook, the Suiyuan shidan, recording recipes and dining philosophy from his gourmet table. His independent persona made him one of the most widely read literary figures of his time.

entries.name: Giovanni da Verrazzano
entries.desc: Italian explorer who, sailing for France, was the first European to chart the Atlantic coast of North America between Florida and Newfoundland.
entries.tldr: Giovanni da Verrazzano was an Italian explorer from the Republic of Florence, best known for his expedition to North America. He led most of his later missions, including the one to America, in the service of King Francis I of France.

entries.name: Jean-François Millet
entries.desc: French painter and co-founder of the Barbizon school, known for his Realist depictions of peasant farmers.
entries.tldr: Jean-François Millet was a French painter and one of the founders of the Barbizon school in rural France. Millet is noted for his paintings of peasant farmers and can be categorized as part of the Realism art movement. Toward the end of his career, he became increasingly interested in painting pure landscapes.

entries.name: Jean-Baptiste Camille Corot
entries.desc: French landscape and portrait painter whose work bridged the Neo-Classical tradition and the plein-air innovations of Impressionism.
entries.tldr: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, or simply Camille Corot, was a French landscape and portrait painter as well as a printmaker in etching. A pivotal figure in landscape painting, his vast output simultaneously referenced the Neo-Classical tradition and anticipated the plein-air innovations of Impressionism.

entries.name: Zewditu I of Ethiopia
entries.desc: Empress of Ethiopia from 1916 until her death in 1930, taking the throne after the dethroning of Lij Iyasu and crowned in February 1917.
entries.tldr: Zewditu was Empress of Ethiopia from 1916 until her death in 1930. She officially adopted the regnal name "Zewditu" at the beginning of her reign, which was triggered by the dethroning of Lij Iyasu in 1916. Her coronation was held on February 11, 1917, in the Cathedral of St.

entries.name: Mikheil Javakhishvili
entries.desc: Mikheil Javakhishvili was a Georgian and Soviet novelist regarded as a leading twentieth-century Georgian writer. He was executed during the Great Purge for resisting Soviet ideology.
entries.tldr: Mikheil Javakhishvili was a Georgian and Soviet novelist who is regarded as one of the top twentieth-century Georgian writers. His first story appeared in 1903, but then the writer lapsed into a long pause before returning to writing in the early 1920s. His recalcitrance to the Soviet ideological pressure cost him life: he was executed during the Great Purge and his writings were banned for nea…

entries.name: Robert Brasillach
entries.desc: Robert Brasillach was a French author and journalist. He was the editor of Je suis partout, a nationalist newspaper which advocated fascist movements and supported Jacques Doriot.
entries.tldr: Robert Brasillach was a French author and journalist. He was the editor of Je suis partout, a nationalist newspaper which advocated fascist movements and supported Jacques Doriot. After the liberation of France in 1944, he was executed following a trial and Charles de Gaulle's express refusal to grant him a pardon.

entries.name: Bruno Schulz
entries.desc: Bruno Schulz was a Polish-Jewish writer, literary critic, visual artist, and art teacher.
entries.tldr: Polish-Jewish writer, graphic artist, and schoolteacher from Drohobycz, whose small body of fiction, chiefly the collection published in English as The Street of Crocodiles, is regarded as a major achievement of interwar modernist literature. His prose fused vivid, dreamlike imagery with memories of his father's shop and provincial Jewish life, drawing comparisons to Kafka. Under German occupation he was forced to paint murals for an SS officer who offered him limited protection, but was shot in the street by a rival officer in 1942. Mural fragments he painted were rediscovered in 2001.

entries.name: Catherine Cornaro
entries.desc: Catherine Cornaro was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Cyprus, also titled Queen of Jerusalem and Queen of Armenia, reigning from 1474 to 1489.
entries.tldr: Catherine Cornaro was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Cyprus, also holding the titles of Queen of Jerusalem and Queen of Armenia. She became queen consort of Cyprus by marriage to James II of Cyprus, and then regent of Cyprus during the minority of her son James III of Cyprus in 1473–1474, and finally queen regnant of Cyprus upon his death. She reigned from 26 August 1474 to 26 February 1489…

entries.name: Vladimir the Great
entries.desc: Prince of Novgorod from 970 and Grand Prince of Kiev from 978 until 1015, canonised as a saint by both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
entries.tldr: Vladimir I Sviatoslavich or Volodymyr I Sviatoslavych, given the epithet "the Great", was Prince of Novgorod from 970 and Grand Prince of Kiev from 978 until his death in 1015. The Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church both canonised him as Saint Vladimir.

entries.name: José Rizal
entries.desc: José Rizal was a Filipino nationalist, writer, and polymath active at the end of Spanish colonial rule in the Philippines. He is popularly considered a national hero.
entries.tldr: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was a Filipino nationalist, writer, and polymath active at the end of the Spanish colonial period of the Philippines. He is popularly considered a national hero of the Philippines, although no official proclamation formally declares him as such. An ophthalmologist by profession, Rizal became a writer and a key member of the Filipino Propaganda Movem…

entries.name: Alexander Griboyedov
entries.desc: Alexander Sergeyevich Griboyedov was a Russian diplomat, playwright, poet, and composer. His one notable work is the 1823 verse comedy Woe from Wit.
entries.tldr: Alexander Sergeyevich Griboyedov was a Russian diplomat, playwright, poet, and composer. His one notable work is the 1823 verse comedy Woe from Wit. He was Russia's ambassador to Qajar Persia, where he and all the embassy staff were massacred by an angry mob in the aftermath of the ratification of the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828), which confirmed the cession to Russia of Persia's northern terri…

entries.name: Manuel L. Quezon
entries.desc: Manuel L. Quezon was a Filipino lawyer, statesman, soldier, and politician who served as the second president of the Philippines from 1935 until his death in 1944.
entries.tldr: Manuel Luis Quezon y Molina, also known by his initials MLQ, was a Filipino lawyer, statesman, soldier, and politician who served as the second president of the Philippines from 1935 until his death in 1944. He was the first Filipino to head a government of the entire Philippines and is considered the second president of the Philippines after Emilio Aguinaldo (1899–1901), whom Quezon defeated i…

entries.name: Amrita Sher-Gil
entries.desc: Amrita Sher-Gil was a Hungarian–Indian painter. She has been called "one of the greatest avant-garde women artists of the early 20th century" and a pioneer in modern Indian art.
entries.tldr: Amrita Sher-Gil was a Hungarian–Indian painter. She has been called "one of the greatest avant-garde women artists of the early 20th century" and a pioneer in modern Indian art. Drawn to painting from an early age, Sher-Gil started formal lessons at the age of eight.

entries.name: Ottokar II of Bohemia
entries.desc: Ottokar II, the Iron and Golden King, was a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who reigned as King of Bohemia from 1253 until his death in 1278, also holding titles across Austria and Styria.
entries.tldr: Ottokar II, the Iron and Golden King, was a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who reigned as King of Bohemia from 1253 until his death in 1278. He also held the titles of Margrave of Moravia from 1247, Duke of Austria from 1251, and Duke of Styria from 1260, as well as Duke of Carinthia and landgrave of Carniola from 1269.

entries.name: Camille Saint-Saëns
