entries.desc: Camille Saint-Saëns was a French composer, organist, conductor and pianist of the Romantic era, known for works including Danse macabre and the opera Samson and Delilah.
entries.tldr: Charles-Camille Saint-Saëns was a French composer, organist, conductor and pianist of the Romantic era. His best-known works include Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso (1863), the Second Piano Concerto (1868), the First Cello Concerto (1872), Danse macabre (1874), the opera Samson and Delilah (1877), the Third Violin Concerto (1880), the Third ("Organ") Symphony (1886) and The Carnival of the A…

entries.name: E. T. A. Hoffmann
entries.desc: E. T. A. Hoffmann was a German Romantic author of fantasy and gothic horror, and also a jurist, composer, and music critic. His story The Sandman is a pioneering work of horror fiction.
entries.tldr: Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann was a German Romantic author of fantasy and gothic horror, a jurist, composer, music critic and artist. His short story "The Sandman" is seen as a pioneering work of horror fiction, while his novella Mademoiselle de Scuderi is regarded as one of the earliest examples of crime fiction.

entries.name: Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Leopold I was Holy Roman Emperor, King of Germany, Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia. The second son of Ferdinand III, he ruled the empire from 1658 until his death in 1705.
entries.tldr: Leopold I was Holy Roman Emperor, King of Germany, King of Hungary, Croatia and Bohemia. The second son of Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, by his first wife, Maria Anna of Spain, Leopold became heir apparent in 1654 after the death of his elder brother Ferdinand IV, King of the Romans. Elected in 1658, Leopold ruled the Holy Roman Empire until his death in 1705, becoming the second-longest-r…

entries.name: Otto II
entries.desc: Otto II, called the Red, was Holy Roman Emperor from 973 until his death in 983. A member of the Ottonian dynasty, he was the youngest son of Otto the Great.
entries.tldr: Otto II, called the Red, was Holy Roman Emperor from 973 until his death in 983. A member of the Ottonian dynasty, Otto II was the youngest and sole surviving son of Otto the Great and Adelaide of Italy.

entries.name: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
entries.desc: Spanish neuroscientist, pathologist, and histologist who shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Camillo Golgi, the first Spaniard to win a scientific Nobel.
entries.tldr: Santiago Ramón y Cajal was a Spanish neuroscientist, pathologist, and histologist specialising in neuroanatomy, and the central nervous system. He and Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1906. Ramón y Cajal was the first Spaniard to win a scientific Nobel Prize.

entries.name: Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Ferdinand III was Archduke of Austria, King of Hungary and Croatia from 1625, King of Bohemia from 1627 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1637 to his death.
entries.tldr: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia who inherited the Thirty Years' War from his father Ferdinand II and, unlike him, worked seriously toward ending it. A capable military commander earlier in his life, as emperor he pursued a more conciliatory religious and political policy, recognizing that outright Habsburg victory was no longer achievable. His diplomacy contributed to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which ended the war, curtailed imperial authority over the German princes, and established a framework of religious toleration. He was also a composer of some skill.

entries.name: Emperor Rudolf II
entries.desc: Rudolf II was Holy Roman Emperor (1576–1612), King of Hungary and Croatia, King of Bohemia (1575–1608/1611) and Archduke of Austria (1576–1608). He was a member of the House of Habsburg.
entries.tldr: Holy Roman Emperor who ruled from Prague rather than Vienna, turning his court into one of Europe's great centers of art, science, and the occult, patronizing astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler alongside alchemists and painters such as Giuseppe Arcimboldo. His famously eclectic Kunstkammer, or cabinet of curiosities, gathered artworks, scientific instruments, and natural wonders from across the known world. Politically he proved far less effective, and crises within the Habsburg lands eventually forced his own family to strip him of most of his powers in his final years.

entries.name: Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Ferdinand II was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, Hungary, and Croatia from 1619 until his death in 1637. He was the son of Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria and Maria of Bavaria.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand II was Holy Roman Emperor, King of Bohemia, Hungary, and Croatia from 1619 until his death in 1637. He was the son of Archduke Charles II of Inner Austria and Maria of Bavaria, who were devout Catholics. In 1590, when Ferdinand was 11 years old, they sent him to study at the Jesuits' college in Ingolstadt because they wanted to isolate him from the Lutheran nobles.

entries.name: Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Ferdinand I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1556, King of Bohemia, Hungary, and Croatia from 1526, and Archduke of Austria from 1521 until his death in 1564.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1556, King of Bohemia, Hungary, and Croatia from 1526, and Archduke of Austria from 1521 until his death in 1564. Before his accession as emperor, he ruled the Austrian hereditary lands of the House of Habsburg in the name of his elder brother, Emperor Charles V, and often served as Charles' representative in developing encouraging relationships with Germ…

entries.name: Henry I the Fowler
entries.desc: Duke of Saxony and King of East Francia from 919, founder of the Ottonian dynasty and generally regarded as founder of the medieval German state.
entries.tldr: Henry the Fowler was the duke of Saxony from 912 and the king of East Francia from 919 until his death in 936. As the first non-Frankish king of East Francia, he established the Ottonian dynasty of kings and emperors, and he is generally considered to be the founder of the medieval German state, known until then as East Francia. An avid hunter, he obtained the epithet "the Fowler" because he wa…

entries.name: Camillo Golgi
entries.desc: Camillo Golgi was an Italian biologist and pathologist awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the central nervous system.
entries.tldr: Camillo Golgi was an Italian biologist and pathologist who was awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his works on the central nervous system. He studied medicine at the University of Pavia between 1860 and 1868 under the tutelage of Cesare Lombroso. Inspired by pathologist Giulio Bizzozero, he pursued research in the nervous system.

entries.name: Victor Emmanuel III of Italy
entries.desc: King of Italy from 1900 until his 1946 abdication, also Emperor of Ethiopia and King of the Albanians following Italy's invasions of those countries.
entries.tldr: Victor Emmanuel III was King of Italy from 29 July 1900 until his abdication on 9 May 1946. A member of the House of Savoy, he also reigned as Emperor of Ethiopia from 1936 to 1941 and King of the Albanians from 1939 to 1943, following the Italian invasions of Ethiopia and Albania. During his reign of nearly 46 years, which began after the assassination of his father Umberto I, the Kingdom of I…

entries.name: Wilhelm I
entries.desc: Wilhelm I was King of Prussia from 1861 and German Emperor from 1871 until his death in 1888. A member of the House of Hohenzollern, he was the first head of state of a united Germany.
entries.tldr: Wilhelm I was King of Prussia from 1861 and German Emperor from 1871 until his death in 1888. A member of the House of Hohenzollern, he was the first head of state of a united Germany. He was regent of Prussia from 1858 to 1861 for his elder brother, King Frederick William IV.

entries.name: Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Charles VI was Holy Roman Emperor and ruler of the Austrian Habsburg monarchy from 1711 until his death, succeeding his brother Joseph I and unsuccessfully claiming the Spanish throne.
entries.tldr: Charles VI was Holy Roman Emperor and ruler of the Austrian Habsburg monarchy from 1711 until his death, succeeding his elder brother, Joseph I. He unsuccessfully claimed the throne of Spain following the death of his relative Charles II of Spain. In 1708, he married Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, by whom he had his four children: Leopold Johann, Maria Theresa, Maria Anna, and M…

entries.name: Anthony van Dyck
entries.desc: Sir Anthony van Dyck was a Flemish Baroque artist, who became the leading court painter in England after success in the Spanish Netherlands and Italy.
entries.tldr: Flemish painter who trained in Antwerp under Peter Paul Rubens before establishing his own reputation across Italy and the Spanish Netherlands. In 1632 King Charles I brought him to England, knighted him, and made him principal court painter, a role in which he produced the elegant royal portraits that came to define the image of the Stuart monarchy. His fluid brushwork and flattering yet naturalistic style set the template for English portraiture for the next two centuries. He died in London in 1641, shortly before the civil war that deposed his patron.

entries.name: Porfirio Díaz
entries.desc: Porfirio Díaz was a Mexican army general and politician who ruled Mexico as dictator from 1876 until his overthrow in 1911, serving as president over thirty years across three terms.
entries.tldr: José de la Cruz Porfirio Díaz Mori, commonly known as Porfirio Díaz, was a Mexican army general and politician who was the dictator of Mexico from 1876 until his overthrow in 1911. Seizing power in a military coup, he served as president of Mexico on three occasions, a total of over thirty years, the longest of any Mexican ruler. This period is known as the Porfiriato and has been called a de f…

entries.name: Maximilian I
entries.desc: Maximilian I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1493 until his death in 1519, and a member of the House of Habsburg. He expanded Habsburg power in Europe chiefly through dynastic marriages.

Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria, reigned 1597–1651
Maximilian I, Prince of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen (1636-1689)
Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria, reigned 1795–1805 and 1806–1825 
Maximilian I of Mexico, reigned 1864–1867

entries.name: Lothair I
entries.desc: Lothair I was a 9th-century Emperor of the Carolingian Empire and King of Italy (818–855) and Middle Francia (843–855).
entries.tldr: Eldest son of Louis the Pious and grandson of Charlemagne, Lothair was crowned co-emperor young but spent much of his early adulthood in rebellion against his father over the repeated redivision of the Carolingian inheritance. After Louis's death, Lothair's claim to supremacy was defeated by his brothers at the bloody Battle of Fontenoy in 841, forcing the settlement known as the Treaty of Verdun in 843. That treaty split the empire into three kingdoms, leaving Lothair the imperial title and an unstable central strip, Middle Francia, which he further divided before dying in 855.

entries.name: Empress Elisabeth of Austria
entries.desc: Elisabeth, nicknamed Sisi, was Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary from her marriage to Franz Joseph I on 24 April 1854 until her assassination in 1898.
entries.tldr: Empress consort of Austria and Queen of Hungary through her marriage to Franz Joseph I, celebrated in her lifetime, and mythologized ever since, for her striking beauty and restless dissatisfaction with the rigid etiquette of the Habsburg court. Known familiarly as Sisi, she spent much of her later life traveling around Europe, often alone, seeking relief from depression and the losses of her son Rudolf's suicide at Mayerling and her sister's death in a fire. In 1898 she was fatally stabbed in Geneva by an Italian anarchist who had originally targeted a different royal.

entries.name: Maximilian II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Maximilian II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1564 until his death in 1576. A member of the House of Habsburg, he was crowned King of Bohemia in 1562 and King of Hungary and Croatia in 1563.
entries.tldr: Maximilian II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1564 until his death in 1576. A member of the Austrian House of Habsburg, he was crowned King of Bohemia in Prague on 14 May 1562 and elected King of Germany on 24 November 1562. On 8 September 1563, he was crowned King of Hungary and Croatia in the Hungarian capital Pressburg.

entries.name: Empress Matilda
entries.desc: Empress Matilda, also known as Empress Maud, was Holy Roman Empress by marriage to Henry V from 1110 until 1125, and later a claimant to the English throne during the civil war called the Anarchy.
entries.tldr: Empress Matilda, also known as Empress Maud, was Holy Roman Empress as the consort of Emperor Henry V from 1110 until his death in 1125, and was subsequently a claimant to the English throne, and Lady of the English, during the civil war known as the Anarchy. Following the death of her father, King Henry I of England, as his only surviving child and nominated heir, she asserted her right to the…

entries.name: Charles Algernon Parsons
entries.desc: Charles Algernon Parsons was an Anglo-Irish mechanical engineer and inventor who designed the modern steam turbine in 1884, revolutionising marine propulsion.
entries.tldr: Sir Charles Algernon Parsons was an Anglo-Irish mechanical engineer and inventor who designed the modern steam turbine in 1884. His invention revolutionised marine propulsion, and he was also the founder of C. A.

entries.name: Henry VI
entries.desc: Holy Roman Emperor and king of Germany, Italy, Burgundy, and Sicily from 1191 until his death in 1197, son of Frederick Barbarossa.

Henry VI, Count Palatine of the Rhine 
Henry VI, Count of Luxembourg

Henry VI, Count of Gorizia (1376–1454)
Henry VI of England (1421–1471)
Henry VI (play), a series of three plays by William Shakespeare
Henry VI, Burgrave of Plauen (1536–1572)
Heinri…

entries.name: Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor was Holy Roman emperor from 1452 until his death in 1493. He was the penultimate emperor to be crowned by the pope, and the last to be crowned in Rome.
entries.tldr: Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor was Holy Roman emperor from 1452 until his death in 1493. He was the penultimate emperor to be crowned by the pope, and the last to be crowned in Rome. He was the fourth king of the Romans and the first Holy Roman emperor from the House of Habsburg, which was to retain the title with one gap until it was declared at an end by Emperor Francis II, in 1806.

entries.name: Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Francis I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1745 to 1765, Archduke of Austria from 1740, Duke of Lorraine and Bar from 1729, and Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1737. He was the last non-Habsburg emperor.
entries.tldr: Francis I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1745 to 1765, Archduke of Austria from 1740 to 1765, Duke of Lorraine and Bar from 1729 to 1737, and Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1737 to 1765. He became the ruler of the Holy Roman Empire and Tuscany through his marriage to his second cousin Maria Theresa of Austria, daughter of Emperor Charles VI. Francis was the last non-Habsburg monarch of the Empire.

entries.name: Elisa Bonaparte
entries.desc: Maria Anna Elisa Bonaparte Baciocchi Levoy, known as Elisa Bonaparte, was an imperial French princess and sister of Napoleon Bonaparte. She ruled as Princess of Lucca and Grand Duchess of Tuscany.
entries.tldr: Maria Anna Elisa Bonaparte Baciocchi Levoy, better known as Elisa Bonaparte, was an imperial French princess and sister of Napoleon Bonaparte. She was Princess of Lucca and Piombino (1805-1814), Grand Duchess of Tuscany (1809-1814) and Countess of Compignano by appointment of her brother.

entries.name: Jérôme Bonaparte
entries.desc: Jérôme Bonaparte was the youngest brother of Napoleon I who reigned as Jérôme Napoleon I, King of Westphalia, between 1807 and 1813.
entries.tldr: The youngest of Napoleon's brothers, Jérôme served briefly in the French navy before his 1803 marriage to the American Elizabeth Patterson was annulled by Napoleon, who wanted his siblings married for dynastic advantage; Jérôme complied, later marrying a Württemberg princess instead. Napoleon rewarded him with the newly created Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807, a patchwork German state Jérôme ruled with a lavish court that also introduced the Napoleonic legal code to the region. He commanded a corps at Waterloo in 1815 and died in 1860, the last surviving Bonaparte sibling.

entries.name: Otto III
entries.desc: Otto III was the Holy Roman emperor and King of Italy from 996 until his death in 1002. A member of the Ottonian dynasty, Otto III was the only son of Emperor Otto II and his wife Theophanu.
entries.tldr: Crowned king of Germany at age three, Otto III was raised amid Byzantine influence by his mother Theophanu, regent until her death when he was eleven. Taking power himself, he moved his court to Rome, installed his own tutor as Pope Sylvester II, and pursued renovatio imperii Romanorum, aiming to revive Rome as a world capital blending Roman, German, and Byzantine power. In 1000 he allied with Poland and Hungary at the Congress of Gniezno and, per a famous account, opened Charlemagne's tomb to view the body. Driven out by hostile Romans, he died of fever at twenty-one, restoration unfinished.

entries.name: Lucien Bonaparte
entries.desc: Lucien Bonaparte, 1st Prince of Canino and Musignano, was a French politician and diplomat of the French Revolution and the Consulate, serving as Minister of the Interior in 1799–1800.
entries.tldr: Lucien Bonaparte, 1st Prince of Canino and Musignano, was a French politician and diplomat of the French Revolution and the Consulate. He served as Minister of the Interior from 1799 to 1800 and as the president of the Council of Five Hundred in 1799.

entries.name: Richard Wagner
entries.desc: Richard Wagner was a German composer, theatre director, essayist, and conductor best known for his operas, for which he wrote both the libretti and the music himself.
entries.tldr: Wilhelm Richard Wagner was a German composer, theatre director, essayist, and conductor, best known for his operas, although his mature works are often referred to as music dramas. Unlike most composers, Wagner wrote both the libretti and the music for all of his stage works. He first achieved recognition with works in the Romantic tradition of Carl Maria von Weber and Giacomo Meyerbeer, but re…

entries.name: Charles the Bold
entries.desc: Charles the Bold was Duke of Burgundy from 1467 to 1477, the only surviving legitimate son of Philip the Good, and rival to his overlord King Louis XI of France.
entries.tldr: Charles the Bold, also called the Rash, was Duke of Burgundy from 1467 to 1477. A member of the House of Valois-Burgundy, he was the only surviving legitimate son of Philip the Good and his third wife, Isabella of Portugal. As heir and as ruler, Charles vied for power and influence with rivals such as his overlord, King Louis XI of France.

entries.name: Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia
entries.desc: Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia was the youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II, the last sovereign of Imperial Russia, and his wife, Tsarina Alexandra Feodorovna.
entries.tldr: The youngest of Nicholas II's four daughters, she grew up isolated within the imperial family's cloistered court, sharing a room with sister Maria and remembered for a mischievous streak. After the 1917 revolution she was held under house arrest, first at Tsarskoye Selo, later Siberia, before being shot with her family by Bolshevik guards in a Yekaterinburg cellar in July 1918. Rumors she alone had survived, supposedly shielded by jewels sewn into her clothing, fueled decades of impostor claims, most famously Anna Anderson's. DNA testing later confirmed she died with the rest of her family.

entries.name: Juan Gris
entries.desc: Juan Gris, born José Victoriano González-Pérez, was a Spanish painter who lived and worked mainly in France. Closely connected to Cubism, his works are among its most distinctive.
entries.tldr: José Victoriano González-Pérez , better known as Juan Gris, was a Spanish painter born in Madrid who lived and worked in France for most of his active period. Closely connected to the innovative artistic genre Cubism, his works are among the movement's most distinctive.

entries.name: Joachim Murat
entries.desc: French Army officer and Marshal of the Empire under Napoleon who served as King of Naples from 1808 until his execution in 1815.
entries.tldr: Joachim Murat was a French Army officer and statesman who served during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Under the French Empire he received the military titles of Marshal of the Empire and Admiral of France. He was the first Prince Murat, Grand Duke of Berg from 1806 to 1808, and King of Naples as Joachim-Napoleon from 1808 to 1815.

entries.name: Olive Schreiner
entries.desc: Olive Schreiner was a South African author, anti-war campaigner and intellectual. She is best remembered today for her novel The Story of an African Farm (1883), which has been highly acclaimed.
entries.tldr: Olive Schreiner was a South African author, anti-war campaigner and intellectual. She is best remembered today for her novel The Story of an African Farm (1883), which has been highly acclaimed. It deals boldly with such contemporary issues as agnosticism, existential independence, individualism, the professional aspirations of women, and the elemental nature of life on the colonial frontier.

entries.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
entries.desc: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, essayist, poet, and travel writer best known for Treasure Island, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and Kidnapped.
entries.tldr: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, essayist, poet and travel writer. He is best known for the novels Treasure Island (1883), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), and Kidnapped (1886) and for the poetry collection A Child's Garden of Verses (1885).

entries.name: Anne of Austria
entries.desc: Anne of Austria was Queen of France from 1615 to 1643 by marriage to King Louis XIII. She was also Queen of Navarre until the kingdom's annexation into the French crown in 1620.
entries.tldr: Anne of Austria was Queen of France from 1615 to 1643 by marriage to King Louis XIII. She was also Queen of Navarre until the kingdom's annexation into the French crown in 1620. After her husband's death, Anne was regent to her son Louis XIV during his minority until 1651.

entries.name: Christian IX of Denmark
entries.desc: Christian IX was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906. From 1863 to 1864, he was concurrently Duke of Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg.
entries.tldr: Christian IX was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906. From 1863 to 1864, he was concurrently Duke of Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg. He became one of the most influential monarchs of 19th-century Europe through the dynastic marriages of his children, earning the nickname "Father-in-law of Europe".

entries.name: Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Leopold II was Holy Roman Emperor, King of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia, and Archduke of Austria from 1790 to 1792. He was a son of Empress Maria Theresa.
entries.tldr: Leopold II was the penultimate Holy Roman Emperor, as well as King of Hungary, Croatia and Bohemia, and Archduke of Austria from 1790 to 1792, and Grand Duke of Tuscany from 1765 to 1790. He was a son of Empress Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I, and the brother of Queen Marie Antoinette of France, Queen Maria Carolina, Duchess Maria Amalia of Parma, and Emperor Joseph II. Leopold was a moder…

entries.name: Vidkun Quisling
entries.desc: Norwegian military officer and politician who headed the puppet government of Norway during its occupation by Nazi Germany in World War II.
entries.tldr: Vidkun Abraham Lauritz Jonssøn Quisling was a Norwegian military officer, politician and Nazi collaborator who headed the puppet government of Norway during the country's occupation by Nazi Germany during World War II.

entries.name: Thomas Carlyle
entries.desc: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher. Known as the "sage of Chelsea", his writings strongly influenced the intellectual and artistic culture of the Victorian era.
entries.tldr: Born in the Dumfriesshire village of Ecclefechan and educated at Edinburgh, Carlyle first made his name introducing British readers to German Romantic philosophy before writing his strange, semi-autobiographical novel Sartor Resartus. His vivid three-volume history of the French Revolution, published in 1837, made his reputation, notably after John Stuart Mill's maid accidentally burned an early manuscript and Carlyle rewrote it from memory. His lectures On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History argued that great individuals drive history, shaping Victorian thought.

entries.name: José Batlle y Ordóñez
entries.desc: José Batlle y Ordóñez was a Uruguayan politician who served two terms as President of Uruguay for the Colorado Party. He introduced Batllism, his welfare-state system, to South America.
entries.tldr: José Pablo Torcuato Batlle y Ordóñez, nicknamed Don Pepe, was a prominent Uruguayan politician who served two terms as President of Uruguay for the Colorado Party. The son of a former president, he introduced his political system, Batllism, to South America and modernized Uruguay through his creation of extensive welfare state reforms.

entries.name: Otto IV, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Otto IV was the Holy Roman Emperor from 1209 until his death in 1218.
entries.tldr: A Welf prince and grandson of England's Henry II, Otto fought a decade-long civil war against Philip of Swabia after their disputed double election of 1198 split Germany. Pope Innocent III backed him at first, then excommunicated him in 1210 when Otto pushed into papal territory in Sicily. His fortunes collapsed at the Battle of Bouvines in 1214, where his English-allied army was routed by France, ending his reign in all but name. Deposed in 1215, he died four years later in quiet obscurity near Brunswick.

entries.name: Mehmed V
entries.desc: Mehmed V Reşâd was the penultimate sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1909 to 1918. Mehmed V reigned as a constitutional monarch.
entries.tldr: Mehmed V Reşâd was the penultimate sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1909 to 1918. Mehmed V reigned as a constitutional monarch. He had little influence over government affairs and his ministries showed little regard for the Ottoman constitution.

entries.name: Abdülaziz
entries.desc: Abdulaziz was sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1861 to 1876, when he was overthrown in a coup. He was a son of Sultan Mahmud II and succeeded his brother Abdulmejid I.
entries.tldr: Abdulaziz was the sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 25 June 1861 to 30 May 1876, when he was overthrown in a government coup. He was a son of Sultan Mahmud II and succeeded his brother Abdulmejid I in 1861.

entries.name: Richard Owen
entries.desc: Richard Owen was an English biologist, comparative anatomist, and palaeontologist regarded as an outstanding naturalist with a remarkable gift for interpreting fossils.
entries.tldr: Sir Richard Owen was an English biologist, comparative anatomist and palaeontologist. Owen is generally considered to have been an outstanding naturalist with a remarkable gift for interpreting fossils.

entries.name: Paul Signac
entries.desc: Paul Victor Jules Signac was a French Neo-Impressionist painter who, with Georges Seurat, helped develop the artistic technique Pointillism.
entries.tldr: Trained briefly as an architect, Signac dropped it after seeing a Monet show at 18 and taught himself to paint from rowboats on the Seine. In 1884 he helped found the Société des Indépendants and met Georges Seurat, with whom he developed pointillism, dotting canvases with unmixed color that blends optically in the eye. After Seurat's death in 1891, Signac became the movement's chief theorist; Matisse painted his 1904 breakthrough Luxe, Calme et Volupté while staying with him at Saint-Tropez. An avid sailor, Signac also painted hundreds of watercolors of French harbors from his own boats.

entries.name: Béla Kun
entries.desc: Béla Kun was a Hungarian communist revolutionary and politician who in 1919 governed the Hungarian Soviet Republic.
entries.tldr: Hungarian journalist and prisoner of war in Russia during World War I who was converted to Bolshevism in captivity and returned home to found the Hungarian Communist Party. In March 1919 he led a coup that established the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic, which he governed as de facto leader for 133 days through nationalization, Red Terror, and war with Romanian and Czechoslovak forces. The republic collapsed that August under a Romanian invasion, and Kun fled to Soviet Russia, where he worked for the Comintern. He fell victim to Stalin's purges and was secretly executed in 1938.

entries.name: Ferdinand I of Bulgaria
entries.desc: Ferdinand I was monarch of Bulgaria from 1887 to 1918, reigning as Prince from 1887 and Tsar from 1908 until his abdication. Under his rule Bulgaria modernized its industry and military.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand I was the monarch of Bulgaria from 1887 to 1918, reigning as Prince of Bulgaria from 1887 to 1908 and Tsar of Bulgaria from 1908 until his abdication in 1918. Under his rule, Bulgaria began rapidly modernising its industry, military, infrastructure and culture. It achieved independence from the Ottoman Empire and fought in the Balkan Wars and World War I, the latter of which ended wit…

entries.name: Henry V
entries.desc: Henry V may refer to:
entries.tldr: Son and successor of Henry IV, Henry V became Holy Roman Emperor in 1111 after years spent leading rebellions against his own father over control of church appointments. He continued the long Investiture Controversy between empire and papacy, seizing and briefly imprisoning Pope Paschal II to extract concessions before the dispute was finally settled by the Concordat of Worms in 1122. His marriage to Matilda, daughter of England's Henry I, tied the German crown to the English royal house.

entries.name: Nicolas Steno
entries.desc: Niels Steensen was a Danish scientist, a pioneer in both anatomy and geology who became a Catholic bishop in his later years. He has been beatified by the Catholic Church.
entries.tldr: Trained as an anatomist, Steno made his name by dissecting a shark's head to prove that fossilized 'tongue stones' were actually shark teeth. He went on to formulate the principle of superposition — that rock strata record a knowable sequence of past events — work later geologists credit as founding stratigraphy. Around 1667 he converted to Catholicism, abandoned science, and was ordained a bishop, ministering to scattered German Catholics with extreme austerity. He died poor in Schwerin and was beatified by John Paul II in 1988.

entries.name: Alexander of Greece
entries.desc: Alexander was King of Greece from 11 June 1917 until his death on 25 October 1920.
entries.tldr: King of Greece from 1917 to 1920, placed on the throne by the Allied powers after they forced his father, Constantine I, into exile for pro-German sympathies during the First World War. With little real authority, he reigned largely as a figurehead while Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos directed policy and led Greece into the war on the Allied side. In October 1920 he died of sepsis after being bitten by a pet monkey at the royal estate, a freak death historians have argued helped trigger his father's return to the throne soon after. He was twenty-seven.

entries.name: Karl Friedrich Schinkel
entries.desc: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was a Prussian architect, city planner, and painter who also designed furniture and stage sets. He led Germany's Neoclassical and Gothic Revival movements.
entries.tldr: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was a Prussian architect, city planner and painter who also designed furniture and stage sets. Schinkel was one of the greatest German architects, a nineteenth century design genius, and a leader in the International Neoclassical and Gothic Revival movements. His most famous buildings are found in and around Berlin, where he influenced the city's design and landscape pro…

entries.name: Ivan VI of Russia
entries.desc: Proclaimed Emperor of Russia as an infant in 1740, he was overthrown within a year and spent most of his life imprisoned until his death.
entries.tldr: Ivan VI Antonovich, also known as Ioann Antonovich, was Emperor of Russia from October 1740 until he was overthrown by his cousin Elizabeth Petrovna in December 1741. He was only two months old when he was proclaimed emperor and his mother, Anna Leopoldovna, named regent, but the throne was seized in a coup after little more than a year. Ivan and his parents were imprisoned far from the capital…

entries.name: Peter III of Russia
entries.desc: Peter III was Emperor of Russia from January to July 1762, when his wife Catherine II overthrew him in a palace coup. He is criticized for undoing Russian gains in the Seven Years' War.
entries.tldr: Peter III Fyodorovich was Emperor of Russia from 5 January 1762 until 9 July of the same year, when his wife, Catherine II, overthrew him in a palace coup d'état. He implemented many notable reforms during his reign, though he is criticised for undoing Russian gains in the Seven Years' War by forming an alliance with Prussia.

entries.name: Edward Cave
entries.desc: Edward Cave was an English printer, editor, and publisher. He coined the term magazine for a periodical, founding The Gentleman's Magazine in 1731.
entries.tldr: Edward Cave was an English printer, editor and publisher. He coined the term "magazine" for a periodical, founding The Gentleman's Magazine in 1731, and was the first publisher to successfully fashion a wide-ranging publication.

entries.name: Piet Mondrian
entries.desc: Piet Mondrian was a Dutch painter and art theoretician regarded as one of the 20th century's greatest artists, and a pioneer of abstract art.
entries.tldr: Pieter Cornelis Mondriaan, known after 1911 as Piet Mondrian, was a Dutch painter and art theoretician, who is regarded as one of the greatest artists of the 20th century. He was one of the pioneers of 20th-century abstract art, as he changed his artistic direction from figurative painting to an increasingly abstract style, until he reached a point where his artistic vocabulary was taken down t…

entries.name: Semerkhet
entries.desc: Horus name of an early Egyptian First Dynasty king, remembered through a tragic legend recorded by the historian Manetho describing a calamity during his reign.
entries.tldr: Semerkhet is the Horus name of an early Egyptian king who ruled during the First Dynasty. This ruler became known through a tragic legend handed down by the historian Manetho, who reported that a calamity of some sort occurred during Semerkhet's reign. The archaeological records seem to support the view that Semerkhet had a difficult time as king and some early archaeologists questioned the leg…

entries.name: Hotepsekhemwy
entries.desc: Egyptian king regarded as founder of the Second Dynasty; the length of his reign is uncertain due to conflicting ancient sources.
entries.tldr: Hotepsekhemwy is the Horus name of an early Egyptian king who was the founder of the Second Dynasty of Egypt. The exact length of his reign is not known; the Turin canon suggests an improbable 95 years while the ancient Egyptian historian Manetho reports that the reign of "Boëthôs" lasted for 38 years. Egyptologists consider both statements to be misinterpretations or exaggerations.

entries.name: Den
entries.desc:
Den may refer to:Den (room), a small room in a house
Maternity den, a lair where an animal gives birth
entries.tldr: Ruler conventionally identified as Den, also called Hor-Den or Udimu, a pharaoh of Egypt's First Dynasty believed to have reigned for several decades, among the longest reigns recorded for the period. Surviving labels and reliefs from his tomb at Abydos preserve the first known depiction of a pharaoh smiting a foreign enemy, an image that became a standard motif of Egyptian royal art for millennia. He appears to have been the first ruler to use the title 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt.' As with most rulers of this era, his exact dates rest on later king-lists rather than contemporary records.

entries.name: Frederick I of Prussia
entries.desc: Frederick I of the Hohenzollern dynasty was Elector of Brandenburg from 1688 to 1713 and Duke of Prussia, a title he raised to royalty in 1701 as the first King in Prussia.
entries.tldr: Frederick I, of the Hohenzollern dynasty, was Elector of Brandenburg (1688–1713) and Duke of Prussia in personal union (Brandenburg–Prussia). The latter function he upgraded to royalty, becoming the first King in Prussia (1701–1713). From 1707 he was also Prince of Neuchâtel.

entries.name: Djet
entries.desc: Djet, also known as Wadjet, Wadj, Zet, and Uadji, was the fourth pharaoh of the First Dynasty, successor of Djer. Djet's Horus name means "Horus Cobra" or "Serpent of Horus".
entries.tldr: Fourth pharaoh of Egypt's First Dynasty, who succeeded his father Djer and is known chiefly through the elegant carved stela that marked his tomb at Abydos, now held in the Louvre. The stela's serpent framed beneath a falcon, spelling his Horus name, is among the most admired examples of early Egyptian relief carving, showing royal artistic conventions were already refined just centuries after unification. His reign, like those of his predecessors, is associated with a subsidiary cemetery of retainer burials around his tomb, a practice that faded out within a few generations.

entries.name: Carlo Bonaparte
entries.desc: Carlo Buonaparte was a Corsican attorney, nobleman and official, best known as the father of Napoleon Bonaparte and grandfather of Napoleon III.
entries.tldr: Carlo Maria Buonaparte, also known as Carlo Maria di Buonaparte and Charles-Marie Bonaparte, was a Corsican attorney, nobleman, and official, best known as the father of Napoleon Bonaparte and grandfather of Napoleon III.

entries.name: Anna Pavlova
entries.desc: Anna Pavlova was a Russian prima ballerina of the Imperial Russian Ballet and the Ballets Russes, best known for creating the role of The Dying Swan.
entries.tldr: Anna Pavlovna Pavlova was a Russian prima ballerina. She was a principal artist of the Imperial Russian Ballet and the Ballets Russes of Sergei Diaghilev, but is most recognized for creating the role of The Dying Swan and, with her own company, being the first ballerina to tour the world, including South America, India, Mexico and Australia.

entries.name: Paul I of Russia
entries.desc: Paul I was Emperor of Russia from 1796 until his assassination in 1801.
entries.tldr: Taken from Catherine the Great at birth and raised in the shadow of his father's murder, Paul spent decades as an embittered heir before finally taking the throne in 1796. He moved fast to undo his mother's legacy, fixing a male-only succession law to end the era of court coups while curbing noble privileges and easing serfs' labor duties. His erratic rule and wild reversals, including a pivot from fighting Napoleon to plotting an invasion of British India, alienated the court. In March 1801 conspirators, apparently with his own son's tacit blessing, broke into his bedroom and strangled him.

entries.name: Jöns Jacob Berzelius
entries.desc: Baron Jöns Jacob Berzelius was a Swedish chemist. Berzelius is considered, along with Robert Boyle, John Dalton, and Antoine Lavoisier, to be one of the founders of modern chemistry.
entries.tldr: Baron Jöns Jacob Berzelius was a Swedish chemist. Berzelius is considered, along with Robert Boyle, John Dalton, and Antoine Lavoisier, to be one of the founders of modern chemistry. Berzelius became a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1808 and served from 1818 as its principal functionary.

entries.name: Alexander I of Russia
entries.desc: Alexander I, nicknamed "the Blessed", was Emperor of Russia from 1801, first King of Congress Poland from 1815, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1809 until his death in 1825.
entries.tldr: Alexander I of Russia, nicknamed "the Blessed", was Emperor of Russia from 1801, the first King of Congress Poland from 1815, and the Grand Duke of Finland from 1809 to his death in 1825. He ruled Russia during the chaotic period of the Napoleonic Wars.

entries.name: James George Frazer
entries.desc: Sir James George Frazer was a Scottish social anthropologist and folklorist influential in the early stages of the modern studies of mythology and comparative religion.
entries.tldr: A Scottish social anthropologist, Frazer became internationally famous for The Golden Bough, a sprawling comparative study tracing myths of dying and resurrecting gods, fertility rites, and sacred kingship across cultures from ancient Rome to contemporary folklore. Though he never conducted fieldwork himself, relying instead on missionary and traveler accounts, the book profoundly shaped early anthropology and inspired writers including T. S. Eliot and James Joyce, even as later scholars criticized its armchair methods.

entries.name: Pierre Laval
entries.desc: Pierre Jean Marie Laval was a French politician. He served as Prime Minister of France three times: 1931–1932 and 1935–1936 during the Third Republic, and 1942–1944 during Vichy France.
entries.tldr: Pierre Jean Marie Laval was a French politician. He served as Prime Minister of France three times: 1931–1932 and 1935–1936 during the Third Republic, and 1942–1944 during Vichy France. After the war, Laval was tried as a Nazi collaborator and executed for treason.

entries.name: Maria-Letizia Bonaparte
entries.desc: Maria-Letizia Bonaparte, commonly known as Letizia Bonaparte, was a Corsican noblewoman and matriarch of the House of Bonaparte, as the mother of Napoleon I, Emperor of the French.
entries.tldr: Maria-Letizia Bonaparte, commonly known as Letizia Bonaparte, was a Corsican noblewoman and the matriarch of the House of Bonaparte, as the mother of Napoleon I, Emperor of the French. Due to her status as the Emperor's mother, she was granted the title "Madame Mère".

entries.name: Ion Antonescu
entries.desc: Romanian military officer who led a wartime dictatorship as Prime Minister during World War II and facilitated the Holocaust in Romania before his 1946 execution.
entries.tldr: Ion Antonescu was a Romanian military officer and marshal who presided over two successive wartime dictatorships as Prime Minister and Conducător during most of World War II. Having been responsible for facilitating the Holocaust in Romania, he was overthrown in 1944, before being tried for war crimes and executed two years later in 1946.

entries.name: Catherine I of Russia
entries.desc: Catherine I was Empress of Russia from 1725 until her death in 1727, having previously been empress consort from 1721 to 1725 as the second wife of Peter the Great.
entries.tldr: Catherine I was Empress of Russia from 8 February 1725 until her death in 1727. She was previously empress consort of Russia from 1721 to 1725 as the second wife of Peter the Great, and tsaritsa consort from 1712 to 1721.

entries.name: Alexandra Feodorovna (Alix of Hesse)
entries.desc: Alexandra Feodorovna was the last empress of Russia as the consort of Nicholas II from their marriage on 26 November [O.S. 14 November] 1894 until his forced abdication on 15 March [O.S.
entries.tldr: Alexandra Feodorovna was the last empress of Russia as the consort of Nicholas II from their marriage on 26 November [O.S. 14 November] 1894 until his forced abdication on 15 March [O.S. 2 March] 1917.

entries.name: Constantine I of Greece
entries.desc: Constantine I was King of Greece from 1913 to 1917 and again from 1920 to 1922. The eldest son of George I of Greece, he succeeded to the throne after his father's assassination in 1913.
entries.tldr: Constantine I was King of Greece from 18 March 1913 to 11 June 1917 and again from 19 December 1920 to 27 September 1922. The eldest son of George I of Greece, he succeeded to the throne following his father's assassination in 1913.

entries.name: Geiseric
entries.desc: Gaiseric, also known as Geiseric, was king of the Vandals and Alans from 428 to 477. He led the Vandal migration to North Africa, playing a key role in the decline of the Western Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: Gaiseric, also known as Geiseric or Genseric was king of the Vandals and Alans from 428 to 477 AD. He ruled over the Vandal kingdom and migrated the kingdom to North Africa, playing a key role in the decline of the Western Roman Empire during the 5th century.

entries.name: Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia
entries.desc: King of Bohemia from 1378 until his death in 1419, and King of the Romans and of Germany from 1376 until his deposition in 1400.
entries.tldr: Wenceslaus IV was King of Bohemia from 1378 until his death in 1419 and King of the Romans and King of Germany from 1376 until he was deposed in 1400. As he belonged to the House of Luxembourg, he was also Duke of Luxembourg as Wenceslaus II from 1383 to 1388.

entries.name: Matthias, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Matthias was Holy Roman Emperor from 1612 to 1619, Archduke of Austria from 1608 to 1619, King of Hungary and Croatia from 1608 to 1618, and King of Bohemia from 1611 to 1617.
entries.tldr: Matthias was Holy Roman Emperor from 1612 to 1619, Archduke of Austria from 1608 to 1619, King of Hungary and Croatia from 1608 to 1618 and King of Bohemia from 1611 to 1617. His personal motto was Concordia lumine maior.

entries.name: August Krogh
entries.desc: August Krogh was a Danish professor of zoophysiology at the University of Copenhagen from 1916 to 1945, known for developing Krogh's principle.
entries.tldr: Schack August Steenberg Krogh was a Danish professor at the department of zoophysiology at the University of Copenhagen from 1916 to 1945. He contributed a number of fundamental discoveries within several fields of physiology, and is famous for developing Krogh's principle.

entries.name: Friedrich Wilhelm II of Prussia
entries.desc: Frederick William II was King of Prussia from 1786 until his death in 1797. He was also Prince-elector of Brandenburg and Prince of Neuchâtel.
entries.tldr: Nephew and successor of Frederick the Great, Friedrich Wilhelm II inherited a powerful state but preferred pleasure, mistresses, and lavish spending to the grinding work of kingship. Alongside his official queen he contracted two morganatic marriages and kept mistresses, most devoted to Wilhelmine Enke, with whom he had several children even before taking the throne. Under him Prussia drifted into costly, indecisive wars against Revolutionary France, though he did leave one lasting legacy by commissioning Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.

entries.name: Tiye
entries.desc: Great Royal Wife of pharaoh Amenhotep III and mother of Akhenaten; in 2010 DNA analysis identified her as the mummy known as the Elder Lady.
entries.tldr: Tiye was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian pharaoh Amenhotep III, mother of pharaoh Akhenaten and grandmother of pharaoh Tutankhamun; her parents were Yuya and Thuya. In 2010, DNA analysis confirmed her as the mummy known as "The Elder Lady" found in the tomb of Amenhotep II (KV35) in 1898.

entries.name: El Lissitzky
entries.desc: El Lissitzky was a Russian and Soviet artist working as a painter, illustrator, designer, printmaker, photographer, and architect. He helped develop suprematism with his mentor Kazimir Malevich.
entries.tldr: El Lissitzky was a Russian and Soviet artist, active as a painter, illustrator, designer, printmaker, photographer, and architect. He was an important figure of the avant-garde, helping develop suprematism with his mentor, Kazimir Malevich, and designing numerous exhibition displays and propaganda works for the Soviet Union.

entries.name: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
entries.desc: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was the husband of Queen Victoria and consort of the British monarch from 1840 until his death in 1861. Victoria granted him the title Prince Consort in 1857.
entries.tldr: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was the husband of Queen Victoria and consort of the British monarch from their marriage on 10 February 1840 until his death in 1861. Victoria granted him the title Prince Consort in 1857.

entries.name: Conrad II
entries.desc: Conrad II, called Conrad the Salic, was Holy Roman Emperor from 1027 until his death in 1039. He was the first of four Salian emperors, a dynasty that ruled Germany, Italy, and Burgundy for a century.
entries.tldr: Conrad II, also known as Conrad the Elder and Conrad the Salic, was the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire from 1027 until his death in 1039. The first of a succession of four Salian emperors, who reigned for one century until 1125, Conrad ruled the kingdoms of Germany, Italy and Burgundy.

entries.name: Alexandra of Denmark
entries.desc: Alexandra of Denmark was Queen of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Empress of India, from 22 January 1901 to 6 May 1910 as the wife of King Edward VII.
entries.tldr: Danish princess who became queen consort of the United Kingdom as the wife of Edward VII, a marriage arranged in 1863 to cement Anglo-Danish relations. Renowned for her beauty and fashion sense, she was so widely imitated that even a limp she developed after illness became a society trend, the "Alexandra limp." Her siblings occupied thrones across Europe, including a sister as Empress of Russia and brothers as kings of Denmark and Greece. As queen dowager she founded Alexandra Rose Day, a charitable flower sale that endures in Britain today.

entries.name: Georges Méliès
entries.desc: French filmmaker, actor, and magician, a pioneer of early cinema known for special effects and the 1902 film A Trip to the Moon.
entries.tldr: Marie-Georges-Jean Méliès was a French filmmaker, actor, magician, and toymaker. He led many technical and narrative developments in the early days of cinema, primarily in the fantasy and science fiction genres. Méliès rose to prominence creating "trick films" and became well known for his innovative use of special effects, popularizing such techniques as substitution splices, multiple exposure…

entries.name: Edvard Beneš
entries.desc: Edvard Beneš was a Czech politician who served as president of Czechoslovakia from 1935 to 1938 and again from 1939 to 1948. He led the Czechoslovak government-in-exile during World War II.
entries.tldr: Edvard Beneš was a Czech politician and statesman who served as the president of Czechoslovakia from 1935 to 1938, and again from 1939 to 1948. During the first six years of his second stint, he led the Czechoslovak government-in-exile during World War II.

entries.name: Ramesses II
entries.desc: Ramesses II, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, regarded as one of its most powerful rulers who led at least 15 military campaigns.
entries.tldr: Ramesses II, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Ramesses II is often regarded as the greatest, most celebrated, and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, which itself was the most powerful period of ancient Egypt. He is also widely considered one of ancient Egypt's most successful warrior pharaohs, conducting no fewer than 15 mili…

entries.name: Isoroku Yamamoto
entries.desc: Admiral who commanded Japan's Combined Fleet during World War II and planned the attack on Pearl Harbor before being killed when his plane was shot down in 1943.
entries.tldr: Isoroku Yamamoto  was an admiral of the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN) and the commander of the Combined Fleet during World War II. He commanded the fleet from 1939 until his death in 1943, overseeing the start of the Pacific War in 1941 and Japan's initial successes and defeats before his plane was shot down by U.S. fighter aircraft over New Guinea.

entries.name: Pasquale Paoli
entries.desc: Pasquale Paoli was a Corsican patriot, statesman, and military leader who led resistance against Genoese and French rule over the island. He became President of Corsica's Executive Council.
entries.tldr: Filippo Antonio Pasquale de' Paoli was a Corsican patriot, statesman, and military leader who was at the forefront of resistance movements against the Genoese and later French rule over the island. He became the President of the Executive Council of the General Diet of the People of Corsica and wrote the Constitution of the state.

entries.name: Béla IV of Hungary
entries.desc: Béla IV was King of Hungary and Croatia from 1235 to 1270 and Duke of Styria from 1254 to 1258, crowned during his father Andrew II's lifetime in 1214.
entries.tldr: Béla IV was King of Hungary and Croatia between 1235 and 1270, and Duke of Styria from 1254 to 1258. As the oldest son of King Andrew II, he was crowned upon the initiative of a group of influential noblemen in his father's lifetime in 1214. His father, who strongly opposed Béla's coronation, refused to give him a province to rule until 1220.

entries.name: Djer
entries.desc: Djer is considered the third pharaoh of the First Dynasty of ancient Egypt in current Egyptology. He lived around the mid 31st century BC and reigned for about 40 years.
entries.tldr: Djer is considered the third pharaoh of the First Dynasty of ancient Egypt in current Egyptology. He lived around the mid 31st century BC and reigned for about 40 years. A mummified forearm of Djer or his wife was discovered by Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, but was discarded by Émile Brugsch.

entries.name: Alfred Adler
entries.desc: Alfred Adler was an Austrian medical doctor and psychotherapist who founded the school of individual psychology, emphasizing belonging and family relationships over Freud's drive theory.
entries.tldr: Alfred Adler was an Austrian medical doctor, psychotherapist, and founder of the school of individual psychology. His emphasis on the importance of feelings of belonging, relationships within the family, and birth order set him apart from Freud and others in their common circle. He proposed that contributing to others was how the individual feels a sense of worth and belonging in the family and…

entries.name: Eugene of Savoy
entries.desc: Prince Eugene of Savoy was a feldmarschall of the Holy Roman Empire and the Austrian Habsburg dynasty in the 17th and 18th centuries, regarded as one of the era's leading military commanders.
entries.tldr: Prince Eugene Francis of Savoy-Carignano, better known as Prince Eugene, was a distinguished feldmarschall in the Army of the Holy Roman Empire and of the Austrian Habsburg dynasty during the 17th and 18th centuries. Renowned as one of the greatest military commanders of his era, Prince Eugene also rose to the highest offices of state at the Imperial court in Vienna, spending six decades in the…

entries.name: Louis the German
entries.desc: Louis the German was the first king of East Francia, ruling from 843 to 876 AD. A grandson of Charlemagne, his kingdom later became known as the kingdom of Germany.
entries.tldr: Louis the German, also known as Louis II of Germany, was the first king of East Francia, and ruled from 843 to 876 AD. Grandson of emperor Charlemagne and the third son of Louis the Pious, emperor of Francia, and his first wife, Ermengarde of Hesbaye, he received the appellation Germanicus shortly after his death, when East Francia became known as the kingdom of Germany.

entries.name: Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Joseph I was Holy Roman Emperor and ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1705 until his death in 1711.
entries.tldr: Joseph I was Holy Roman Emperor and ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1705 until his death in 1711. He was the eldest son of Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor from his third wife, Eleonor Magdalene of Neuburg. Joseph was crowned King of Hungary at the age of nine in 1687 and was elected King of the Romans at the age of eleven in 1690.

entries.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
entries.desc: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator. His original works include the poems "Paul Revere's Ride", The Song of Hiawatha, and Evangeline.
entries.tldr: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator. His original works include the poems "Paul Revere's Ride", The Song of Hiawatha, and Evangeline. He was the first American to completely translate Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy and was one of the fireside poets from New England.

entries.name: Maria Theresa of Spain
entries.desc: Maria Theresa of Spain was Queen of France from 1660 to 1683 as the wife of King Louis XIV. Born an Infanta of Spain and Portugal, she was also an Archduchess of Austria.
entries.tldr: Maria Theresa of Spain was Queen of France from 1660 to 1683 as the wife of King Louis XIV. She was born an Infanta of Spain and Portugal as the daughter of King Philip IV and Elisabeth of France, and was also an Archduchess of Austria as a member of the Spanish branch of the House of Habsburg.

entries.name: Ramesses I
entries.desc: Ramesses I was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, whose brief reign around 1292–1290 BC mainly marked the transition after Horemheb had stabilized Egypt.
entries.tldr: Menpehtyre Ramesses I was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt's 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292–1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295–1294 BC. While Ramesses I was the founder of the 19th Dynasty, his brief reign mainly serves to mark the transition between the reign of Horemheb, who had stabilized Egypt in the late 18th…

entries.name: Frederick William of Brandenburg
entries.desc: Frederick William of Brandenburg, known as the Great Elector, was ruler of Brandenburg-Prussia in the 17th century. Three later Hohenzollern kings of Prussia share his name.
entries.tldr:
Frederick William of Brandenburg may refer to:Frederick William, the Great Elector (1620–1688)
Frederick William I of Prussia (1688–1740), also Elector of Brandenburg
Frederick William II of Prussia (1744–1797), also Elector of Brandenburg
Frederick William III of Prussia (1770–1840), also Elector of Brandenburg until 1806

entries.name: Frederik VIII of Denmark
entries.desc: Frederik VIII was King of Denmark from 29 January 1906 until his death in 1912.
entries.tldr: Frederik spent over four decades as crown prince before becoming king in 1906 at age 62, an apprenticeship that made him unusually sympathetic to Denmark's new parliamentary system. His children and grandchildren went on to occupy thrones across Europe, including Norway and Greece, earning the Danish royals the nickname father-in-law of Europe. His reign ended abruptly in 1912 when, traveling home from Nice under a pseudonym, he collapsed and died on a Hamburg street at night; his body lay unidentified in the city morgue for hours before officials realized the dead man was a king.

entries.name: Max Linder
entries.desc: Max Linder, born Gabriel-Maximilien Leuvielle, was a French actor, director, screenwriter, producer, and comedian of the silent film era, cited as the first international movie star.
entries.tldr: Gabriel-Maximilien Leuvielle, known professionally as Max Linder, was a French actor, director, screenwriter, producer, and comedian of the silent film era. His onscreen persona "Max" was one of the first recognizable recurring characters in film. He has also been cited as the "first international movie star" and "the first film star anywhere".

entries.name: Caroline Bonaparte
entries.desc: Caroline Bonaparte was an Imperial French princess, the youngest sister of Napoleon I, who served as queen of Naples during her husband's reign and as regent in his absences.
entries.tldr: Carolina Maria Annunziata Bonaparte, better known as Caroline Bonaparte, was an Imperial French princess; the seventh child and third daughter of Carlo Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino, and a younger sister of Napoleon I of France. She was queen of Naples during the reign of her spouse there, and regent of Naples during his absence four times: in 1812–1813, 1813, 1814, and 1815.

entries.name: Pauline Bonaparte
entries.desc: Pauline Bonaparte was an imperial French princess, the first sovereign Duchess of Guastalla, and a sister of Napoleon, the first emperor of the French.
entries.tldr: Paula Maria Bonaparte Leclerc Borghese, better known as Pauline Bonaparte, was an imperial French princess, the first sovereign Duchess of Guastalla, and the princess consort of Sulmona and Rossano. She was the sixth child of Letizia Ramolino and Carlo Buonaparte, Corsica's representative to the court of King Louis XVI. Her elder brother, Napoleon, was the first emperor of the French.

entries.name: Umberto Boccioni
entries.desc: Umberto Boccioni was an influential Italian painter and sculptor. He helped shape the revolutionary aesthetic of the Futurism movement as one of its principal figures.
entries.tldr: Umberto Boccioni was an influential Italian painter and sculptor. He helped shape the revolutionary aesthetic of the Futurism movement as one of its principal figures. Despite his short life, his approach to the dynamism of form and the deconstruction of solid mass guided artists long after his death.

entries.name: Ramesses III
entries.desc: Ramesses III was the second pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, considered the last New Kingdom pharaoh to wield substantial power.
entries.tldr: Usermaatre Meryamun Ramesses III was the second Pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty in Ancient Egypt. Some scholars date his reign from 26 March 1186 to 15 April 1155 BC, and he is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power.

entries.name: Gérard Desargues
entries.desc: Girard Desargues was a French mathematician and engineer, who is considered one of the founders of projective geometry. Desargues's theorem, the Desargues graph, and the crater Desargues on the Moon are named in his honour.
entries.tldr: A military engineer and architect from Lyon who also worked on Parisian water-supply projects, he moved in the Paris circle of mathematicians around Marin Mersenne alongside Descartes and Pascal, who admired him as a mentor. In a dense, jargon-heavy 1639 treatise, he introduced points and lines "at infinity," laying foundations of projective geometry as an alternative to Euclidean methods. His eponymous theorem on triangles in perspective proved essential centuries later to drawing and geometry alike, though his odd vocabulary meant it was ignored until rediscovered in the nineteenth century.

entries.name: Hans von Aachen
entries.desc: Hans von Aachen was a German painter who was one of the leading representatives of Northern Mannerism.
entries.tldr: Trained in Cologne and then in Italy for fourteen years, absorbing the Mannerist styles of Tintoretto's followers, he became a leading painter of the Northern Mannerist court style. In 1592 Emperor Rudolf II appointed him court painter, a post he could fulfill from home rather than living at Rudolf's Prague court, and the two formed a friendship contemporaries likened to Alexander and his painter Apelles. Alongside portraits, he produced sensuous mythological nudes prized by the secretive, art-obsessed Rudolf. He briefly served Rudolf's successor Matthias before dying in Prague in 1615.

entries.name: Li Si
entries.desc: Li Si was a Chinese calligrapher, philosopher, and official of the Qin dynasty. He served as chancellor from 246 to 208 BC, first under Qin Shi Huang and then under Qin Er Shi.
entries.tldr: Li Si was a Chinese calligrapher, philosopher, and official of the Qin dynasty. He served as Qin state Chancellor from 246 to 208 BC, first under King Zheng — who later became Qin Shi Huang, the "First Emperor" of the Qin dynasty. He then served under Qin Er Shi, Qin Shi Huang's eighteenth son and second emperor.

entries.name: Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria
entries.desc: Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria was the only son of Emperor Franz Joseph I and Empress Elisabeth, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne from birth. In 1889 he died in a suicide pact at Mayerling.
entries.tldr: Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria was the only son and third child of Emperor Franz Joseph I and Empress Elisabeth of Austria. He was heir apparent to the imperial throne of the Austro-Hungarian Empire from birth. In 1889, he died in a suicide pact with his mistress Baroness Mary Vetsera at the Mayerling hunting lodge.

entries.name: George II of Greece
entries.desc: George II was King of Greece from 27 September 1922 until 25 March 1924, and again from 25 November 1935 until his death on 1 April 1947.
entries.tldr: Eldest son of King Constantine I, George ascended the Greek throne in 1922 after his father's forced abdication, only to be deposed himself in 1923 after a failed royalist coup and the declaration of a republic, which stripped him of his nationality and property. A 1935 coup and plebiscite restored the monarchy and brought him back from exile, whereupon he let his prime minister, Ioannis Metaxas, establish a dictatorship. Driven out again by the Axis invasion in 1941, he returned to Greece in 1946 and died less than a year later.

entries.name: Henry III
entries.desc: Henry III may refer to: Henry III, Holy Roman Emperor (1017–1056); King Henry III of Castile (1379–1406); King Henry III of England (1207–1272); and other medieval monarchs sharing the name.
entries.tldr: Henry III may refer to Henry III, Holy Roman Emperor (1017–1056), King Henry III of Castile (1379–1406), King Henry III of England (1207–1272), King Henry III of France (1551–1589), King Henry III of Navarre (1553–1610), and several other medieval and early modern rulers who shared the regnal name.

entries.name: Lisa del Giocondo
entries.desc: Lisa del Giocondo was an Italian noblewoman of the Gherardini family of Florence and Tuscany. Her name was given to the Mona Lisa, her portrait painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
entries.tldr: Lisa del Giocondo was an Italian noblewoman and member of the Gherardini family of Florence and Tuscany. Her name was given to the Mona Lisa, her portrait commissioned by her husband and painted by Leonardo da Vinci in the Italian Renaissance.

entries.name: Ion C. Brătianu
entries.desc: Ion Constantin Brătianu was one of the major political figures of 19th-century Romania. He was the son of Dincă Brătianu and the younger brother of Dumitru Brătianu, as well as the father of Ion I.
entries.tldr: Ion Constantin Brătianu was one of the major political figures of 19th-century Romania. He was the son of Dincă Brătianu and the younger brother of Dumitru Brătianu, as well as the father of Ion I. C.

entries.name: Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg
entries.desc: Wife of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria; their 1914 assassination in Sarajevo set off the chain of events that led, four weeks later, to World War I.
entries.tldr: Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg was the wife of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Their assassination in Sarajevo sparked a series of events that led, four weeks later, to World War I.

entries.name: Władysław Sikorski
entries.desc: Polish military and political leader who organised underground independence movements before World War I and fought in the Polish Legions and Polish–Soviet War.
entries.tldr: Władysław Eugeniusz Sikorski was a Polish military and political leader. Before World War I, Sikorski established and participated in several underground organizations that promoted the cause of Polish independence. He fought with distinction in the Polish Legions during World War I, and later in the newly created Polish Army during the Polish–Soviet War of 1919–1921.

entries.name: Elias Lönnrot
entries.desc: Elias Lönnrot was a Finnish physician, philologist, and collector of traditional Finnish oral poetry. He is best known for compiling the Finnish national epic, the Kalevala, from gathered oral verse.
entries.tldr: Elias Lönnrot was a Finnish polymath, physician, philosopher, poet, musician, linguist, journalist, philologist and collector of traditional Finnish oral poetry. He is best known for synthesizing the Finnish national epic, Kalevala from short ballads and lyric poems he gathered from Finnish oral tradition during several field expeditions in Finland, Russian Karelia, the Kola Peninsula and Baltic regions.

entries.name: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac
entries.desc: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac was a French chemist and physicist known for his law on combining gas volumes and for showing water is two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.
entries.tldr: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac was a French chemist and physicist. He is known mostly for his discovery that water is made of two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen by volume, for two laws related to gases, and for his work on alcohol–water mixtures, which led to the degrees Gay-Lussac used to measure alcoholic beverages in many countries.

entries.name: Ramesses IV
entries.desc: Ramesses IV was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, the second son of Ramesses III. He became crown prince in 1164 BC after his elder brother Amenherkhepshef died at fifteen.
entries.tldr: Usermaatre Heqamaatre Setepenamun Ramesses IV was the third pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty of the New Kingdom of Ancient Egypt. He was the second son of Ramesses III and became crown prince when his elder brother Amenherkhepshef died aged 15 in 1164 BC, when Ramesses was only 12 years old. His promotion to crown prince is suggested by his appearance in a scene of the festival of Min at the Ramesseum.

entries.name: Jean Le Rond d'Alembert
entries.desc: Jean Le Rond d'Alembert was a French mathematician, physicist, philosopher, and music theorist. Until 1759 he was, together with Denis Diderot, a co-editor of the Encyclopédie.
entries.tldr: Jean Le Rond d'Alembert was a French mathematician, physicist, philosopher, and music theorist. Until 1759 he was, together with Denis Diderot, a co-editor of the Encyclopédie. His most famous achievements include the wave equation, also known as d'Alembert's equation, and D'Alembert's formula for solving said equation.

entries.name: Josiah Willard Gibbs
entries.desc: Josiah Willard Gibbs was an American mechanical engineer and scientist whose work on thermodynamics helped transform physical chemistry into a rigorous science.
entries.tldr: Josiah Willard Gibbs was an American mechanical engineer and scientist who made fundamental theoretical contributions to physics, chemistry, and mathematics. His work on the applications of thermodynamics was instrumental in transforming physical chemistry into a rigorous deductive science. entries.name: Ben Turpin
entries.desc: Bernard "Ben" Turpin was an American comedian and actor, best remembered for his work in silent films. His trademarks were his cross-eyed appearance and adeptness at vigorous physical comedy.
entries.tldr: Bernard "Ben" Turpin was an American comedian and actor, best remembered for his work in silent films. His trademarks were his cross-eyed appearance and adeptness at vigorous physical comedy. A sometime vaudeville performer, he was "discovered" for film while working as the janitor for Essanay Studios in Chicago.

entries.name: Anna Petrovna of Russia
entries.desc: Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia was the eldest daughter of Emperor Peter I of Russia and Empress Catherine I. Her younger sister, Empress Elizabeth, ruled between 1741 and 1762.
entries.tldr: Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia was the eldest daughter of Emperor Peter I of Russia and Empress Catherine I. Her younger sister, Empress Elizabeth, ruled between 1741 and 1762. While a potential heir in the reign of her nephew Peter II, she never acceded to the throne due to political reasons.

entries.name: Meritaten
entries.desc: Meritaten was an ancient Egyptian royal woman of the Eighteenth Dynasty, daughter of Pharaoh Akhenaten. She held official titles and became Great Royal Wife to Pharaoh Smenkhkare.
entries.tldr: Meritaten, also spelled Merytaten, Meritaton or Meryetaten, was an ancient Egyptian royal woman of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Her name means "She who is beloved of Aten"; Aten being the sun-deity whom her father, Pharaoh Akhenaten, worshipped. She held several titles, performing official roles for her father and becoming the Great Royal Wife to Pharaoh Smenkhkare, who may have been a brother.

entries.name: Joseph Banks
entries.desc: Sir Joseph Banks, 1st Baronet was an English naturalist, botanist, and patron of the natural sciences.
entries.tldr: A wealthy English landowner with a passion for natural history, Banks financed his own participation in James Cook's first Pacific voyage aboard HMS Endeavour, returning in 1771 with vast collections of previously unknown plants and animals, including specimens from Australia, that made him instantly famous. He went on to serve as president of the Royal Society for over four decades, directing British scientific patronage and the exchange of plants across the empire through Kew Gardens. He was central to recommending Botany Bay as a site for British settlement in Australia.

entries.name: Joseph Radetzky von Radetz
entries.desc: Joseph Radetzky von Radetz was a Czech nobleman and Austrian field marshal who served as chief of the general staff of the Habsburg monarchy during the Napoleonic Wars.
entries.tldr: Johann Josef Wenzel Anton Franz Karl, Graf Radetzky von Radetz was a Czech nobleman and Austrian field marshal. He served as chief of the general staff in the Habsburg monarchy during the later period of the Napoleonic Wars and contributed to the Trachenberg Plan and the Leipzig Campaign, which led to the Battle of Leipzig. Afterwards, he embarked on military reforms of the Austrian army.

entries.name: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher
entries.desc: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher was a Prussian Generalfeldmarschall, later made Fürst von Wahlstatt. He is best known for leading his army against Napoleon at Leipzig in 1813 and Waterloo in 1815.
entries.tldr: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, Graf (count), later elevated to Fürst (prince) von Wahlstatt, was a Prussian Generalfeldmarschall. He earned his greatest recognition after leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

entries.name: Albrecht von Wallenstein
entries.desc: Albrecht von Wallenstein was a Bohemian military leader and statesman, a major figure of the Thirty Years' War who commanded the Catholic armies of Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II.
entries.tldr: Albrecht Wenzel Eusebius von Wallenstein, Duke of Friedland, also von Waldstein, was a Bohemian military leader, statesman and a major figure of the Thirty Years' War, fighting on the Catholic side as supreme commander of the armies of Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II. His successful martial career made him one of the richest and most influential men in the Holy Roman Empire by the time of his death.
